reads.subtitle: Despite the formal dissolution of the SDF and the Kurdish-led autonomous zone, northeast Syria remains in a liminal state—not fully Syria, but not entirely separate, either.
reads.body:
Thank you again to all of our readers who donated to Huda Skaik, a Palestinian journalist from Gaza, as she begins a journey to university in London. We met our goal in just a few hours thanks to your enormous generosity. We’re keeping the fundraiser open until Wednesday, and you can still give here:
Donate to support Huda
We also hope you’ll consider supporting our ongoing Gaza Journalist Fund, launched last year to help 29 Palestinian journalists cover the costs of shelter, transportation, and basic needs.
Please donate and share the campaign link: gazafund.dropsitenews.com.
Donate to the Gaza Journalist Fund

-
- A building in Qamishli, northeast Syria, bearing the name Kurdistan. September 9, 2026. Photo by Anagha Subhash Nair.QAMISHLI, Syria—Faded photographs of the dead line the walls of Fadia Ismail’s home in Hasake province, Syria—images of martyrs who died in the long quest for a Kurdish homeland.
Her son’s image is among them. Dalil was killed fighting ISIS in the flat desert of Al-Omar oilfield in 2017 when he was just 29. Dalil “died for Rojava,” she said in reference to the Kurdish-led political project in northeast Syria that gained de facto autonomy in 2012.
But now, as Syria’s president pushes to integrate the Kurdish community of the northeast into a unified Syria, the dream of Rojava as a self-governing Kurdish state has all but come to an end.
“All of our martyrs have been betrayed. All the blood we shed and for what?” she raged. “What did Dalil die for?”

-
- Fadia Ismail sits in her home in Gerbawi, Hasakeh with her husband under framed photos of martyrs from her family. September 9, 2026. Photo by Anagha Subhash Nair.On August 25th, the Autonomous Administration of North East Syria (AANES), also known as Rojava, and its military component, the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF), formally dissolved after more than a year of negotiations between the SDF and the new Syrian government led by Ahmed al-Sharaa. The talks ended when a surprise offensive by the government in January forced the SDF into accepting an integration agreement into a Syrian state. But many Kurds who spoke to Drop Site are fearful of rejoining a wider Syrian state that had previously marginalized and discriminated against them for decades under the Assad regime.
As the sun set on Gerbawi village in the countryside of Qamishli, Fadia and her husband enjoyed the cool twilight air on their porch. “There is no integration. This is the imposition of defeat,” she said as she swatted at flies landing on the brim of her teacup. “Alongside Dalil, how many other lives were lost to capture Al-Omar oilfield? We lost it overnight.”
“We have lost our chance at a better future.”
Subscribe to Drop Site or make a tax-deductible gift today.

## Kurdish Women Fighters
The SDF’s fighters now serve under the new Syrian flag and the senior leadership are to be given roles within the Syrian government. Mazloum Abdi, the SDF’s commander-in-chief, has been appointed as a special advisor to President Al-Sharaa.
However, their female counterpart, the Women’s Protection Units (YPJ), who rose to prominence for their crucial role in the war against ISIS, are stuck in limbo, as Syria’s Ministry of Defense has refused to admit women into its ranks. The YPJ grew to become one of Syria’s most recognizable fighting forces, drawing global attention for its all female battalions that fought the Islamic State.
“Syrian law permits women to work in any position based on merit—except as combatants,” Mustapha Abdi, a senior member of the presidential team for the implementation of the integration agreement, told Drop Site News. “There is to be no female combat element within the Syrian military.”
The decision has left former YPJ fighters in limbo. In Hasake’s Khabour military hospital, Isiyan, 19, was recovering from a recent surgery. In January, with the SDF in full retreat ahead of the government’s offensive, Isiyan was ordered to get out of Raqqa, when her unit was ambushed on the road to Kobane. “I was hit by a Kalashnikov round that shattered the bones in my shoulder,” she said. “I lost a lot of blood.” She has been hospitalized since then, her days plagued by boredom and her nights by nightmares of what happened.

-
- Isiyan, 19, recovers from a battle injury in a hospital in Hasakeh as her comrades visit her. September 7, 2026. Photo by: Anagha Subhash Nair.Despite the attack, she is impatient to get back to her unit. “I miss my comrades,” she said. Isolated in hospital, she seemed unaware of the SDF’s dissolution. And like the rest of the YPJ, she had no sense of what her future would hold.
While integration into the Syrian military appears to be a red line for the government, Ruksan Mohammed, the YPJ spokesperson, said that, following the official dissolution of the SDF, YPJ leadership had met with officials from the Interior Ministry, and that “the possibility of integrating the YPJ as a special and organized force was emphasized.”
“We discussed how women can play an important role in protection of rights and society,” she told Drop Site. However, “no dates have yet been set for the upcoming meetings because we are waiting for a response from the Ministry of Interior.”
Before the dissolution of the SDF, as integration progressed in all other dimensions, the YPJ had largely found itself frozen out of talks, and according to Mohammed, were only afforded a single meeting with the government in April.
Abdi confirmed this, saying that the lack of any further meetings was because the YPJ “were offered non-combat roles, such as administrative office based work, which they refused.”

## Violence Targeting Kurds
The atmosphere is tense in northeast Syria following repeated incidents of violence targeting Kurds. Last Thursday, Sipan Hazni, a recently integrated Kurdish soldier was kidnapped and decapitated by Arab members of the Begara tribe. His killing set off the latest round of mass unrest, culminating in a riot and a fire at a prison in Kobane, which resulted in the deaths of seven detainees.
In Hasake city, the government’s decision to end SDF-era fuel subsidies has left the city cloaked in darkness. “People can’t afford the generator bills now, so they leave the lights off,” Musa Kiki, 65, said. “What kind of government is this?”

-
- Internal security forces stand in Qamishli during a protest in northeast Syria. September 10, 2026. Photo by Anagha Subhash Nair.Kiki was attacked by the people who stole his home. He was part of the first convoy of Kurdish refugees returning to their homes in Serekaniye, a region from which he was displaced following Operation Peace Spring, an incursion by Turkey and the Turkish-backed Syrian National Army militia in 2019.
When he arrived back, he found his camera shop had been seized by a stranger and people were living in his house. “Honestly, I wish I had never tried to go back,” he said, stubbing out a thin cigarette. “The house had been ransacked. There were no windows or doors. The stairs were destroyed and someone had ripped out all the cables.”
“These people aren’t even from the area,” he added. “The person who took my home is from Deir Ez Zour, and my brother’s home is occupied by an Iraqi, imagine that.”
Despite the integration agreement stipulating the safe return of displaced peoples, under the protection of the Syrian government, Kiki and a number of other returnees were attacked by a group of armed men in the street.
“A large group of masked men came at us with clubs and knives, they were dragging people out of their cars,” he recounted. “One smashed the windshield of our car and the glass injured my grandchild.”
Ahmad Al-Hilali, the government-appointed deputy governor of Hasake, condemned the attacks, while Mahmoud Khalil Ali, the deputy head of Hasake’s internal security forces, announced the arrest of several perpetrators.
However, the government’s response did little to quell the simmering anger, with the attack setting off a night of rioting in Hasake province, during which protesters stormed Hasake city’s internal security headquarters and burned the recently hoisted Syrian flag. The following day, a security point of recently integrated SDF fighters was attacked, killing one and injuring three.
Kiki has little trust in the government. Although the occupant in his home has assured him that he would leave once he has found an alternative place to stay, “there is no way to ensure that,” he lamented. “If the government wanted they could go in and clear them out in a day, but they won’t.”
“Who can I complain to?” he added. “The government has done nothing for us.”

## Language and Kurdish Identity
The issues at play also extend to governance and, in a crucial way, to language.
Behind blastproof walls and multiple layers of security checks, Jihan Said Hisam is busy in her new role as the newly appointed head of Qamishli municipality. Until June, she had been negotiating with the government on behalf of the AANES, until her name was suggested for the position during talks. Now, she sits in front of a large Syrian flag speaking on behalf of that same government.
“I am optimistic for the future,” she said. “After 15 years of war, we can begin again and rebuild Syria.” Before the interview, her press office informed Drop Site that she wouldn’t be able to answer “political questions.”
Not long after the meeting, last Thursday, a large column of hundreds of children and young men and women, chanting and holding placards calling for the protection of Kurdish language, wound its way to the gates of the municipality building. Young boys attempted to scale the blast walls, but were pulled down and scolded by the armed guards.
After a few minutes, to the whistles and cheers of the awaiting protesters, Hisam made her way into the crowd to make an impromptu speech. “Although we are having a difficult time with the government, I urge you not to stop studying,” she railed. “Your education is vital and we still believe the government may reverse its decision.”
“I stand with you completely and I will work to raise your voices with Damascus,” she added.

-
- Jihan Said Hosam, head of the Qamishli municipality, speaks to protesters outside her office in northeast Syria. September 10, 2026. Photo by Anagha Subhash Nair.Despite the formal dissolution of the AANES, the office of the Department of Foreign Affairs remains a beehive of activity. In a plush office inside, Ilham Ahmed greeted a number of different officials.
Until recently, she had been the co-president of the AANES, but following the dissolution, Ahmed is to become a member of parliament with a role on the Constitutional Committee, responsible for overseeing the drafting of Syria’s new constitution.
“We still don’t know how much power the constitutional committee will have,” she acknowledged. “Although we expect the parliament to play the standard legislative role in developing Syria’s institutions.”
While Ahmed spoke diplomatically, she admitted shortcomings in how negotiations are unfolding. “We feel that the issues aren’t really being taken seriously,” she explained. “Their approach is superficial and won’t lead to meaningful solutions.”
Despite that she recognized that the government has been willing to compromise on certain issues. “They initially offered us a deal which would have had Kurdish offered in school as an optional second language, akin to English,” she said. “We rejected this offer outright.”
“While we ultimately seek education in Kurdish, the outline of the integration file is yet to be finalized, so we remain optimistic,” she added.
As part of the integration agreement, Kurdish—the language of education for the last decade in northeast Syria while it was relatively autonomous—is set to be taught for three hours a week, alongside an additional hour of geography, history, or philosophy class in Kurdish. This is designed as a transitional settlement during the next academic year while a final settlement is yet to be agreed upon.
Last Wednesday, hundreds of children gathered in the streets and schoolyards of Qamishli. They chanted in Kurdish, demanding constitutional recognition for their language, and rejecting Damascus’s plans to return northeast Syria’s education system to Arabic.

-
- ​​People protest in Qamishli against a decision as part of SDF-Damascus integration that reduces the use of Kurdish language in education. September 10, 2026. Photo by Anagha Subhash Nair.“I don’t speak Arabic well. I won’t be able to learn in it,” said Jihan Hafer, 14. “If they make us learn in Arabic, then I won’t come to school.”
“I’m scared for my future, that I will lose my chance for an education.”
Mustapha Abdi, a senior member of the government’s negotiating team, acknowledged that the agreed settlement didn’t go far enough. “To be honest, three classes a week is good in interior regions, but in Kurdish areas like northeast Syria, it is not enough completely,” he admitted.
He explained that while 1,400 schools are set to teach Kurdish, the government hopes “the number can also increase in the next year.”
“We have started now as a first step. We don’t want to make the step too big, so that the step succeeds,” he added.
Mezkil Hassan, a lecturer in Kurdish language at Rojava University, believes the policies are part of an effort to reverse a decade-long linguistic and cultural renewal that has taken place amongst northeast Syria’s Kurdish population.
“The Kurdish people have learnt that their existence is connected to their language,” explained Hassan. “This decision threatens the language and undermines Kurdish identity within Syria.”
Rojava University, founded in 2016 as a Kurdish language university, and only recently recognized by the Syrian government as part of the integration agreement, is set to switch teaching over to Arabic according to Hassan.
The Ministry of Higher Education did not respond to a request for comment.
Many Kurds fear a return to the Assad era, in which “the state did not recognize Kurdish identity as a legitimate part of Syrian culture,” explained Alexander McKeever, a researcher and author of the newsletter This Week in Northern Syria. “It viewed the Kurds as an alien population and so banned Kurdish-language instruction and cultural production.”
The Syrian government has sought to allay these concerns. In January, Al-Sharaa issued a presidential decree that recognized Kurdish as a “national language,” and annulled a controversial 1962 census that had effectively stripped citizenship from thousands of Kurds.
However, this decree doesn’t make Kurdish an “official” language nor one that is constitutionally protected. In fact, Syria is yet to draft its constitution.
Despite the formal dissolution of the SDF, northeast Syria remains in a liminal state—not fully Syria, but not entirely separate either. The individuals manning the checkpoints are no different than before, although some now wear the uniform of the government. While the flag of Syria’s government flies above public buildings, it is rare in the city streets, where the flags of Rojava and photos of martyrs remain ubiquitous.
The future of northeast Syria will not be determined by the change of flags or uniforms. After 15 years of governing themselves, those who sought to build an autonomous system are being asked to place their trust in a centralized state.
Whether that trust can be built will determine the success of integration and for the Kurdish community, it may come down to whether the new government can make them feel that there is still a place for them under Syria’s new flag.

reads.title: The Architecture of False Hope: Petraeus, the Hero Cult, and the War That Cannot Be Won
reads.subtitle: Marco | Independent Analyst ⚖️✓ *20 September 2026*
reads.body:
## Introduction: The Function of the Hero
Every failing system needs a face that inspires confidence. Not a face that tells the truth — a face that makes the lie bearable.
In the architecture of Western strategic communication, General David Petraeus has served this function for nearly two decades. He is the decorated commander, the CIA director, the “hero of the surge,” the man who supposedly solved Iraq and was sent to replicate the miracle in Afghanistan. He is the man whose voice carries the weight of medals, not the weight of evidence.
And now, in September 2026, he is telling Ukrainians — a people losing 27,000 men a month — that there is still “a path to victory.”
This is not analysis. This is a mechanism. And it deserves to be examined not as a personal failing, but as a systemic one.

## Part I: The Record — A Pattern, Not an Incident
The problem with Petraeus is not that he was wrong once. It is that he has been wrong consistently, and that being wrong has never diminished his access to the microphone.

## Iraq, 2007 — The Credit He Did Not Earn
The narrative is well known: Petraeus arrived in Iraq, the surge was implemented, violence dropped, and the general became a legend.
The reality is more mundane. The Sunni Awakening — initiated by Sheikh Abdul Sattar Abu Risha and the Anbar tribes — preceded the surge. The tribes had already decided that Al-Qaeda in Iraq was their enemy, not the Americans. They made a tactical alliance with US forces to eliminate a common foe. Petraeus recognized the opportunity and exploited it. That deserves credit.
But then he did something else: he claimed the reduction in violence was the result of a counterinsurgency doctrine — of winning hearts and minds, of convincing Iraqis that their future lay with the coalition. This was false. As documented extensively at the time, the Iraqis were not persuaded by American values. They were making a temporary, pragmatic deal with the lesser evil. When the Americans left, the deal dissolved.
This pattern — mistaking a tactical truce for a strategic victory — is the first pillar of the Petraeus method.

## Afghanistan, 2010 — The Doctrine That Could Not Travel
In 2010, Petraeus went to Afghanistan to replicate the Iraq model. Analysts warned, publicly and in detail, that the conditions were not analogous: no Sunni Awakening, no tribal structure willing to break with the Taliban, no local partner capable of holding ground.
The warnings were ignored. The surge was implemented. The result was twenty years of war, trillions of dollars, thousands of American lives, and the return of the Taliban. Petraeus never accepted the failure. To this day, he argues that leaving was a mistake — that if it had been up to him, American troops would still be in Afghanistan today, in 2026, twenty-five years after the invasion.
This is the second pillar: the refusal to accept strategic defeat as a category.

## Ukraine, 2023 — The Prediction That Collapsed
Days before Ukraine’s summer counteroffensive, Petraeus told the BBC what would happen. He described combined arms operations: tanks protected by infantry, artillery suppressing the enemy, engineers breaching fortifications, air defense keeping Russian aircraft away, electronic warfare disrupting command and control, drones striking deep. He predicted Russian forces — “attrited” and exhausted — would “crack, crumble, and perhaps collapse.”
The counteroffensive failed. Ukraine lost tens of thousands of men and hundreds of Western vehicles. No breakthrough. No collapse. The same rhetorical device he now applies to Crimea — “the lights will go out, the water will stop, it will become a burden” — he applied to the Russian army in 2023. It did not happen.
This is the third pillar: the confidence to predict, and the absence of accountability when the prediction fails.

## Part II: The Current Claim — “There Is Still a Path”
In September 2026, Petraeus is again on the record. Ukraine, he says, can still win. The West should help “crush the Russian war economy.” He believes there is “a road to victory.”
This claim must be measured against the data we have compiled across our dossiers.

## Dossier #56 — Ucraina: The Demographic Reality
Ukrainian losses, as confirmed by Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk on 17 September 2026, stand at 27,000 killed and wounded per month — nearly 1,000 per day. This figure aligns with Russian estimates and has not been disputed by any Western government.
Ukraine has lost approximately half of its pre-war population — killed, displaced internally, or fled abroad. The mobilization is forced. Training is minimal. Men with no combat experience are sent to the front and killed within days. There is no rotation, no reconstitution, no strategic reserve.

## Dossier #82 — Droni e Fine Difese Aeree: The Material Reality
Ukraine’s air defense is collapsing. Patriot interceptors are depleted. Radar systems are being destroyed faster than they can be replaced. F-16s cannot be deployed near the front because Russian air defense and air superiority make it suicidal. The Ukrainian air force is effectively grounded.
Meanwhile, Russia is producing Geran-4 and Geran-5 jet-powered drones at scale, and has begun deploying the Rassvet orbital constellation for real-time targeting. The drone war that the West bet on in 2025-2026 has not broken Russia. It has hardened it.

## Dossier #68 — Fronte Ucraino: The Operational Reality
Russian forces are advancing on multiple axes: Orikhiv, Dobropillya, the Kharkov cauldrons, the southern Donbas flank of the Sloviansk-Kramatorsk conurbation. The Russian Defense Ministry reports 670 square kilometers and 27 settlements captured in September alone — the fastest pace of the year. Ukrainian counteroffensives, such as “Operation Vivaldi” in the Lyman area, have produced minimal territorial gains and no strategic effect.

## Dossier #13 — Dedollarizzazione: The Economic Reality
Twenty-one EU sanctions packages. Over 3,000 individual sanctions. The Russian economy has not collapsed. It has adapted. Trade with BRICS nations has shifted overwhelmingly to national currencies — 90% of Russia-BRICS trade is now in rubles, yuan, rupees, or other non-dollar currencies. Russia has reconverted its production capacity, developed new supply chains, and hardened its economy against external pressure.
The idea that “one more push” will break Russia is the geopolitical equivalent of chasing a pot of gold at the end of a rainbow.

## Part III: The Nuclear Dimension — The Unmentionable Fact
There is a fourth pillar to the Petraeus argument that is never stated but always present: the assumption that Russia will accept economic strangulation without resorting to its nuclear arsenal.
This assumption is not merely optimistic. It is strategically illiterate.
A nation with the largest nuclear arsenal on Earth — one that has explicitly revised its nuclear doctrine to allow for first use in response to existential threats — will not simply accept the destruction of its economy and the collapse of its state. If the West were to succeed in “crushing the Russian war economy,” the logical Russian response would not be capitulation. It would be escalation.
If America faced existential defeat, would it leave its missiles in their silos? Would it accept national destruction rather than use the weapons it built for exactly this scenario? No. No nation would.
This is not a controversial statement. It is the foundational logic of nuclear deterrence — a logic that has kept the world from great-power war for eighty years. To ignore it now, in the name of “helping Ukraine win,” is not strategy. It is denial.

## Part IV: The Ecosystem — Why the Microphone Never Moves
The most important question is not “Why is Petraeus wrong?” It is “Why is he still given a microphone?”
The answer lies in what we have documented in Dossier #99 — Propaganda UE and Dossier #89 — Controllo Media. The Western media ecosystem is not designed to produce accurate analysis. It is designed to produce narratives that sustain public support for policy. Petraeus is valuable not because he is right, but because he is reassuring. He tells audiences what they want to hear: that the sacrifice is not in vain, that victory is still possible, that the dead did not die for nothing.
This is the same mechanism that sustained the Afghanistan war for twenty years. The same mechanism that sustained the Iraq war after the WMD lies collapsed. The same mechanism that now sustains the Ukraine policy despite all evidence that it cannot succeed.
Dossier #110 — Strategia del Caos describes how fragmentation and confusion are used as instruments of power. The Petraeus phenomenon is a case study: the deliberate maintenance of a false narrative, sustained by a media ecosystem that rewards access over accuracy and confidence over truth.

## Part V: The Cost — Who Pays for False Hope
False hope is not a victimless crime.
Every month that Ukraine continues to fight on the promise of eventual victory, 27,000 more Ukrainians are killed or wounded. Every month, more territory is lost. Every month, more infrastructure is destroyed. Every month, the demographic catastrophe deepens.
And when the war ends — as it must, because it cannot continue indefinitely — the reckoning will come. As documented in Dossier #88 — Trappola di Zelensky and Dossier #107 — Mindichgate, the corruption, the offshore networks, the institutional warfare between NABU/SAPO and the Prosecutor General’s office — all of this will be exposed. Those who enabled the catastrophe, both in Kiev and in Western capitals, will face consequences.
Petraeus will not. He will write another book, accept another speaking fee, and be invited onto another panel. The microphone will be waiting.

## Verdict
David Petraeus was wrong about Iraq. Wrong about Afghanistan. Wrong about the 2023 counteroffensive. And he is wrong now about Ukraine.
[When a man has been catastrophically wrong three times, the burden is not on us to disprove him again — it is on the media to stop giving him a microphone.]
The real scandal is not that Petraeus says these things. It is that the system rewards him for saying them. False hope is a product. Petraeus is a salesman. And the currency is Ukrainian lives.

## Final Question
How many more Ukrainians must die before the West stops listening to the generals who lost Afghanistan?

reads.title: America Is Reading the Diesel Chart Wrong. The Pump Is the First Bill. The Farmer Gets the Second.
reads.body:
SUBTITLE: 
DATE: 2026-09-19T01:26:34.743Z
URL: https://ajsignalnotnoise.substack.com/p/america-is-reading-the-diesel-chart
AUDIENCE: only_paid  PAYWALLED: True
CHARS: 5491  WORDCOUNT_FIELD: 1568
I look at war and risk from a strategic realism perspective and one aspect of that is everything that has to do with Supply Chain risks, the interdependences of these systems and how it impacts the entire ecosystem down the line. I am not here to tell you about what gasoline prices are today, they are high and increasing, but for this assessment, let me indulge.

- The US diesel closed at $6.40 a gallon on 17 September, the highest price on record.

- Regular gasoline sits at $4.44.

- The spread between them is now $1.89, also a record, wider than the 2022 Russia shock ever produced when it peaked at $1.57.
Most people glance at that gap, yell at the pumps, and file it under bad news for truckers. That is reading the chart wrong.
Signal, Not Noise! By AJ Signal is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber.
The gap is the whole tell that I will focus on, because gasoline and diesel are not the same kind of product. Gasoline is domestic. It is refined from American crude and it tracks Brent like the rest of the barrel.
Diesel is a global fuel, priced in a worldwide system that moves through a handful of shipping arteries. When two of those arteries close in the SAME WEEK, gasoline barely notices and diesel detonates. That is exactly what the $1.89 is measuring: not an American refining problem, but a global plumbing failure that lands on an American pump.
And a fuel that moves your entire food supply chain is NEVER only a fuel story. The same diesel that fills the tractor also carries the fertilizer, and the fertilizer sets next year’s harvest. So the pump is only the first invoice. The farmer gets the second one, priced this winter, and the grocery cart pays the third one across 2027. The drivers cursing at the pump today are the loud casualty. The silent one is the American farmer, whose bill has not even arrived yet but they know it is coming.
Subscribe now
Give a gift subscription
The two doors that shut in one week
Diesel’s global system runs through two doors, and both of them slammed inside seven days.

- The first was the Aramco East-West pipeline. On 11 September, drones out of Iraq (allegedly) struck the line, and Aramco turned the entire pipeline off, as they said, “out of abundance of caution”. Roughly four to five million barrels a day move through that pipe. Since Hormuz closed in March 2026, it was the ONLY large-volume route carrying Saudi crude west to the Red Sea and out to the world. Aramco called the outage a matter of weeks. The terrain, the elevation of the stations that were hit, and the logistics of reaching them, I have argued require three months or more, an assessment I laid out in detail in my pipeline investigation.

- The second door was Bab al-Mandeb. In the same week, the Houthis took Perim Island and the western channel of the Strait, the gate between the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden. Tanker traffic through it fell 91%, from around 30~ ships a day to 4~. Anything sailing from Saudi Arabia’s Yanbu Oil Terminals toward Europe or the US Gulf Coast now goes the long way around Africa, adds weeks and cost, or does not sail at all. That is -IF- the Yanbu terminal itself is even running, since it was among the targets hit on 11 September.
One door feeds the barrel into the sea. The other door is the sea. Losing both at once is why the price of a global fuel moved the way it did while a domestic one stayed calm.

-
- First-order effect: the pump, and the export trap
Europe feels this before America does, and that is what pulls the American pump up. Europe banned Russian diesel in 2023 and has leaned on Gulf and US Gulf Coast cargoes to stay supplied ever since. Both of those sources just went dark in the same week.
So European buyers are now bidding for the same US refinery output that American truckers need, and the European bid is winning. US distillate exports ran at a record pace in August while the American pump printed its own record in September. The country is exporting its diesel and then paying the export price for the barrels that stay home.
Subscribe now
Give a gift subscription
Get 7 day free trial
That sets up the political lever. On 15 September the Senate floated a diesel export ban, a move I have flagged as the predictable next step for months. The logic writes itself for a president watching his approval slide with every cent at the pump in a midterm year. He is holding a lever marked keep American diesel in America, and if diesel holds above $6 into October, he pulls it.
The refiners will argue, correctly, that a ban adds not one barrel of supply and may push them to cut runs. Their argument loses to a photograph of $7 on a pump sign. The economics are sound and the politics are stronger, and the politics decide.
Second-order effect: the field
Here is the casualty nobody is naming. Fertilizer moves on the same water as the diesel, through the same two doors.
Through the Gulf and Bab al-Mandeb comes roughly 17 percent of US urea and close to 20 percent of the DAP and MAP phosphate the country consumes, most of it landing at New Orleans, along with the sulphur that feeds domestic phosphate production. Saudi Arabia alone accounts for about 39 percent of US phosphate imports. Two inputs stay safe: ammonia, which is 88 percent made at home, and potash, which comes overland from Canada. Neither touches the Gulf. Everything else that a spring crop needs does.

reads.title: Oil: The Middle East Oil Tap Is Closing for Good, and Markets Have Not Priced It. It CANNOT Be Defended.
reads.subtitle: Every defence I built assumed you could route around a failure. Against a 20,000 dollar drone that returns tomorrow, there is nothing left to route to. The only defence left is removing the intent.
reads.body:
I have spent the last 20+ years making things survivable. Security, resiliency and crisis management, supply chain security, primary and secondary risk. I find the single point of failure in a system, then I build the infrastructure from ground up and find the workaround and the redundancy that gets most of what sits in your home to you on time from your electricity, to your tooth paste to your cigarettes and your botox.
I have built and run those frameworks for some of the largest companies on the NYSE, for London Stock Exchange and the Toronto Stock Exchange, and the discipline has one article of faith at its core: whatever breaks, you can route around it. That has been my experience through war, conflict, coup d’eta or natural disasters.
Subscribe now
Share
This Existential War in the Middle East has forced me to a conclusion I NEVER EVER expected to say out loud, and never thought I would put in writing. The redundancy that holds up global critical national infrastructure, and the oil and gas grid at the centre of it, is now exposed to a long-term collapse that has no military answer. Nothing in the standard toolkit of deterring, deny, detect, delay, defend, demarcate, destroy, routes a country out of this against an enemy that is state-level, competent, determined, qualified, and can deliver a warhead or a drone for cheap.
The reason is simple, and it sits underneath every plan I have ever drawn. Redundancy ONLY protects you when the enemy cannot reach the fallback. You harden the primary node, and when it goes you drop to the secondary, and the system keeps breathing.
The moment an adversary can strike the primary, the secondary and the tertiary, cheaply, and repeat it tomorrow and the day after, the workaround is dead. There is nothing left to route to. The whole architecture of modern infrastructure defence assumes failures are isolated and fallbacks are safe, and a cheap drone breaks both assumptions at once.
Signal, Not Noise! By AJ Signal is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber.
The threat, measured the way I was trained to measure it
A real threat needs three things present together: capability, intent, and opportunity. Take any one away and the threat is theoretical. What has changed in this war is that all three now sit in the same hands at the same time. Iran, the Ansarallah Houthis, and the Unity of Arenas structure behind them are capable, they are motivated, and the opportunity is the entire map. Thousands of aim points. Pumping stations, pipelines, compressor stations, terminals, most of them standing on open desert or buried ten to twenty metres under sand, none of them movable, all of them mapped.

-
- For twenty years, defending critical national infrastructure and multibillion dollar factories, or power-plants against terrorism was a solvable problem because the attacker was rarely capable, rarely persistent, and rarely cheap. Remove those limits and the problem inverts.
I cannot write a plan that protects an entire regional oil network, pump by pump, across thousands of kilometres, against a patient and qualified enemy who comes back the next morning at scale, every morning.... The honest answer is that no such plan exists, and I say that as someone whose profession is to produce workarounds provide soautlions and exactly that plan a client, a company, a CEO or the board expects from me.
The math that breaks the defence
Even if we remove the politics from the current situation the problem is still an arithmetic problem, and the arithmetic does not favour the defender. To hold the line of defence or your forward line of defence, the defender (You and me) has to succeed everywhere, every time, along the full length of the system.
The attacker (or the capable, determined and the on budget enemy) has to succeed JUST ONCE, with a drone that costs ten or twenty thousand dollars, and then do it again next week. No air-defence screen, no radar picket, no budget closes a gap shaped like that across a whole country. A single interceptor can cost more than the drone it kills by 100x or even 1000x more, and there are more targets than interceptors will ever exist to cover. The cost-exchange ratio runs the wrong way, permanently, and cost-exchange is what decides a war of attrition against infrastructure.
That forces a question larger than any one pipeline or field. Set aside this station or that terminal and ask the general version. Which piece of critical national infrastructure anywhere is safe against a cheap kamikaze drone in this world of cheap drones? On the current balance, the answer is ZERO, and that answer is not specific to the Gulf. It is the new baseline condition of the industrial world that everyone is keeping hush because we do not yet have any solutions.
The order of effects
The first-order effect is a forced, repeatable stoppage with no reliable fallback, which turns what used to be a temporary outage into a standing liability forever. A node is not down until it is repaired. It is down until the war that can reach it is over.
The second-order effect is financial, and it is the one the market has not priced. Once infrastructure cannot be defended by hardware, the risk premium on it stops being cyclical and becomes structural. Insurers, lenders and shippers reprice the whole asset class, capital backs away from exposed nodes, and the century-old logic of building redundancy as protection inverts, because a second and third node are now additional targets rather than additional safety. You cannot buy your way to resilience in a domain where every new asset is one more thing the enemy can hit for twenty thousand dollars.

reads.title: Support Gaza Journalist Huda Skaik's Journey to University of London
reads.subtitle: We have until Wednesday to help a Drop Site contributor raise $50,000
reads.body:
About a year and a half ago, we launched a fundraising campaign to help a Pakistani student, Areeba Fatima, cover expenses for the journalism program she’d been accepted into at Columbia University. This summer, she walked across the stage a graduate, and along the way, produced some terrific reporting for Drop Site, including this investigation into state violence in Kashmir or her recent story on fellow Columbia student Mahmoud Khalil’s new lawsuit against Columbia itself.
All of that was thanks to the generosity of Drop Site readers. Areeba’s success, and your generosity, emboldened us to try it again.
We now have a new opportunity we wanted to get in front of you. Huda Skaik is a young Palestinian journalist from Gaza and a Drop Site contributor. She has been accepted to the University of London, where she wants to sharpen her already formidable journalistic skills. Everything is approved, but for the final visa she needs to raise money to cover her funding gap—unfortunately by this coming Wednesday.
Drop Site is launching a campaign to raise the remaining $50,000 she needs by September 23 to support Huda’s journey from Gaza to the University of London.
Donate to support Huda
Full funding for Huda’s remaining two years of study and living costs has to be secured to meet the financial requirements of the UK visa process. And she’s on a hard deadline. Between the costs the scholarship doesn’t cover, accommodation and living expenses, her visa, and her evacuation and travel out of Gaza, the total comes to about $116,000. We’ve raised part of it, but we still need to raise the remaining $50,000 by Wednesday, September 23.
I think we can do it. If 2,000 people reading this email give $25 each, we’ll hit the target by the end of the afternoon. (Double-check my math, but I think that’s right.) 100% of the contributions will go toward her scholarship and we will of course cover the processing fees and all that on our end.)
If you’d like to make a larger gift to help close the gap, please reach out to majorgiving@dropsitenews.com or ryan@dropsitenews.com and we can let you know how to earmark it directly to Huda.

-
- Huda Skaik, 21, reporting from Gaza Alongside video reports and documentaries, Huda has published more than 70 articles at outlets around the world, including The Nation, Al Jazeera, and Middle East Eye.
Huda earned an “unconditional scholarship” offer to study journalism at the London university, entering directly into her second year. Her passport is ready. The university recognized both her academic record and the exceptional circumstances she’s working under.
That’s where you come in.
Currently displaced and living under extraordinarily difficult conditions, Huda remains committed to her work, sharing her vital perspective on the genocide in Gaza with the world.  We’re asking you to chip in whatever you can. $5, $20, $100—it all adds up. If enough of us pitch in, we can make this happen for Huda.
Donate to support Huda
“I am not asking for help simply to attend university. I am asking for the chance to continue telling stories, studying journalism, and using my work to make sure the experiences of people in Gaza are heard.” - Huda Skaik
Every dollar you give goes directly toward Huda’s evacuation, education, and living costs. If you can’t support directly, please consider sharing Huda’s fundraising page with others in your network.
Let’s do this together,
Ryan and the Drop Site team

reads.title: USA & Iran: Iran Now Fights on Martyrdom. America Fights on Ambition. Nobody Left to Say Wait.
reads.subtitle: The seasoned war planners on both sides are home, off the field. The men who replaced them read fear on one side and ambition on the other, and neither is inclined to say the word wait.
reads.body:
Every analysis of this war counts hardware. Missiles, interceptors, carrier groups, pipeline stations, tanker traffic. The count that decides how this ends is a different one that I keep track of: the number of experienced people still sitting in the two rooms where the decisions get made.
Signal, Not Noise! By AJ Signal is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber.
Over the past twelve months, both the IRGC and the Pentagon have emptied those Strategic and Operations rooms of the men who built the current doctrines, and the chairs have been refilled by people with the opposite instincts of the ones who left.
The decision to fire a weapon sits with a person, and that person either carries the memory of a war gone wrong or he does not. “Institutional memory” is the quiet stabilizer of every standoff. It is the reason the Cold War produced a hundred near-misses incidents for war but ZERO exchanges.

-
- Signal, Not Noise by AJ is now a Substack BESTSELLER in the category of #5 Rising in World PoliticsThe people in the room had internalized the cost, knew where the off-ramps were, and knew the difference between a Signal and an attack. If we have these institutional memories of both out of both rooms in the same year and you have not changed a single weapon on either side. You have changed the only thing that governs whether the weapons are used.
That is the variable the pace of this war has buried but I want you to keep note of it anyways. Everyone is tracking the arenas week to week, so no one is tracking the slower and more decisive shift underneath: the seasoned diplomats and old war planners on both sides are home now, seeing it play out on television, and the men who replaced them carry fear on one side and ambition on the other, with thin experience common to both.
Subscribe now
Share
What experience actually buys in a standoff
Under my thinking and my form of strategic realism, I treat “military deterrence” as a a language or as a “communication system” before it is a “firepower system”. Two adversaries avoid the WORST outcome by reading each other correctly, holding the line without stepping over it, and leaving each other a way down or an off-ramp that does not look like surrender.
Every part of that is a judgment call, and judgment is the product of qualified experience. The veteran commander knows that a “probing strike” is a message and not the opening of a general or a broader war. He knows which threats are theatre and which are real. He knows that pressure is meant to be survived, not necessarily answered in kind at every rung. He is, above all, the man in the room most willing to say the single most stabilizing word in any crisis, which is “wait”.
Remove him and you do not just lose the “institutional memory”, but you lose the interpreter of that Signal, to read what was meant by every action and counter action. The new man reads the same “probing strike” as the first blow of the war he was told his whole career was coming, and he answers it as such.
The escalation that follows is NOT caused by any new weapon or any new intent. It is caused by a misreading the experienced man would not have made. This is how most wars that nobody wanted begin, through the compounding of small misreadings by people who lack the memory to place them correctly.
Iran: a chair filled by martyrdom, and why that breaks the math
Iran’s loss is very specific. The assassination campaign of the past year has killed a disproportionate share of its military architects, the “cool-headed” planners who designed the layered doctrine Iran now fights with that I have written about and explained here over the past few months. The men who build a system understand its limits and its purpose. The men who inherit it after their mentors are killed tend to understand only that they are owed vengeance.
So the IRGC chair is now filled by commanders operating on something of anger, and martyrdom or perhaps even fear after a year of losses and public assassinations. They have said openly that they “seek victory, and that even in death, they remain victorious”.

To me, that single sentence is one of the most blinding sentences to have ever been translated in this war and it belongs in the “strategic column”, because it rewrites the entire payoff matrix that American power is built to exploit.
Every single coercion model the United States military and the “American Institutions” use assumes that their adversaries prefers living to dying.
Deterrence only works by raising the cost of an action until the price of pursuing it exceeds the value of the prize, and the ultimate price on the table is DEATH.
Against an actor or an adversary who scores HIS OWN DEATH as a “win”, that lever is completely disconnected from the machine.
You cannot threaten to impose a “cost your opponent has already priced” as a benefit. Truly, America has NEVER EVER fought an organized military that is truly a determined force that literally sought death on this scale, not in Iraq (the Iraqi forces surrendered in mass), not in Afghanistan at the command level (they were irregular militias and armies), and not in Vietnam.
The “seeking of martyrdom as a posture” removes the top step of the American escalation ladder, which means the usual method of buying restraint by threatening annihilation buys nothing at all here.
America: a chair filled by ambition, and a principal who is replaceable
The American loss runs in the opposite direction and produces the mirror-image danger. The seasoned combat Generals were pushed toward the exit out of the Pentagon forever, and the department is now led, at the political level, by a media personality elevated to the newly returned “Secretary of War” during the prelude to a possible regional or even a Global war.
Below him, the uniformed chairs are increasingly held by officers who are newer, hungry, and aware that this is the “first war” of real consequence in their command, the first with the size, the scale, and the potential to widen into a regional or even global war, and the one their entire lineage of mentors since 1979 has waited their whole careers to fight.
Ambition is a different failure mode than fear, and in some ways a worse one for stability. Fear makes a commander jumpy and prone to preemption, which is dangerous enough. Ambition gives him a “positive incentive” to act, to be THE man who broke Iran, to leave a legacy in the sand rather than a stalemate.
The restraining instinct that comes from having already earned your reputation is missing in someone still trying to make it. When the frightened and the ambitious face each other across a line, the frightened side over-reads threats and the ambitious side under-weights costs, and both are pushing the same direction.
Layered on top is a second-order instability that has no equivalent on the Iranian side: the American principal is himself replaceable in the middle of the crisis. A Secretary of War who can be fired or forced to resign, in an administration that runs on the logic of “the fall guy”, means the chain of command can turn over at the worst possible moment.
“Command continuity” is one of the few things a country in a standoff cannot afford to lose, and here it is NOT guaranteed. A crisis that arrives during a leadership turnover at the top of the war department is a crisis being managed by people still learning where the light switches are.
Subscribe now
Share

> SIGNAL, not noise is a reader supported platform, please consider becoming a paid subscriber if you find my work insightful or if it resonates with you.
Kindly share, like, and restack to help amplify my SIGNAL.
The order of effects

- The first-order effect is a higher baseline rate of miscalculation. Two rooms full of inexperienced readers of each other’s signals will misread more often, and each misread carries a live chance of a response the situation did not require. The probability of an accidental escalation is a function of WHO is interpreting the incidents, and both interpreters just got worse in the same year.

- The second-order effect is the loss of the brake. In a mature standoff, a tactical incident is contained because someone senior on each side has both the standing and the memory to absorb it and step back.

With the veterans gone, an incident that would once have been walked back instead runs up the ladder, because the men holding the rungs are motivated to climb rather than to stop. The system loses its shock absorber at the exact moment it needs it most.

reads.title: FIR Counterintelligence Brief: Daniel McAdams & the Ron Paul Institute
reads.body:
SUBTITLE: 
DATE: 2026-09-18T00:25:54.907Z
URL: https://thefulkintelligencereport.substack.com/p/fir-counterintelligence-brief-daniel
AUDIENCE: everyone  PAYWALLED: False
CHARS: 21874  WORDCOUNT_FIELD: 3420
-
- Link to download the fully footnoted PDF here.

## BLUF

- The Ron Paul Institute (RPI) was launched in April 2013 by Ron Paul. Daniel McAdams has been its executive director since 2013. Coinciding with the launch of the RPI, Daniel McAdams became a contributor to Kremlin-funded Russia Today (RT) by October 2013. The second article published on RPI during its launch established a longstanding practice, that continues to the present, of reprinting articles from the U.S. Treasury-sanctioned Russian Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR)-controlled Strategic Culture Foundation.

- FIR manually verified by clicking through the RT.com website that Daniel McAdams has at least 130 video interviews/appearances on RT.com with an additional 46 transcripts of interviews. FIR manually verified by clicking through RT.com that the board members of RPI have a combined 162 video interviews/appearances on RT.com in addition to appearances by McAdams.

- FIR manually verified by clicking through ronpaulinstitute.org that RPI has republished at least 150 SVR-controlled SCF articles since 2013.

- Daniel McAdams has publicly stated that he admires Vladimir Putin. In 2010, three years before RPI launched, he registered the domain name dailyputin.com.

- Andrew Napolitano, an RPI advisory board member, interviewed and praised U.S. Treasury-sanctioned Aleksandr Dugin, who is on the Presidium of the International Club of National Unity (MKNE). MKNE lists individuals from the Russian government, military, and intelligence services among its members and Napolitano is a member.

## Introduction

According to Daniel McAdams’s bio on ronpaulinstitute.org, he worked as a journalist based in Budapest, Hungary, from 1993 to 1999 while traveling through the former communist bloc as a human rights monitor and election observer. The Foundation for Defense of Democracies says McAdams monitored elections for the British Helsinki Human Rights Group (BHHRG) during this period. The Guardian noted that BHHRG was criticized for taking the side of authoritarian regimes, saying:

> Founded in 1992, the BHHRG sends observers to elections and writes reports which - along Laughlandish lines - almost invariably dispute the accounts given by better known human rights organisations. This stance has led to the BHHRG being criticised by the International Helsinki Federation for Human Rights (established in 1976) as preferring “the role [is to take] PR flak for a new breed of authoritarian rulers in Europe” to the business of actually monitoring abuses.
One of the trustees of BHHRG was John Laughland and its chairman was Mark Almond. Both Laughland and Almond ended up serving on the academic board of the Ron Paul Institute. By 2013, Laughland had a meeting with the Russian Aleksandr Dugin who by that time had been working on building alliances with the European right and the right in the United States. Edward Lozansky offered up U.S. conservative contacts to Dugin in a 2008 meeting. McAdams would become a fellow at Lozansky’s American University in Moscow by the summer of 2012, according to the earliest web snapshot of Lozansky’s fellows page on his website.

-
- By 2016, McAdams had also become affiliated with the Centre for the Study of Interventionism which was administered by Laughland. McAdams was listed as the Center’s U.S. Associate. Two other groups that Laughland was associated with are Thierry Baudet’s Forum for Democracy International (FVD) and the Institute for Democracy and Cooperation. Laughland was listed as the director of Baudet’s FVD and Baudet had a meeting with Dugin in 2018 for multiple hours. While the men disagreed on some things, Dugin praised Baudet’s victory in his Provincial Council election. FVD’s youth magazine De Dissident also interviewed Dugin in 2022, and in an article for FVD, Laughland noted how FVD defended Dugin and objected to the sanctions imposed against him saying “he is sanctioned for thoughtcrime.” McAdams, Laughland and Baudet were all at the 2025 RPI DC conference.
The other group Laughland was a part of, the Institute for Democracy and Cooperation (IDC), was founded with Putin’s approval by a Russian lawyer (who later represented Edward Snowden) named Anatoly Kucherena, who in 2013 was serving as a member of a board that oversaw the Russian Federal Security Service (FSB). The Paris branch is run by Natalia Narochnitskaya and Laughland was listed as the director of studies (the IDC website is down as of writing this brief). Narochnitskaya was described by British journalist Catherine Belton as a “barely concealed Russian intelligence agent” who was close to both Vladimir Yakunin (a former KGB general) and a “protégée of the spymaster Yevgeny Primakov at the Institute for World Economy in Moscow during the time of the perestroika reforms.” Belton said the IDC was, “part of a PR offensive that began when Putin’s government set up RT, the global English-language TV network aimed at challenging the hegemony of Western channels such as CNN and the BBC.”

-
-

## McAdams Lands a Job with Ron Paul
Following his work as a journalist, McAdams became an advisor to U.S. Congressman Ron Paul from 2001 until Representative Paul’s retirement in 2012. During that period, the Kremlin-funded RT news station launched in 2005 and interviewed Ron Paul during his term in office multiple times. A foreign news station interviewing U.S. politicians is not out of the ordinary, but RT has a particular interest in promoting voices that are non-interventionist like Paul’s. While Ron Paul was in Congress and McAdams was serving as his advisor, McAdams penned articles for antiwar.com and lewrockwell.com. Lew Rockwell ran the latter while Eric Garris of antiwar.com was the webmaster for Rockwell’s website. Lewrockwell.com was sponsored and administered by the Center for Libertarian Studies (published under the Mises Institute where Lew Rockwell was president from 1982-2009) which was also the sponsor of antiwar.com where the co-founder of BHHRG, Christine Stone, had a regular Thursday column according to the Guardian.
Lew Rockwell served as Ron Paul’s chief of staff in the late 1970s to early 1980s and then founded lewrockwell.com in 1999 with Burt Blumert to “carry on the anti-war, anti-state, pro-market work of Murray N. Rothbard.
At a Ron Paul Institute Conference in 2019, McAdams said he got his job working with Ron Paul through Rockwell. Quoting McAdams, he said:

> My ticket to go work for my hero for Ron Paul came…was punched by my articles that I wrote for Lew Rockwell before I was hired…
Relevant here: FIR previously published a brief documenting that LewRockwell.com republishes Russian Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR) controlled Strategic Culture Foundation articles, Russian Military Intelligence (GRU) linked infobrics articles and SVR directed New Eastern Outlook articles.

## The Launch of the Ron Paul Institute and Russian State Media Appearances by its Members
After Ron Paul retired from Congress, he founded the Ron Paul Institute (RPI) in April 2013, and McAdams was named as the executive director. RT provided favorable coverage on the RPI in July 2013.  On October 26 of that year, McAdams sent an email to Robert Wenzel’s Economic Policy Journal saying:
My first piece as an RT contributing analyst...
..it's all about expanding the RPI influence!
I am officially on the roster of the RT editorial writers!
Since launching RPI, McAdams gave at least 130 video interviews/appearances on RT.com. FIR manually clicked RT.com to verify each of the 130 interviews and appearances and found another 46 articles where there are transcripts of interviews. Additionally, FIR found, by clicking through the RT.com website, RT interviews of the following board members of RPI:
•	John Laughland (RPI academic board) - 74 video interviews/appearances.
•	Ron Paul (RPI chairman) - 24 video interviews/appearances.
•	Lew Rockwell (RPI advisory board) – 9 video interviews/appearances.
•	Michael Scheuer (RPI academic board) - 12 video interviews/appearances.
•	Andrew Napolitano (RPI advisory board) - 3 video interviews/appearances.
•	Dennis Kucinich (RPI advisory board) - 24 video interviews/appearances.
•	Eric Margolis (RPI academic board) – 5 video interviews/appearances.
•	Col. (Ret.) Lawrence Wilkerson (RPI academic board until 2020) - 14 video interviews/appearances.
The U.S. Department of State does not consider RT in the same class as traditional fact-based Western news outlets. Specifically, the State Department said on September 13, 2024, that:

> RT moved beyond being simply a media outlet and has been an entity with cyber capabilities. It is also engaged in information operations, covert influence, and military procurement.
Earlier that year on July 9, the U.S. Department of Justice issued a press release stating that the Russian Federal Security Service (FSB) used active RT employees to build out a private intelligence unit which operated nearly 1,000 social media bots.  In September 2024, U.S. filings alleged RT employees set up a shell company structure to fund Tennessee-based TENET Media with nearly $10 million to in turn fund U.S. based influencers.  According to news reports, one of those influencers was Lauren Southern who previously met with Aleksandr Dugin. Another was Matt Christiansen who co-hosted a show with Rebecca Hargraves; Hargraves promotes Hitler and hosted Dugin on her program and co-hosted a Multipolar Press event with Dugin popularizer Constantin Hoffmeister. RT, according to the Department of State, also lacks fiscal transparency and the U.S. Treasury says it is funded by the Kremlin and placed it under sanctions.
Worthy of note, before the launch of RPI, McAdams registered a website on May 28, 2010, under his email dlmcadams@gmail.com called dailyputin.com.  Furthermore, in case there is any question about McAdams’s position on Vladimir Putin and Russia, he said:

> “OMG you admire Putin”!!!
Yes no shit! I absolutely admire Putin! Suck on that, NAFO! Putin is right. He actually protects his own national interest as opposed to Biden, who only protects his crackhead son. Putin! Daily Putin!

-
-

## Spotlight on Some of the Authors that RPI Republishes

Some of the authors RPI regularly republishes have connections to Russian intelligence tasked organizations and Russian propaganda organizations besides RT. Andrew Napolitano, who is on the advisory board of RPI, has at least 140 articles on ronpaulinstitute.org all but one article between 2021-2026, according to his author archive on the website. In March of 2025, Napolitano traveled to Moscow to interview Aleksandr Dugin and Sergey Lavrov. On that trip with him were Larry Johnson and Mario Nawfal. Elon Musk interacted with Nawfal on X “at least 1,200 times” between August of 2024 and April of 2025. Larry Johnson, who will be discussed more, is frequently interviewed by Nawfal.
Napolitano said in his interview with Dugin that:

> [Start of interview]: I am privileged, deeply and profoundly privileged to be interviewing today one of the smartest philosophers in the world the great Professor Aleksandr Dugin…Thank you for giving me this opportunity to speak with you.
Professor Aleksandr Dugin a brilliant, brilliant scholar, a wonderful philosopher, fearless and courageous person, thank you very much for allowing me the privilege to spend this time with you and to interview you. [End of interview]

-
- Napolitano’s interview did not address Dugin’s published geopolitical program or his associates’ documented role in information and unconventional warfare, which FIR has treated separately in a 65-page report.  For example, Dugin wrote a book, developed with the assistance of military officers in the department of strategy at the Russian General Staff Academy in 1997 titled Foundations of Geopolitics. In that book, he calls for retaking Ukraine, “wrest[ing] Europe from US (NATO) control,” establishing a “planetary New Empire” with the US as its scapegoat, destabilizing the US through supporting dissidents, racists, isolationists, etc., and ultimately geopolitically destroying the United States.
In 2025, both Napolitano (on the independent review board of media experts) and Dugin (on the Presidium) were listed as part of the Russian organization called the International Club of National Unity (MKNE) which has members and leadership with links to the Russian government, military and intelligence services.  Ron Paul appeared on video with MKNE podcast host and co-founder of the American Communist Party Christopher Helali. ’  While an extensive look into MKNE is beyond the scope of this counterintelligence brief (X user @Restitutor_ produced a comprehensive report on them already), it is relevant to mention that Sergey Panteleyev is listed as a member of MKNE, and he was also identified as a member of Russian Military Intelligence Unit 54777 which conducts psychological operations against the West.  ‘  Panteleyev heads an institute called the Institute of the Russian Diaspora which was the project implementer of a legal fund called Pravfond, and Pravfond’s First Deputy Executive Director is Vladimir Pozdorovkin who is a former member of the Russian Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR).  Pravfond helped Viktor Bout (who was convicted of terrorism-related charges in the U.S.) and Simeon Boikov (AKA Aussie Cossack) the latter of whom promotes disinformation linked to GRU backed Storm-1516 and has tried to fund a neo-Nazi group. ’ '  Storm-1516 is linked to an American defector named John Mark Dougan who works with a long-time associate of and lieutenant of Aleksandr Dugin’s named Valery Korovin. Korovin submitted a letter to the Russian Ministry of Defense in 2019 suggesting they organize “an internet war against the United States on its own territory.” ’  Both Bout and Boikov were listed as members of MKNE.  Laughland, while on the RPI academic advisory board, was interviewed by MKNE member Stanislav Krapivnik six times and Daniel McAdams was interviewed by Krapivnik twice. ’  Krapivnik raises money for and supplies components, such as 3D printers, to the Russian Slavinsk Brigade’s drone shop.

-
- Larry Johnson is also republished on the Ron Paul Institute, and he has over 100 articles from 2019 to August 2026 on ronpaulinstitute.org; he was a guest speaker at a Ron Paul Institute conference (with another MKNE member and RT show host Rick Sanchez). Johnson was also listed as a member of the MKNE presidium as of August 2026. Johnson interviewed Dugin in July of 2024 and said in that interview that:

> …I’m really pleased to have my new friend Aleksandr Dugin today…What I really want to do today is get your story out there…You’ve been a victim of sanctions. [Start of interview]
I thank you for the courage you and your wife demonstrate…I regret that you have been persecuted by my own country, because it’s unjustified, it’s unfair and you’re just a man of ideas and your ideas, I think, give us some hope for the future. [End of interview]
Scott Ritter is another person RPI republishes, and he has 47 article entries there from 2019-2024 and has been a speaker at a RPI conference. ’  Ritter’s name is also on MKNE documents and MKNE has their own photo page for Ritter which includes a photo of him with convicted Russian terrorist Viktor Bout.
Caitlin Johnstone was regularly republished by the FSB-tasked outlet SouthFront, where she published more than 150 articles from 2018–2020. SouthFront is now under U.S. Treasury sanctions. RPI has republished her work (140 articles from 2017 to the present) and hosted her as a 2018 conference speaker. ’  RPI now regularly republishes her, and she has 140 articles on RPI from 2017-present.  She was also a speaker at a RPI conference in 2018.

## RPI Republishes the Russian Foreign Intelligence Service Controlled Strategic Culture Foundation
Recapping some of what was discussed already in this report, in 2013 RPI launched and that same year RT gave it favorable coverage. Also that year, their executive director became a contributor to RT and has subsequently appeared on video 130 times on RT.com. What has not been discussed yet is that also in 2013 on the first day RPI launched, RPI began republishing the Russian Foreign Intelligence Service controlled Strategic Culture Foundation (SCF) articles, and the first link to SCF on RPI was to an article that a retired Russian colonel wrote.  A quick brief on the SCF is necessary because of the longstanding republishing ties between SCF and RPI.
Yuri Prokofiev is the co-founder of the SCF, and he serves as the president of the foundation. ’  He was a member of the Politburo of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union (CPSU) Central Committee and First Secretary of the Moscow City Committee of the CPSU. ’  Prokofiev was an official in the final days of the Soviet Union and once said, “A person cannot live without faith. You believe in God, in the afterlife. I believe in communism.”

-
- The SCF is registered in Russia and the last internet protocol host address linked to the website is 192.145.97.84 on the Delta Ltd network out of Moscow, Russia.
On July 28, 2020, the New York Times said the Strategic Culture Foundation was directed by the Russian Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR) “according to two American officials,” and that it was being investigated by the FBI for its ties to the SVR “according to another official.”  A few days later, the U.S. Department of State’s Global Engagement Center published its Pillars of Russia’s Disinformation and Propaganda Ecosystem, and also noted the SCF “is directed by Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR).”  On April 15, 2021, the U.S. Department of the Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) designated SCF and stated that it is “controlled by the SVR’s Directorate MS (Active Measures).”  Furthermore, the Treasury said that SCF:

> publishes conspiracy theorists, giving them a broader platform to spread disinformation, while trying to obscure the Russian origins of the journal so that readers may be more likely to trust the sourcing.
On October 18, 2024, the FBI and CISA issued a PSA listing SCF as one of the websites “operated by Russian malign influence actors.”

-
- FIR manually verified by clicking through ronpaulinstitute.org that RPI has republished SCF at least 150 times. All the articles FIR found that RPI republished from SCF are in Appendix I of this report. Ron Paul’s welcome letter to RPI was posted on April 16, 2013, and that same day an excerpt from SCF was featured on the RPI website along with a link to SCF at the bottom of the article. A screenshot from that article (using the Wayback Machine to access the link) is provided below in figure 8.

- The link to the SCF found in the RPI article referenced in figure 8 takes the user to SCF’s old domain www.strategic-culture.org. A screenshot of the article on the SCF’s old domain is provided in figure 9.

-
- Most of the SCF article reprints at ronpaulinstitute.org have at the end of the article the line “Reprinted with permission from the Strategic Culture Foundation” with SCF hyperlinked to the article origin on the SCF website. The following three figures are additional examples of SCF reprints on the ronpaulinstitute.org with the corresponding article on the SCF’s website.

## Conclusion

The pattern documented in this brief is systematic rather than incidental. From its first day of operation in April 2013, the Ron Paul Institute has republished material originating from the SVR-controlled Strategic Culture Foundation. FIR manually verified at least 150 such republications. The same year RPI launched, its executive director, Daniel McAdams, became a contributing analyst for Kremlin-funded RT and has since accumulated at least 130 video appearances on RT.com, with additional transcripts. RPI board and advisory figures add a further combined 162 verified RT appearances.
The republication practice and the RT appearances have continued after official U.S. attributions of SCF as SVR-controlled (State GEC 2020; Treasury/OFAC 2021) and after official characterizations of RT as an instrument of covert influence rather than a conventional news outlet (State Department 2024; Treasury sanctions). Parallel associations documented here include RPI advisory board member Andrew Napolitano’s 2025 Moscow interviews with Aleksandr Dugin and Sergey Lavrov; Napolitano’s listing with the International Club of National Unity (MKNE); and RPI’s regular republication of authors who also appear on sanctioned or intelligence-tasked platforms.
From a counterintelligence perspective, these practices create a durable, low-friction English-language pathway for content and messaging originating from, or aligned with, Russian intelligence-linked outlets into a non-interventionist and libertarian-leaning audience (McAdams describes himself as closer to a Catholic anarchist).[1] The volume, duration (2013–present), and coincidence of launch timing distinguish this from occasional or isolated reprinting.
This brief does not allege that Daniel McAdams, Ron Paul, or the Ron Paul Institute is directed, funded, or controlled by Russian intelligence services. It does not allege a command-and-control relationship. The findings are limited to observable republication, documented media appearances, public statements, and publicly recorded associations with individuals and organizations that the U.S. government and Western agencies have identified as controlled, directed, or tasked by Russian intelligence services, or as participants in Russian influence activity.
Continued monitoring of RPI republication practices, RT appearances by RPI principals, and overlapping memberships (including MKNE) is warranted based on the volume and persistence of the pattern documented here.
