reads.title: THE ENERGY WINTER: IRAN, REFINING, AND THE COMMISSION'S OWN GOAL
reads.subtitle: Record-low gas, diesel shortages, shrinking refining: Europe's winter of crisis. Marco | Independent Analyst 18 September 2026
reads.body:
## Introduction
Europe enters the winter of 2026 with gas storage at 15-year lows, diesel supplies approaching five-year lows, and a refining industry in structural decline. Three forces are converging: the war in Iran, the collapse of European refining capacity, and the political choices of the European Commission. This article examines all three.

## I. The Iran War: The Trigger
The war in Iran, which began in late February 2026, has disrupted the Strait of Hormuz—through which approximately one-fifth of the world’s oil and LNG flows.
The impact on Europe has been immediate:

- EU oil and gas import bill: +€6 billion since the war began

- European gas prices (TTF): +70% since the war started

- Brent crude: +50% since the war started

- Diesel prices at the pump (EU): Record €2.11 per litre in April 2026
Europe was particularly exposed because it had become dependent on Gulf refined products after cutting off Russian supplies. In 2025, the EU imported approximately 35% of its jet fuel and 20% of its diesel. The Gulf was the primary supplier, providing 56% of jet fuel imports and 34% of diesel imports.
When Hormuz was disrupted, those supply chains broke. European refineries pushed jet fuel production to maximum capacity, at the expense of diesel. But it wasn’t enough. By late August, jet fuel stocks were 6% below the five-year minimum.
The Iran war exposed a vulnerability that had been building for years. But it did not create it. It merely accelerated a crisis that was already underway.

## II. The Refining Crisis: The Structural Problem
Europe has enough crude. What it lacks is the industrial capacity to turn that crude into the fuels that heat homes, power trucks, and keep planes in the air.
Europe’s refining capacity has been declining since 2009:

- -20% capacity lost since 2009

- ~30 refineries closed across Europe, including 5 in Italy alone

- 9 million barrels/day projected capacity by 2035, down from 14 million at the start of the century
Europe’s Refining CapacityCurrent capacity~11 million b/dProjected 2035 capacity~9 million b/dDecline since 2009-20%Refineries closed~30 (5 in Italy)Diesel import dependence~20%Jet fuel import dependence~35%
Gianni Murano, president of Italy’s Unem, described the paradox: “While Europe reduces production capacity, other regions of the world are building new, ever-larger and more efficient refineries. Refining is not just about the future of fossil fuels, but above all about Europe’s ability to preserve a strategic industrial base during the energy transition.”
The consequence: Europe imports crude, ships it to refineries in the Middle East and Asia, and buys back the refined products at a premium. The refining margin—the “crack spread”—has become the most profitable part of the oil business, and Europe has largely given it away.
Murano added: “There was a conviction that from tomorrow it would be possible to move everyone by electric vehicle and that refineries could be done without. It didn’t work out that way.”

## III. The Commission’s Policy: The Political Choice
Here is the fact that official communications rarely mention: the decision to stop buying Russian gas was made in Brussels, not in Moscow.
On 26 January 2026, the 27 EU member states formally adopted the regulation on the gradual phase-out of Russian pipeline gas and LNG imports. The regulation was published in the Official Journal and entered into force the following day. The ban on LNG imports takes effect from the beginning of 2027; the ban on pipeline gas from autumn 2027.
This is not a Russian embargo. It is European legislation. The text was negotiated by the Council and the European Parliament, with an agreement reached on 3 December 2025. The von der Leyen Commission guided the entire process, presenting the roadmap on 6 May 2025 and pushing for rapid adoption.
The REPowerEU Regulation — Key FactsAdopted by the Council26 January 2026Entered into force27 January 2026LNG import banFrom beginning of 2027Pipeline gas banFrom autumn 2027Sanctions for non-complianceUp to €40 million or 3.5% of global turnover
Yet the Commission’s public narrative tells a different story.
On 1 July 2026, Commission President Ursula von der Leyen stated that Russia “used energy as a weapon and cut off gas supplies to Europe”. Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova responded: “Ursula is an excellent liar. Russia has never cut off gas for Europe. Any EU citizen can sue her for this lie and win.”
On 11 March 2026, von der Leyen declared that returning to Russian fossil fuels would be a “strategic mistake” that would make Europe “more dependent, more vulnerable and weaker.”
On 20 March 2026, she categorically ruled out buying Russian gas “even in the event of power outages in the EU.”
These statements confirm that the Commission made a political choice not to buy Russian gas, regardless of the consequences for prices and energy security. It was not Russia that closed the taps. It was Brussels that decided to stop buying.
The costs of this choice are now visible. On 27 August 2026, von der Leyen herself admitted that “energy prices in Europe are still 2-3 times higher than in the United States and China” and that “energy is now the main factor limiting our competitiveness and our independence.” She also revealed that dependence on imported fossil fuels has already cost over €50 billion more since the beginning of the Middle East crisis.

## IV. The Court of Auditors: “The Strategy Is Stalled”
On 9 September 2026, the European Court of Auditors published a special report that effectively demolished the Commission’s energy strategy. The auditors concluded that:

- The REPowerEU plan “still lacks effective governance tools to guide its implementation”

- EU funding has played “only a secondary role” in ending dependence on Russian oil and gas

- “Not enough investment has been induced” to accelerate the clean energy transition and strengthen cross-border connections

- Four years after its launch, “REPowerEU is stalled, despite several hundred billion euros made available”

- “Russian fossil fuels are still imported indirectly into the EU through third countries (e.g., Turkey, China or India)”
Mihails Kozlovs, the Court member responsible for the report, stated that the Commission’s claims about the plan’s effectiveness “contradict the statements of the Commission President, who instead boasted of its effectiveness by telling only part of the truth.”
In simple terms: the EU’s energy strategy has been a documented failure, according to the EU’s own audit institution. Not only has it cost hundreds of billions, it has not even achieved its stated goal of eliminating energy dependence on Russia.

## V. Gas Storage: 15-Year Lows
As of 9 September 2026, EU gas storage was 67.33% full—12.3 percentage points below the 79.63% recorded at the same date in 2025. The level is well below the five-year average of 84%.
EU Gas Storage — September 2026Storage level (9 Sept)67.33%Year-on-year change-12.3 percentage pointsFive-year average84%Germany54.98% (from 74.22%)Italy84.06% (from 89.68%)France74.69% (from 89.21%)
The reasons for the low storage levels are counterintuitive. During the summer, spot prices were higher than forward prices for winter. This eliminated the economic incentive for operators to inject gas into storage. Why buy gas at €60/MWh in July to sell it at €55/MWh in January?
Now, Europe faces the winter with thin inventories and rising prices:

- TTF gas price: ~€80/MWh, +150% year-on-year, the highest since January 2023

- EU winter gas bill: Projected at €117 billion, or 0.6% of GDP

- Inflation impact: Could push eurozone inflation toward 4%

- ECB response: Two additional rate hikes expected

## VI. What This Means for Citizens

## Italy: The Hardest Hit

- Household electricity price: €0.345/kWh (vs. G20 average of €0.163)

- September 2026 electricity bill estimate: €0.3193/kWh, up from €0.2875 a year earlier

- Gas price: €1.37 per cubic metre, up from €1.05 a year earlier

- Annual household cost increase: ~€877 for a typical family
Italy — Household Energy Costs (2026)Electricity (Sept 2025)€0.2875/kWhElectricity (Sept 2026)€0.3193/kWhGas (Sept 2025)€1.05/m³Gas (Sept 2026)€1.37/m³Annual increase (energy)€515Annual increase (fuel)€362Total annual increase€877

## Germany and the UK
German household electricity prices are €0.356/kWh, more than double the G20 average. UK prices are €0.324/kWh.

## VII. The Ukraine War: A Marginal Factor
The war in Ukraine has added a third layer of stress. Ukrainian drone attacks on Russian refineries have intensified, hitting targets as far as Omsk, 2,675 kilometres from the border.
Since March 2026, Russian refining capacity has fallen by approximately 1.3 million barrels per day—a quarter of the total. In August, capacity dropped to 4 million b/d against the usual 5.5 million.
Russia has responded by banning gasoline exports in April and diesel exports in July. For Europe, which historically imported 23% of its diesel from the former Soviet Union, the loss of approximately 850,000 barrels per day of Russian exports has been significant.
But here is the key point: the Ukraine war is marginal compared to the structural refining crisis and the Iran war. The real problem is not Russian refineries being hit. The real problem is that Europe no longer has its own refineries to compensate.

## VIII. Conclusion
Europe’s energy crisis is not a story about scarcity. It is a story about the destruction of industrial capacity—and the political decisions that made it worse.
Three factors are converging:

- The Iran war disrupted Gulf refined product supplies that Europe had become dependent on.

- The refining crisis has left Europe unable to process its own crude into the fuels it needs.

- The Commission’s political choices—the REPowerEU regulation adopted on 26 January 2026—severed energy ties with Russia without building adequate alternatives.
The wars in Iran and Ukraine have exposed this vulnerability, but they did not create it. They merely accelerated a decline that has been underway for two decades.
And the decision to sever energy ties with Russia was not a Russian action. It was a European one. The Commission’s claims that Russia “cut off” the gas are contradicted by the legislative record and by the statements of the Commission’s own auditors.
The cost is being borne by European households, who face record bills for electricity, gas, and fuel. A typical Italian family will pay approximately €877 more in 2026. German and British families face similar increases. And the worst may be yet to come.
Until Europe rebuilds its refining capacity and acknowledges the true cost of its political choices, it will continue to pay the price of its own deindustrialisation.

## Sources and Dossiers
Primary Sources:

- Council of the European Union: “Divieto progressivo di importazione di gas russo: via libera definitivo del Consiglio” (26 January 2026)

- European Court of Auditors: Special Report 21/2026 on REPowerEU (9 September 2026)

- TASS: “Von der Leyen ‘excellent liar’ saying Russia cut off gas supplies to Europe — Zakharova” (2 July 2026)

- Unem / Gianni Murano interview: “Raffinerie europee affossate dal green” (15 September 2026)

- Teleborsa / AGSI: EU gas storage data (9 September 2026)

- Nomisma Energia: Italian household energy cost estimates (August-September 2026)
Related Dossiers:

- Dossier #125: The Money Laundering of War

- Dossier #126: Istanbul 2022 and the War of Locomotives

- Dossier #130: European Censorship
Independent analysis. No ideology. Just facts.
Marco | Independent Analyst ⚖️

reads.body:
- Satellite image shows a large smoke plume rising from Aramco’s Jizan Bulk Plant storage tanks in Jazan City, Saudi Arabia, on September 8, 2026, after Ansarallah strikes. Photo by Gallo Images/Orbital Horizon/Copernicus Sentinel Data 2026.Friday, September 18, 2026 – Ansarallah leader claims U.S. is directly supporting Saudi Arabia, rejects accusations of striking Mecca. Fighting continues in Taiz as government forces claim 30 Ansarallah fighters killed. One killed, two wounded after Saudi intercepts drone over Taif. Over 112,000 displaced in Yemen. Saudi Aramco tells European customers they will receive no crude next month after pipeline attack. U.S. clears possible $24.3 billion sale of 48 F-35s to Saudi Arabia. Italy prepares naval mission, calls for more ships in Red Sea. Iran strikes tanker in Hormuz. Massive government rally in Tehran. U.S. approves visas for Iranian president, foreign minister to attend UN General Assembly. South Korea rules out involvement in Hormuz “conflict,” says “minimum level” of action needed to protect shipping. FT: Iran shifts trade overland as U.S. blockade disrupts Gulf routes. Iran-U.S. war and Hormuz disruption cost Arab economies nearly $150 billion in the first month, UN agency says. Amnesty: Iranian authorities committed crimes against humanity in 2022 protest crackdown. Two women shot by Israeli forces in central Gaza. Five children rescued from damaged home as Gaza government announces emergency plan for buildings at risk of collapse. Israeli settler attacks injure at least six Palestinians across the occupied West Bank. Israel adds 2,167 units to E1 settlement plan, bringing total to 3,401. “The whole case is related to her journalistic work”: Palestinian-American journalist detained by Israel at Hasharon. Qatar pledges 1.3 million liters of fuel for Gaza, enough for just 16 days of health sector needs. Two wounded as Israeli ceasefire violations continue in southern Lebanon. Early voting begins in midterm elections. Forty-six Senate Democrats demand Pentagon accounting of Iran war costs. White House withdraws Lance Schroyer’s nomination to lead ICE. Trump administration weighs at least 12 data center projects on federal public lands. Microsoft executive calls AI “largest theft of labor in human history.” Man who sprayed Rep. Ilhan Omar with vinegar sentenced to 14 months in prison. Pentagon reinstates mandatory testosterone screening for male service members over 30. Pakistan mosque bombing kills at least 16. Spanish police clear migrants from Ceuta. Russians vote in first parliamentary election since Ukraine invasion. Belarus continues military drills near NATO border. Chinese coast guard ship collides with Philippines government vessel near Palawan. Philippines school shooting leaves three dead in third deadly attack since June.
This is Drop Site Daily, our free news recap We send it Monday – Friday

## Yemen

- Ansarallah leader claims U.S. is directly supporting Saudi Arabia, rejects accusations of striking Mecca: Ansarallah leader Abdul-Malik al-Houthi claimed the U.S. is directly supporting Saudi military operations against Yemen, saying Washington has deployed “a joint force of 200 military experts” who are “managing the operations” from Saudi Arabia. He said Saudi forces are fighting “with aircraft obtained from America” and “bombs purchased from America,” and claimed Riyadh is seeking greater direct U.S. involvement in the war.

- On Sunday, Ansarallah told U.S. officials it would limit Red Sea attacks to Saudi ships and continue to uphold the U.S.-Ansarallah ceasefire during Oman-facilitated talks in Muscat, Reuters reported.

- Al-Houthi said that an end to the conflict requires Saudi Arabia to halt its attacks on Yemen and lift its blockade. “This is what we want, this is our issue: for Saudi Arabia to stop its aggression against us,” he said, adding that Riyadh must “end its blockade of our people” and stop depriving Yemenis of the country’s oil and gas resources.

- Al-Houthi also rejected Saudi allegations that Ansarallah had targeted Mecca, calling the accusation “a great lie” and accusing Riyadh of using it to encourage other countries to join the conflict. “Our lives, our souls, our wealth, and everything we possess are a sacrifice for Mecca and the Islamic holy sites,” he said.

- Fighting continues in Taiz as government forces claim 30 Ansarallah fighters killed: Yemeni forces, backed by Saudi airstrikes, are attempting to regain a foothold in the contested mountainous district of Al-Waziyah in western Taiz governorate, along the approaches to Yemen’s Red Sea coast and the Bab al-Mandab Strait. Saudi-backed forces claimed 30 Ansarallah fighters were killed and 60 wounded, figures that could not be independently verified. They also reported airstrikes on positions around Al-Dhikra Junction, Al-Damna and Al-Rahida.

- In nearby Mocha, a strategic Red Sea port captured by Ansarallah last week, Saudi-backed forces said airstrikes targeted Ansarallah movements, reinforcements, and supply routes as they seek to regain territory along the coast.

- One killed, two wounded after Saudi intercepts drone over Taif: one person was killed and two others wounded, one critically, by falling debris after an Ansarallah drone was intercepted and destroyed over Taif, Saudi Civil Defense said on Thursday. Several buildings and vehicles were also damaged.

- Over 112,000 displaced in Yemen: More than 112,000 people have been displaced in Yemen in the last two weeks amid renewed fighting between Ansarallah and Saudi-backed government forces, according to the UN migration agency. Nearly 3,000 others have fled by sea to Djibouti, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) said.

- “Our resources are very, very, very limited and our stocks will be depleted very soon,” Abdusattor Esoev, IOM’s Chief of Mission in Yemen, said in a statement.

- Saudi Aramco tells European customers they will receive no crude next month after pipeline attack: Saudi Aramco told at least two European refiners they will receive no Saudi crude under their regular contracts next month, with the decision applying to all European buyers, Bloomberg reported on Friday.

- The move follows last week’s drone attack that forced Saudi Arabia to shut its key East-West pipeline to the Red Sea. The pipeline is expected to partially restart within days but could take up to six weeks to return to full operation.

- U.S. clears possible $24.3 billion sale of 48 F-35s to Saudi Arabia: The State Department approved a possible Foreign Military Sale of 48 F-35 Lightning II fighter jets and related equipment to Saudi Arabia and notified Congress of the proposed deal.

- The Saudi Embassy in Washington welcomed the proposed sale, saying, in a post on X, it reflects the “strength and enduring nature of the Saudi-U.S. strategic partnership” and the continued advancement of defense cooperation between the two countries.

- Italy prepares naval mission, calls for more ships in Red Sea: Italy is preparing to deploy additional naval assets to the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandab amid concerns over merchant shipping, Al-Monitor reported.

- Italy, which participates in Aspides, the European Union’s naval mission to protect commercial shipping in the Red Sea, said Thursday it was preparing its own naval mission rather than waiting for a broader EU response. “After what I said, something moved within Aspides, but we need more ships,” Defense Minister Guido Crosetto told Reuters, adding that “the only nations really supporting [security efforts] are Italy and Greece.”

- Rome has not specified how many ships it could send or detailed the measures under consideration.

## Iran

- Iran strikes tanker in Hormuz: Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said it struck a Togo-flagged oil tanker in the Strait of Hormuz on Friday, according to the state broadcaster. The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations separately said a tanker had been hit by an unknown projectile in the strait, though it was unclear if it was referring to the same incident.

- Massive government rally in Tehran: Hundreds of thousands of Iranians rallied in Tehran on Friday in the biggest government-organized demonstration since the U.S. and Israel launched the war on Iran in February. The state broadcaster estimated over 300,000 people in the demonstration, which featured drones and weaponry on parade.

- Tens of thousands of Iranians who have registered with volunteer units, or who wish to sign up, joined the rally. Tehran’s Republican Guard chief, Gen. Hassan Hassanzadeh, told the state broadcaster that over 600,000 had registered to participate in the training.

- U.S. approves visas for Iranian president, foreign minister to attend UN General Assembly: The Trump administration approved visas for Iran’s “core delegation,” including President Masoud Pezeshkian and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, to attend next week’s UN General Assembly meetings in New York.

- The decision comes more than six months into the U.S.-Iran war, with negotiations over reopening the Strait of Hormuz and returning to nuclear talks remaining stalled.

- On Wednesday, the Trump administration denied visas to a high-level Palestinian delegation, including Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas, for the same UN General Assembly gathering, marking the second consecutive year Palestinian officials have been denied entry. The State Department cited, among other reasons, the Palestinian Authority’s pursuit of legal action against Israel at the International Court of Justice and International Criminal Court.

- The U.S. is barring Iranian officials attending the UN General Assembly from purchasing luxury goods or obtaining wholesale club memberships. “On one side stands a brutal economic war, deliberately designed to inflict maximum pain and suffering on every Iranian citizen,” Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei wrote on X, criticizing the measure. “On the other stands the theatrical announcement of measures to stop Iranian officials from supposedly shopping at an American wholesale club.”

- South Korea rules out involvement in Hormuz “conflict,” says “minimum level” of action needed to protect shipping: South Korean President Lee Jae Myung said Friday that Seoul will not deploy troops in a way that could involve the country in an overseas conflict, Yonhap reported.

- Lee said South Korea nevertheless needs to undertake a “minimum level of activities” to protect its citizens, vessels, and crude oil transportation routes. Seoul is reviewing ways to strengthen those measures, while its Cheonghae naval unit has expanded the scope of its activities in the region.

- Last week, a South Korean assessment team returned from the United Arab Emirates after reviewing security conditions in the region. U.S. President Donald Trump is pressing allies to contribute to securing freedom of navigation through the Strait.

- FT: Iran shifts trade overland as U.S. blockade disrupts Gulf routes: Iran is increasingly routing trade through its land borders, particularly Turkey, after the U.S. naval blockade and disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz curtailed maritime trade, the Financial Times reports.

- Before the war, more than 80% of Iran’s roughly 180 million tons of annual trade moved by sea from its Gulf coast. Iran’s non-oil exports fell 28% and imports 26% in the five months ending August 22 compared with last year.

- Trade with Turkey rose 19% to $3.2 billion in the first half of the year, while imports through the Gürbulak-Bazargan land crossing surged 250% in the five months to August 12.

- But long border delays and limited infrastructure mean even doubling overland and Caspian trade cannot replace lost maritime trade, experts told the FT. Moving Iran-China trade overland rather than by sea could also add an estimated $18 billion a year in costs.

- Iran-U.S. war and Hormuz disruption cost Arab economies nearly $150 billion in the first month, UN agency says: The ongoing conflict and disruption to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz caused losses equivalent to roughly 4% of Arab states’ combined GDP during the first month alone, according to the UN Economic and Social Commission for Western Asia (ESCWA).

- ESCWA Executive Secretary told a UN Security Council meeting on maritime security that the disruption is affecting far more than oil and gas, driving up freight and insurance costs, threatening food security, and weighing on investment across the region.

- Around 25% of global seaborne oil trade and 19% of LNG shipments have historically passed through Hormuz.

- U.S. sanctions on Iranian airlines threaten supply chain for essential medicines, researchers warn: The Trump administration’s latest sanctions on Iran’s aviation sector threaten the supply chain for essential medicines and medical supplies in Iran, Bourse & Bazaar Foundation researchers wrote.

- Over 60% of Iran’s medical imports arrive by air, making them roughly seven times more dependent on aviation than Iranian imports generally.

- Over 30% of medical imports through Tehran’s main airport are hormone-based medications, including insulin and cancer treatments, the report noted. Another 10% are vaccines and 6% blood products.

- U.S. offers up to $15 million for information on IRGC financial networks: The State Department’s Rewards for Justice program issued a new appeal for information about Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps’s (IRGC) alleged use of digital asset exchanges and other financial mechanisms to evade sanctions and access international financial systems. The reward offers up to $15 million for information leading to the disruption of the IRGC’s financial mechanisms.

- Amnesty: Iranian authorities committed crimes against humanity in 2022 protest crackdown: A new report by Amnesty International has found that Iranian authorities committed crimes against humanity during their suppression of the nationwide “Woman Life Freedom” uprising in 2022. The report, more than 1,000 pages long, details the use of “murder, torture, enforced disappearance, imprisonment, rape and persecution on political, gender, ethnic and religious grounds.” It also identifies 87 officials it says should be criminally investigated for crimes against humanity.

- “[Iranian authorities] waged a widespread and systematic attack against a civilian population demanding dignity, human rights and fundamental political change, pursuant to a state policy of using lethal force to obliterate dissent,” Agnès Callamard, Amnesty International’s Secretary General, said in a statement. “This report is being published at a time when people in Iran are also facing the devastating consequences of unlawful attacks by the USA and Israel. Amnesty International unequivocally opposes violations of international law by all parties and rejects any attempt to instrumentalize the suffering of victims of human rights violations in Iran to justify unlawful attacks that inflict further civilian harm.”

## Palestine

- Two women shot by Israeli forces in central Gaza:

- Two Palestinian women were wounded by Israeli gunfire toward residential homes and tents sheltering displaced Palestinians in the Nuseirat and Bureij refugee camps in Central Gaza on Friday, according to WAFA.

- Five children rescued from damaged home as Gaza government announces emergency plan for buildings at risk of collapse:

- Civil Defense crews rescued five children who became trapped on the second floor of their home after its staircase collapsed in the Sabra neighborhood, south of Gaza City. The families were evacuated and warned not to return to the house, which had been damaged by Israeli attacks and remains at risk of collapse.

- Two days ago, the collapse of another residential building in Gaza City killed 21 Palestinians, including 12 children and five women.

- The IDF responded to Drop Site on the collapse, saying “the IDF did not strike the building in question during the war.” The building, however, showed visible cracks and signs of damage from Israel’s assault on Gaza, which damaged 80% of structures across the Strip, including two-thirds that were destroyed, according to the UN.

- More than 2,000 damaged buildings across Gaza are at risk of collapse, according to Civil Defense. Gaza authorities and representatives from international, UN, and Arab organizations agreed Friday on an emergency plan to address hundreds of war-damaged buildings at risk of collapse across the Strip, according to Gaza’s Government Media Office. The meeting called for the immediate entry of heavy machinery, specialized equipment, fuel, and oil, as well as the allocation of land for shelters for residents living in unsafe buildings.

- Israeli settler attacks injure at least six Palestinians across the occupied West Bank:

- Hebron: Armed Israeli settlers, protected by Israeli forces, attacked Palestinian farmers trying to reach their land in Wadi Al-Shannar, east of Halhul, on Friday. The settlers assaulted and detained several farmers, according to WAFA.

- Ramallah: Five Palestinians were injured after Israeli settlers threw stones at their vehicle near the entrance to Yabroud, east of Ramallah, causing the vehicle to overturn.

- Jericho: A Palestinian was injured when Israeli settlers attacked families in Khirbet Allan, north of Jericho in the Jordan Valley. The settlers attempted to steal sheep, attacked residents with stones, and damaged a Palestinian-owned vehicle.

- East Jerusalem: Israeli forces beat a Palestinian man outside Lions’ Gate, one of the entrances to Al-Aqsa Mosque.

- Israel adds 2,167 units to E1 settlement plan, bringing total to 3,401: Israel added a tender for 2,167 housing units to its E1 settlement expansion plan in the occupied West Bank, Reuters reported, on top of 1,234 units announced in August.

- The E1 project would cut the occupied West Bank off from East Jerusalem and disrupt territorial contiguity between its northern and southern areas. Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich has said the plan would “bury” the idea of a Palestinian state.

- Bidding is scheduled to open October 25, two days before Israel’s parliamentary election.

- “The whole case is related to her journalistic work”: Palestinian-American journalist detained by Israel at Hasharon: Palestinian-American journalist and Drop Site contributor Naqaa Hamed is being held in Hasharon, a temporary detention facility in central Israel, and is expected to be transferred to Damon Prison, where most Palestinian female prisoners are held.

- Hamed’s lawyer told Drop Site she was accused of incitement against Israeli settlers and the army, communicating with the enemy, and cooperating with the enemy during a military court session on Thursday.

- Her lawyer argued that Hamed was a professional journalist and her arrest came solely because of a campaign targeting her by Israeli settlers. He told Drop Site “the whole case is related to her journalistic work.” The military court ruled to extend her detention by six days to complete their “investigation.” Mahajneh submitted an appeal.

- The Committee to Protect Journalists condemned Hamed’s detention, saying “Unsubstantiated espionage allegations must not be used to criminalize journalism, and the systemic harassment and intimidation targeting her work in the occupied West Bank must end.”

- Maryland Senator Chris Van Hollen called for her immediate release, saying in a post on X, “Another American citizen wrongfully detained by the Israeli govt.”

- Report: Israel kills one, wounds 15 on Thursday, total ceasefire violations reach 4,931: Israel committed 19 ceasefire violations in Gaza on Thursday, killing one Palestinian and wounding 15 others, bringing the total documented violations since the ceasefire took effect to 4,931, according to a document shared by the Palestinian side with mediators and obtained by Drop Site News.

- Since the ceasefire took effect, 1,387 Palestinians have been killed in Israeli attacks—including 297 children, 140 women, and 42 elderly people—and 4,784 wounded, nearly half of them children, women, or elderly.

- The World Health Organization estimates that Gaza’s health sector needs about 80,000 liters daily. At that rate, Qatar’s 1.3 million-liter grant would cover only about 16 days of healthcare operations. - Earlier this week, the Supreme Court rejected President Donald Trump’s bid to restrict mail ballots.

Elissa Slotkin, sent a letter demanding Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth provide a full breakdown by Sept. 30 of costs incurred in the Iran war and details on the administration’s $67 billion supplemental funding request.

reads.title: THE UNELECTED EMPEROR: VON DER LEYEN'S POWER GRAB AND THE DEMOCRATIC DEFICIT
reads.subtitle: She has no mandate. She was not elected by anyone. Yet she speaks for 450 million Europeans. Marco | Independent Analyst 18 September 2026
reads.body:
## Introduction
There is a question that European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has never been able to answer convincingly: who elected you?
She was not on any ballot. She did not campaign for the job. She was not the lead candidate of any European political family. In 2019, EU leaders bypassed the Spitzenkandidaten process—the system designed to give the Commission presidency democratic legitimacy—and nominated her in closed meetings. In 2024, she was re-elected by the European Parliament with 401 votes in favour and 284 against. A parliamentary vote, yes. But not a popular mandate.
Now, in 2026, von der Leyen is making decisions that would normally require the consent of elected heads of state and government. She is speaking on foreign policy, trade, and the future of the Union as if she were a sovereign leader. And the leaders who do have a mandate are watching their own legitimacy collapse.
This article examines three cases—Iran, Canada, and Mercosur—that expose a structural problem at the heart of the European Union: the Commission President is accumulating powers that no treaty grants her, while the democratic legitimacy of the entire system erodes.

## I. The Mandate Question
The European Commission President is not directly elected by European citizens. This is not an opinion. It is a fact of EU law.
Under the Treaty on European Union, the Commission President is proposed by the European Council—the heads of state and government of the 27 member states—and then elected by the European Parliament. The Spitzenkandidaten system, introduced in 2014, was supposed to link the Commission presidency to the European Parliament elections. But it was abandoned in 2019 when von der Leyen was nominated.
How von der Leyen Got the Job2019Nominated by the European Council in closed meetings, bypassing Spitzenkandidaten2019Elected by the European Parliament (vote not disclosed publicly)2024Re-elected by the European Parliament: 401 in favour, 284 againstDirect popular voteNone
As one analysis put it: “Von der Leyen has no democratic mandate. She is not elected. She was nominated to her current position in closed meetings of bureaucrats. She represents no population.”
This is the foundation on which everything else rests. When von der Leyen acts unilaterally, she is not just overstepping her role—she is doing so without the democratic legitimacy that would justify such action.

## II. Iran: The First Overreach
The war in Iran, which began in late February 2026, exposed the problem in real time.
Within days of the US-Israeli campaign, von der Leyen positioned herself as the EU’s chief diplomatic voice. She signalled support for regime change in Tehran—a position that went far beyond the consensus of member states. She held no fewer than a dozen calls with EU and Gulf leaders. She spoke as if she were the EU’s head of state.
The reaction from European diplomats was swift and brutal.
Nine diplomats, EU officials, and lawmakers from both small and large European countries told POLITICO that von der Leyen had gone beyond her mandate. One senior EU diplomat put it bluntly: “She is saying things that are not in her mandate.”
Nathalie Loiseau, a centrist French lawmaker on the European Parliament’s Foreign Affairs Committee, said: “I felt I was hallucinating… watching Ursula von der Leyen call the heads of Gulf states. She has no diplomatic service, speaks without a mandate or intelligence briefings. Her words have no value beyond her individual statement.”
Another diplomat added: “The problem is the president going out with ideas and somehow committing the European Union without consulting countries beforehand.”
The formal EU position on the Iran war was not set out by von der Leyen. It was defined by Kaja Kallas, the High Representative for Foreign Affairs, in a statement coordinated with all 27 member states. The Commission’s own spokesperson confirmed this. Yet von der Leyen spoke first, and louder.
Gérard Araud, former French Ambassador to the United States, was even more direct. He told Euronews that von der Leyen was “acting outside of competence” and pointed out that “the European Union treaties, which form the basis of the EU, do not give it any particular competence in foreign policy.”
Von der Leyen on Iran — Key FactsPosition takenSupport for regime changeConsultation with member statesNone documentedCalls with Gulf leaders“No fewer than a dozen”Formal EU positionDefined by Kaja Kallas, not von der LeyenReactionDiplomats from nine countries accused her of overreachTreaty basisNone — foreign policy is a member state competence

## III. Canada: The Invention of a Power
On 16 September 2026, during her State of the Union address, von der Leyen announced that the EU would explore “associate membership” for Canada.
She said: “I would like to work with you on opening the door for Canada to be the first associate member of the EU.”
There is just one problem: “Associate member” does not exist in the EU Treaties. No such category is provided for. Article 49 of the Treaty on European Union states that only a “European State” may apply for membership. Canada is not a European state.
The reaction from member states was one of surprise and concern. Three diplomats told POLITICO that national capitals were “caught off guard” and had never been asked to sign off on the idea before the speech. One diplomat said: “Nobody really knows what it means.” Another added: “Member states have tried to manage expectations. There are only warm feelings for Ottawa, but we need to know what the details are.”
A third diplomat was even more blunt: any associate membership status would require changes to the EU’s fundamental treaties—which is “impossible” due to a lack of support.
Granting membership to the EU is a responsibility of the European Council, not the Commission President. Von der Leyen announced the initiative without consulting either the Council or the European Parliament. She invented a new category of membership on live television, before the 27 governments she is supposed to serve had any chance to discuss it.
Manon Aubry, a Left MEP, asked the question that no one in the Commission has been able to answer: “Who gave you a democratic and popular mandate for that?”
Von der Leyen on Canada — Key FactsAnnouncementState of the Union, 16 September 2026Proposal“Associate membership” for CanadaLegal basisNone — the category does not exist in EU lawConsultation with member statesNone — capitals were “caught off guard”Consultation with CouncilNoneTreaty change requiredYes — considered “impossible”ReactionMEP Manon Aubry: “Who gave you the mandate?”

## IV. Mercosur: The Precedent
The Canada case is not an isolated incident. It is the continuation of a pattern that began with Mercosur.
In February 2026, von der Leyen announced that the EU would provisionally apply its trade agreement with the South American Mercosur bloc—before the European Parliament had voted on it. France, which had ardently opposed the deal, was furious. One EU diplomat said: “Von der Leyen went further than any Commission president before in the interpretation of her mandate.”
The Left group in the European Parliament submitted a motion of censure against the entire Commission, citing its “detrimental trade deals with no democratic mandate” and accusing von der Leyen of having “forced through destructive trade deals such as Mercosur without a democratic mandate.”
The pattern is clear:

- Iran — Von der Leyen spoke on foreign policy without a mandate, going beyond the consensus of member states.

- Mercosur — Von der Leyen provisionally applied a trade deal before the European Parliament voted on it.

- Canada — Von der Leyen invented a new category of membership without consulting anyone.
In each case, she acted as if the Commission President has the authority of a head of state. In each case, the treaties say otherwise.
The Pattern of Unilateral ActionIran (March 2026)Spoke on foreign policy without mandate; criticised by 9 countriesMercosur (February 2026)Applied trade deal before Parliament vote; motion of censure filedCanada (September 2026)Invented “associate membership”; capitals caught off guard

## V. The Leaders Who Do Have a Mandate
Here is the uncomfortable reality: the leaders who do have a democratic mandate are watching their own legitimacy collapse.

## Friedrich Merz (Germany)
Merz became Chancellor in May 2025. He was elected by the Bundestag, not by popular vote—but his coalition government commands a parliamentary majority. He has a mandate, however indirect.
His approval ratings are catastrophic. According to an INSA poll for Bild published on 12 September 2026, 78% of Germans say Merz is not the right person to be Chancellor. Only 14% say yes. Among his own CDU voters, 58% say he is not suitable.
Friedrich Merz — ApprovalSatisfied14%Not the right Chancellor78%CDU/CSU voters: not suitable58%SourceINSA / Bild, 12 September 2026

## Emmanuel Macron (France)
Macron was elected twice by popular vote. He has the strongest democratic mandate of any leader in Europe.
His approval rating has hit a historic low. According to an Ipsos BVA-CESI poll published on 12 September 2026, only 16% of French people have a favourable opinion of Macron—down five points from July. 81% hold a negative view.
Emmanuel Macron — ApprovalFavourable opinion16%Unfavourable opinion81%Change from July 2026-5 pointsSourceIpsos BVA-CESI, 12 September 2026

## The Contrast
LeaderMandateApprovalEmmanuel MacronElected twice by popular vote16% favourableFriedrich MerzElected by Bundestag majority14% satisfiedUrsula von der LeyenNominated in closed meetings; parliamentary vote onlyNo direct mandate
The leaders who were elected by voters are deeply unpopular. The leader who was never elected by anyone is making decisions for all of them.

## VI. What Von der Leyen’s Approval Numbers Actually Show
Unlike Merz and Macron, von der Leyen has no national approval rating. She is not accountable to a national electorate. But polling data does exist, and it reveals something deeper than unpopularity: many Europeans do not even know who she is.
A POLITICO poll conducted by Public First across Germany, France, and Spain in September 2026 found:

- Germany: ~20% say she is doing a good job; 45% say she is doing a bad job

- France: Only 12% say she is doing a good job; nearly one-third say she is doing a bad job

- Spain: ~20% say she is doing a good job; nearly one-third say she is doing a bad job

- France: More than one in five respondents did not know who von der Leyen was

- Spain: 10% did not know who she was

- Germany: 5% did not know who she was
These are the numbers of a leader without a mandate. She is not unpopular in the way Merz and Macron are unpopular. She is unknown. And an unknown leader with unchecked power is not a recipe for democratic accountability.
Von der Leyen — Polling (Sept 2026)Germany — good job~20%Germany — bad job45%France — good job12%France — don’t know who she is1 in 5Spain — don’t know who she is10%SourcePOLITICO / Public First, 16 September 2026

## VII. The Treaty Problem
The pattern of unilateral action is not just a matter of political style. It is a question of legality.
Under Article 24(1) of the Treaty on European Union, the Commission has no power of initiative or negotiating mandate in the field of the Common Foreign and Security Policy. Foreign policy is the exclusive competence of the Council. Von der Leyen has no treaty authority to speak on Iran, negotiate with Gulf leaders, or promise Ukraine’s accession to the EU.
Under Article 49 TEU, only a “European State” may apply for EU membership. Canada is not a European state. There is no legal basis for “associate membership.” Von der Leyen invented it.
On trade, the Commission does have a mandate. But the provisional application of the Mercosur agreement—before the European Parliament voted—was widely seen as a democratic bypass. A motion of censure was filed against the entire Commission.
The Commission’s own spokesperson defended von der Leyen by saying she was demonstrating “political leadership of the Commission’s external policies” in line with EU treaties. But when asked for the specific treaty article that authorises her actions on Iran or Canada, the Commission has not provided one.

## VIII. Conclusion
The European Union is facing a structural crisis of legitimacy. And von der Leyen’s power grab is both a symptom and a cause.
The symptom is this: the leaders who were elected by voters—Macron, Merz—are deeply unpopular. Their mandates are eroding. The centre cannot hold. In that vacuum, the Commission President steps in.
The cause is this: von der Leyen is accumulating powers that no treaty grants her. She speaks on foreign policy without a mandate. She invents new categories of membership without consulting member states. She applies trade deals before parliaments vote on them. And she does all of this without ever having faced a single European voter.
The question is not whether von der Leyen is personally popular—she is not. The question is whether the European Union can function when its most powerful official has no democratic mandate, and the officials who do have mandates are too weak to stop her.
When MEP Manon Aubry asked von der Leyen “Who gave you a democratic and popular mandate for that?”—the Commission President did not answer. She could not. Because the answer is: nobody.
And that is the problem.

reads.title: THE UNSEEN HAND: MEDIA CONTROL IN EUROPE
reads.subtitle: SUBTITLE: How Brussels Funds Narratives, Suppresses Dissent, and Manages the Information Space DATE: September 18, 2026
reads.body:
INTRODUCTION
The European Union presents itself as the global guardian of press freedom. Every year, Brussels publishes reports denouncing media concentration in third countries, political pressure on journalists, and information manipulation. Yet a closer examination of the EU’s internal practices reveals a different reality: an increasingly sophisticated system of conditional funding, unchecked mergers, regulatory pressure, and coordinated narratives. This is not censorship in the classic sense. It is something subtler, harder to contest, and therefore more effective.
This dossier (#89) is not based on theories. It is based on official EU documents, Court of Justice rulings, Media Pluralism Monitor reports, budget data, and public statements. The facts are verifiable. The conclusions are uncomfortable.
1. THE MONEY — FUNDING THE NARRATIVE
The most direct mechanism of control is financial. In 2026, the European Commission proposed a budget of approximately €8.6 billion for the cultural and creative sector as part of the new AgoraEU program — double the current funds. This program merges the previous CreativeEurope and CERV (Citizens, Equality, Rights and Values), and — crucially — the “media” component applies to both cinema and news.
The question is simple: who decides which “news” deserves funding? The answer is equally simple: those who control the funds.
In 2026, the Commission allocated €7.4 million to three European newsrooms for coverage of European affairs. The beneficiaries include consortia coordinated by Arte, OKO.press, and AFP. It is no coincidence that these organizations are historically aligned with Brussels’ positions on integration, foreign policy, and migration. A report by MCC Brussels, cited by journalist Marius Tucă, estimates that the EU has spent at least €80 million to promote pro-European messages in mainstream media, with the total figure potentially approaching €1 billion.
National Review described it precisely: a “slush fund” financed by taxpayers for NGOs and media that promote “rights” and “EU values.” And among the funded projects, one of the most significant was to “provide technical, content-related, and organizational support to prevent hate speech, especially online.” Translated: funding speech moderation.
2. OWNERSHIP — THE INFORMATION OLIGARCHS
While Brussels funds “friendly” media, ownership of Europe’s major media groups is concentrating into ever fewer hands. The Media Pluralism Monitor 2026 identified media concentration as the highest risk to pluralism in Europe. The indicators “Plurality of media providers” and “Plurality in digital markets” top the list of problems.
In France, eleven billionaires control nearly 80% of the national press. Bernard Arnault, Europe’s richest man with an estimated fortune of $145 billion, has progressively extended his empire from luxury goods to media, adding influential weeklies to his portfolio. Vincent Bolloré, Rodolphe Saadé, and other magnates are all competing to influence the media and political landscape ahead of the 2027 presidential election.
In Spain, Atresmedia and Mediaset España control over 80% of the national advertising market.
In Italy, the government is believed to influence 93% of the radio market, 52% of evening newscasts, 48% of national newspapers, and 100% of regional newspapers.
This is not an exclusively European dynamic. But in Europe it takes on particular significance, because it occurs under the supervision of an institution that presents itself as the guarantor of plurality. The European Media Freedom Act (EMFA), which entered into force in August 2025, provides for a “media pluralism test” (Article 22) that should assess mergers based on their impact on plurality, not just economic criteria. As of June 2026, only 4 countries had national rules compliant with this article. In most cases (16 countries), mergers are still assessed only with economic competition criteria. The EMFA is, in practice, a dead letter.
3. THE LAW — CENSORSHIP BY REGULATION
The Digital Services Act (DSA) is the most powerful tool in the Commission’s hands. Officially, it protects users by guaranteeing them explanations, appeals, and redress when content is removed. In practice, according to a U.S. congressional report cited in a European parliamentary question, the Commission has met with digital platforms to limit political speech in the days before at least eight elections in six member states since 2023.
A European Parliament resolution motion from February 2026 states that the Commission has systematically used regulatory pressure under the DSA to influence the moderation of political content by major online platforms. The text concludes that applying the DSA to political content during elections violates Article 10 of the European Convention on Human Rights (freedom of expression).
To this is added the European Democracy Shield, an initiative signed by 32 European countries in November 2025, which extends moderation mechanisms to artificial intelligence and the media. According to MEP Catherine Griset, the project “could once again result in censorship of opposition media and social media, and in the use of European taxpayers’ money to fund media and ‘trusted flaggers’.”
4. RESISTANCE — THOSE WHO DO NOT ALIGN
Media control is not uniform. In Hungary, the EU Court of Justice ruled in February 2026 that the government violated European law by revoking the license of independent radio Klubrádió for minor issues. The ruling is a recognition that pressure on independent media exists — but it is also an exception. In the Czech Republic, the government has been accused of non-compliance with the EMFA, with the Director General of Czech Radio publicly criticizing the draft budget.
In Germany, the situation is more complex. The AfD has denounced what it calls “state censorship” through the media regulatory authorities of the Länder. In July 2026, the Landesmedienanstalt NRW was accused of censorship attempts against critical media. The podcast “Ungeskriptet” was hit with measures after an interview with Björn Höcke, with the podcaster explicitly speaking of “censorship.” Julian Reichelt’s portal Nius has sued against a similar measure by the Berlin-Brandenburg authority.
At the same time, German intelligence services have intensified surveillance of the AfD ahead of the elections in Saxony-Anhalt, according to reports from Belarusian and Arab sources. In Saxony-Anhalt, the AfD has threatened to withdraw from the public broadcaster MDR, opening a direct confrontation over the funding and control of public media.
5. THE KASPAROV CASE — WAR NARRATIVE AS MAINSTREAM
While European media moderate internal political discourse, voices calling for the destruction of sovereign states find ample space in mainstream outlets. On September 10, 2026, The Telegraph published a column by Garry Kasparov titled “Five devastating blows that can finally defeat Putin’s Russia.” Kasparov’s thesis is that “nothing short of the destruction of the Russian state in its current form will be sufficient to protect the continued peace and prosperity of the West.”
This is not a marginal opinion. It is published in one of the most influential newspapers in the United Kingdom, picked up by dozens of international outlets, and presented as strategic analysis. The message is clear: coexistence with Russia in its current form is impossible. The war must continue until the dissolution of the adversary state.
There is no censorship on this. No moderation. No “hate speech prevention.” There is only one narrative — the war narrative, Atlanticist, anti-Russian — that enjoys unlimited access to the European media space.
6. THE CONFIDENCE CRISIS — THE NUMBERS
The result of this system is an unprecedented crisis of trust. The European Council on Foreign Relations (ECFR) and the European Cultural Foundation conducted 5,834 interviews in six countries (France, Germany, Italy, Poland, the Netherlands, United Kingdom) between April and May 2026. The result is devastating: nearly 70% of respondents rate the EU negatively and speak of “general deterioration” or “loss of normality.” Only 12% see signs of a “European awakening.” 74% believe Europe is not handling its main challenges well.
The study, published on September 8 by Paweł Zerka, concludes that the problem is not that Europeans do not want a stronger Europe. The problem is that they no longer believe it is possible to achieve one. The “discrepancy between imagination and reality,” as Zerka puts it, is the exact measure of the European project’s failure.
CONCLUSION
Media control in Europe is not a conspiracy. It is a documented strategy, implemented through conditional funding, unchecked mergers, selective regulation, and coordinated narratives. Media that align receive funds. Those that do not face regulatory obstacles, lawsuits, surveillance, and isolation. Voices calling for the destruction of sovereign states find space on front pages. Those calling for peace are labeled “disinformation.”
The question is not whether this system exists. The question is: how long will European citizens continue to believe their media are free?
The ECFR numbers suggest the answer is: not much longer.

- National Review — The EU and Propaganda, July 20, 2026

- European Commission — AgoraEU program, 2026 budget

- Reuters — Bolloré’s Lagardère buying stake in hard-right media firm, September 4, 2026

reads.body:
Hey all!
Nicholas from the Unusual Whales team, here! This week is a bit of an extension of last week’s issue on advanced options strategies. This time, we’re covering some VERY high risk strategies (risk of ruin), and should not be attempted by inexperienced traders. I want to preface as well that the strikes utilized in this write-up were chosen for simplicity for explanation; NOT to represent a suggestion for a trade anyone should take.
With that said, let’s dive on in.

## The Short Straddle
A trader who wants to speculate on a decrease in volatility and relatively little movement in AAPL can sell a Short Straddle. The trader receives a credit, or premium, for selling both a Put and a Call at the same strike price and expiration. The short Put carries the obligation to buy 100 shares at the strike price if assigned, while the short Call carries the obligation to sell 100 shares at the strike price if assigned.
You sell an AAPL $335 Short Straddle expiring September 28, 2026, selling the $335 Call for approximately a $5.80 credit and selling the $335 Put for approximately a $4.62 credit, receiving a total net credit of approximately $10.42 per share, or $1,042.40, to express this view. Your two breakeven prices at expiry are approximately $324.58 on the downside ($335 - $10.42) and $345.42 on the upside ($335 + $10.42).

-
- The maximum profit at expiry is approximately $1,042.40, which occurs if AAPL finishes exactly at the $335 strike price, allowing both options to expire worthless. Since the time component of your trade plan may not extend all the way to expiration, you should be prepared to buy to close at a variety of AAPL prices as the market value of your $335 Short Straddle changes.
Because AAPL can theoretically rise without limit, the short Call creates unlimited upside loss potential. The downside risk is also substantial, though technically limited because AAPL cannot fall below $0. Selling a Straddle therefore carries a high risk of ruin, as a large adverse move in either direction, such as an unexpected earnings result, major news event, or acquisition announcement, can result in very large losses.

## The Short Strangle
A trader who wants to speculate on a decrease in volatility and a relatively neutral AAPL price can sell a Short Strangle. The trader receives a credit, or premium, for selling both the Put and the Call. The short Put carries the obligation to buy 100 shares at the Put strike price if assigned, while the short Call carries the obligation to sell 100 shares at the Call strike price if assigned.
You sell an AAPL $327.50 / $342.50 Short Strangle expiring September 28, 2026, selling the $327.50 Put for approximately a $2.05 credit and selling the $342.50 Call for approximately a $2.55 credit, receiving a total net credit of approximately $4.60 per share, or $460.40, to express this view. Your breakeven prices at expiry are approximately $322.90 on the downside ($327.50 - $4.60) and $347.10 on the upside ($342.50 + $4.60).

-
- The maximum profit at expiry is $460.40, which occurs if AAPL finishes between $327.50 and $342.50, allowing both options to expire worthless. Since the time component of your trade plan may not extend all the way to expiration, however, you should be prepared to buy to close at a variety of AAPL prices as the market value of your $327.50 / $342.50 Short Strangle changes.
Because AAPL can theoretically rise without limit, the short Call creates unlimited upside loss potential. The downside risk is also substantial, though technically limited because AAPL cannot fall below $0. A sharp adverse move, such as an unexpected earnings result, major news event, or acquisition announcement, can therefore result in very large losses. The fixed-risk version of a Short Strangle is a Short Iron Condor.

## The Synthetic Short
A trader who wants to speculate on decreasing price and increasing volatility can open a Synthetic Short. The trader may pay a small debit, receive a small credit, or open the trade for exactly $0.
Suppose stock XYZ is trading at $25.50. You forecast a decrease in price and an increase in volatility.
You open a $25 Synthetic Short at exactly $0.00, no cost, to express this view. How is this possible? The $25 Call bid price is $3.00 and the $25 Put ask price is also $3.00, so when you sell the $25 Call you receive exactly $3.00 and you use that credit to pay for the $25 Put.

-
- The breakeven price for this trade is the exact price of the underlying when you entered since this structure behaves almost exactly like shorting 100 shares of XYZ: theta, vega, and gamma are all roughly zero and delta is roughly -100.
The max loss on this position at expiry is theoretically unlimited, since XYZ price can increase indefinitely. The max gain of a Synthetic Short is large but theoretically capped, since XYZ price can only decrease to $0. Since the loss on a Synthetic Short is theoretically unlimited, this structure carries a high “risk of ruin”. The unlimited loss can be mitigated by buying a further OTM Call, which caps upside losses but makes the position more expensive to open (i.e. the debit becomes larger) and removes some of the similarities to shorting 100 shares: theta becomes negative, vega and gamma become positive, and delta drops below -100.

## The Synthetic Long
A trader who wants to speculate on increasing price and increasing volatility can open a Synthetic Long. The trader may pay a small debit, receive a small credit, or open the trade for exactly $0.
Suppose stock XYZ is trading at $27. You forecast an increase in price and an increase in volatility.
You open a $27 Synthetic Long at exactly $0.00, no cost, to express this view. How is this possible? The $27 Put bid price is $3.25 and the $27 Call ask price is also $3.25, so when you sell the $27 Put you receive exactly $3.25 and you use that credit to pay for the $27 Call.

-
- The breakeven price for this trade is the exact price of the underlying when you entered since this structure behaves almost exactly like owning 100 shares of XYZ: theta, vega, and gamma are all roughly zero and delta is roughly +100.
The max loss on this position at expiry is theoretically very high but capped, since XYZ price can only decrease to zero. The max gain of a Synthetic Long is theoretically unlimited, since XYZ price can increase indefinitely. Since the loss on a Synthetic Long is theoretically very high (but not technically unlimited), this structure carries a high “risk of ruin”. The unlimited loss can be mitigated by buying a further OTM Put, which caps downside losses but makes the position more expensive to open (i.e. the debit becomes larger) and removes some of the similarities to owning 100 shares: theta becomes negative, vega and gamma become positive, and delta drops below +100.
Hopefully these strategy breakdowns are helpful! Again, the above strategies have significantly higher risk than some of those we’ve looked at in the past, and definitely aren’t for use by beginners!
Thank you as always for reading! Happy trading, and stay safe out there during all this headline risk!
NOTE: This post is not financial advice. The stock market is risky, and any trade or investment is expected to have some, or total, loss. Please do research before any trade. Do not use this information for investment decisions. Check terms on site for full terms. Agree to terms before considering this information.

reads.title: Many of the “Michigan Jewish Dems” Backing Mike Rogers Are Actually Already Republican Supporters, Analysis Finds
reads.subtitle: A close look at the signatories reveals many have been involved in past GOP efforts—including “Jews For Mitt” in 2012.
reads.body:
- Michigan Republican Senate candidate at the 2026 Republican National Convention at the American Airlines Center on September 10, 2026 in Dallas, Texas. Photo by Alex Wong/Getty Images.Story by Tom Perkins
Over 400 alleged Michigan Jewish Democratic and independent voters signed a pledge in late August to vote for Republican U.S. Senate candidate Mike Rogers, igniting a controversy and generating questions about whether Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed was losing critical support among a group that typically votes blue by about a 2:1 ratio.
But a Drop Site review of signatories in the “Michigan Jews Against Extremism” campaign finds many of the Jewish community leaders involved have deep ties to the GOP, as well as to pro-Israel activist groups such as AIPAC. Nearly 50 were involved in a nearly identical gambit in 2012 that went by the name “Jews for Mitt.” Then-President Barack Obama, the group argued, was so “anti-Israel” that their consciences drove them to abandon the Democratic Party to support Republican nominee Mitt Romney.
Among those who signed both the Romney and Rogers pledges are six members of the Schostaks, a politically powerful family behind a major Michigan development company. Bobby Schostak, the former head of the Michigan Republican Party, signed the Jews For Mitt pledge, but this time did not pretend to be a Democrat—he now serves as the Rogers campaign’s finance chair.
Dozens of signatories either work with the GOP, have served in office as Republicans, have run as Republicans, or donate to right-wing candidates, including Donald Trump.
The operation, however, has been extraordinarily effective, garnering enormous media attention, which frames the group as genuine Democrats who were finally pushed over the edge by El-Sayed.
Taken together, nearly 90% of the first 430 signatories are either connected to pro-Israel activist groups, GOP aligned, Jews for Mitt voters, or may not live in Michigan.
Drop Site is supported by readers. Make a gift or subscribe for free:
The Michigan Jews campaign appears to be an “astroturf operation” led by AIPAC and other Republican-affiliated activists, said Jess Newman, a former special assistant for AIPAC’s vice CEO. She now works with the Democratic Socialists of America.
Many of the top signatories are well-known Jewish community leaders, Newman added, and the campaign seeks to “create a permission structure to vote for Rogers” for less politically active Democratic Jews who do not know that most of these leaders are connected to Republicans, or are Republicans.
“They are using this brazen tactic because they know that people aren’t going to look deeply into it, and some Jewish voters will say ‘Oh, I recognize a few names on this list so I can find a way to hold my nose and vote for the Republican,” Newman said. “The implication is that this is a list of Democrats who otherwise would vote for Democrats, had a red line not been crossed.”
The campaign’s website states, “Many of us have been fiercely supportive of Democratic candidates and principles.” But FEC records show many signatories have donated to GOP candidates, including Trump, Rick Snyder, Kelly Loeffler, Marco Rubio, Mike Lee, Rick Santorum, the Republican National Congressional Committee, and PACs that support a wide range of Republican candidates, including GOP Michigan House Leader Matt Hall.
Among the signatories are current and former leadership for AIPAC, as well as groups that have led the charge against pro-Palestinian advocates in Michigan and nationally, including the Jewish Federation, Hillel, and Anti-Defamation League.
Drop Site did not include in its 90% figure people who simply are connected with a Jewish communal group, or a synagogue not involved in Israel activism. However, it did include those in leadership at synagogues Adot Shalom and Shaarey Zedek, which openly work with AIPAC, support the IDF, and make pro-Israel activism a central component of their mission.
The list’s first signer is Adam Kaplan, a Hillel donor, AIPAC donor, former Jewish Federation committee member, and an appointee in the administration of Republican former Michigan Gov. Rick Snyder.
Some signatories have run for office as Republicans, including Bubba Urdan, a West Bloomfield resident who ran for the GOP nomination in the Michigan state house, and has served on Jewish Federation boards. Urdan did not respond to a request for comment.
A spokesperson for Michigan Jews Against Extremism said the letter “was not organized by AIPAC or in coordination with it or any other organization.” She did not address questions about the Republican ties.
The signatories’ AIPAC-GOP connections run deep. Among them is David Handelman, a Mitch McConnell donor and former AIPAC Michigan president who once organized a Detroit pro-Israel event with the 2002 Iraq War architect and diplomat John Bolton as the featured speaker.
Former AIPAC national president David Victor still sits on its national board, and donated to Mike Rogers in 2010. He also donated to John McCain and GOP Ohio Congress members John Boehner and Rob Portman, as well as many Democrats.
Max Newman is a metro Detroit attorney and AIPAC activist who also works with Hillel. Campaign finance records show he donated to Rogers multiple times in the aughts, Rudy Giuliani, the National Republican Congressional Committee and many Democrats.
Joshua Opperer is the executive director of AIPAC’s National New Leaders Network and Jewish Federation of Detroit’s executive committee recently donated $10,000 to AIPAC, and published a Substack article titled, “Fireworks in Rafah,” that includes a picture of Israeli soldiers celebrating Israel’s independence day by lighting off fireworks in Rafah. He has donated to several Republicans, as well as Democrats.
The 2012 Jews For Mitt ad declares “We are Michigan Jews. Four years ago many of us voted for Barack Obama. Today we are voting for Mitt Romney.” The ad alleges Obama had “anti-Israel policies,” and claims Mitt Romney would “aggressively combat Muslim extremism” and “fortify America’s crucial relationship with Israel.”
Among the 49 people who are a part of both campaigns are the Schostacks, Urdan, Max Newman, Victor, and Handelman, who are all Republicans or have donated to Republicans. It includes many other AIPAC activists, like Margo Woll.
“They are dusting off their old strategy of trying to create a grass-tops campaign that makes it look like Jewish people in general are not going to vote for the Democratic nominee,” said former Democrat Congress member Andy Levin, who was defeated in a 2022 election bid by the AIPAC-backed Haley Stevens in a metro Detroit district. Only about one-third of Michigan Jews are Republicans, and Levin said he believes most Jews will still vote for El-Sayed.
The campaign spokesperson told Drop Site, “For some signatories, our concern is much more personal: as Jews we do not feel safe when political rhetoric minimizes antisemitism, excuses or contextualizes violence against Jews, or embraces an agenda we believe is hostile to our community, our safety and our children’s safety.”
 “We are speaking for ourselves, exercising our right as Michigan voters, and asking to be heard without being reduced to a political label.”
Among those who do not appear to live in Michigan is Hannan Lis, who told Detroit ABC affiliate WXYZ in March that he moved to Israel several years ago to be closer to his grandkids, and who has been described as an “Israeli citizen” in older media reports. He was part of the Jewish Federation’s board of governors and the AIPAC National Council. Lis told Drop Site he is a dual citizen who splits time between Israel and Michigan. He is registered to vote in Michigan.
“The key question here is ‘Who speaks for the Jews and who are the Jews?’” said Levin, a former Michigan synagogue president.
“This idea that these right wing-on-Israel groups are the Jewish people or they represent the Jewish people is just demonstrably false,” Levin added. He said there is an intense organizing effort in Michigan’s Jewish community for El-Sayed, but the media and the vast amount of attention goes to a statistically small number of voters who are pledging to cast a ballot for Rogers.
Levin’s father, former Rep. Sandy Levin, 95, who served as the powerful chair of the House Ways and Means Committee, made an unusual foray back into politics to endorse El-Sayed this week.  On Wednesday, a list of over 600 Michigan Jews pledging to support El-Sayed was released.
Jewish voters make up about 1% of Michigan’s electorate, and right-wing Jewish voters may represent as little as .3% of voters statewide. The number of Democrats who may switch is even more miniscule within the context of the state’s electorate. That raises questions about the outsize media attention to this tiny group of voters, Levin said.
Some on the list, and some Jewish Democrats, genuinely may not be able to vote for El-Sayed, Jess Newman said. She added that the campaign is “preying on latent Islamophobia.”
“It’s about depressing voter turnout for El-Sayed and getting people on the margins, and if they have to lie to get there, then they will,” Newman added.
