reads.title: UN experts cite possible U.S. war crimes in Iran strikes; Fed hikes interest rates for first time in 3 years; OpenAI flags “concerning” AI behavior
reads.subtitle: Drop Site Daily: September 17, 2026
reads.body:
- The icon for the AI app ChatGPT by OpenAI is highlighted alongside other rival products on the screen of a tablet device on September 16, 2026. Photo illustration by Leon Neal/Getty Images.Thursday, September 17, 2026 – Saudi-led coalition strikes Yemen as fighting intensifies near Bab al-Mandab. AP: Saudi Arabia running low on missile interceptors, seeks foreign air-defense support. Bloomberg: Saudi Arabia seeks to restore half of East-West oil pipeline capacity “within days.” Trump claims U.S. “towards the end” of Iran war; Tehran says it does not trust Washington. U.S.-contracted vessel carrying American personnel struck in Iranian attack near Strait of Hormuz, Fox News reports. Global oil market short 5 million barrels a day as China’s crude prices hit record high. UN inquiry finds grounds to believe U.S. committed war crimes in Iran strikes that killed at least 178 civilians. Israeli forces carry out demolitions and raids across occupied West Bank. Toll of Gaza’s Israeli-damaged building collapse rises to 21 killed and 45 wounded. 21-year-old Palestinian prisoner dies in Ofer prison. Gaza Health Ministry: Israel cuts approved medical evacuations from 136 to 61. Israel extends detention of journalist Naqaa Hamed for six days. U.S. extends visa restrictions barring Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas from UN General Assembly; Palestinian FM calls decision “Unjustified.” Israel and Morocco expand diplomatic ties. Ireland withdraws from Eurovision 2027 over Gaza. Israeli attacks continue across southern Lebanon despite ceasefire; bodies of two young men recovered. Lebanese President Joseph Aoun, French President Emmanuel Macron, and Jordan’s King Abdullah II meet in Paris to discuss support for Lebanese army. Federal Reserve raises interest rates. Democrat puts hold on Trump plan to sell more bombs to Israel. House recesses early to avoid vote on War Secretary Pete Hegseth impeachment. Top general says U.S. must be prepared to fight on moon. OpenAI discloses new AI transgressions. U.S. raids vessels in Eastern Pacific. Russian missile and drone barrages hit Kyiv, Odessa, and Zaporizhzhia. North Korea says U.S.-led military buildup justifies expanding nuclear arsenal. Russia says new U.S. sanctions will undermine peace efforts. Japanese PM reshuffles cabinet amid economic crisis. Scientists say climate change likely helped trigger catastrophic Nepal glacier collapse. Argentine judge orders halt to Falklands oil project as sovereignty dispute intensifies. U.S. drone maker with ties to Trump family signs Pakistan Army deal.
This is Drop Site Daily, our free news recap We send it Monday – Friday

## Yemen

- Saudi-led coalition strikes Yemen as fighting intensifies near Bab al-Mandab: Saudi-led coalition warplanes struck three telecommunications towers in Yemen’s Taiz province, damaging homes and injuring two, according to Ansarallah-run Al-Masirah. Two coalition strikes also hit Abs in Hajjah province, killing one person, wounding another, destroying four vehicles, and damaging a house, the outlet reported.

- Meanwhile, fighting continued around the strategic Kahbub mountains overlooking the Bab al-Mandab Strait and Mayyun Island. Yemeni Saudi-backed forces claimed they repelled Ansarallah infiltration attempts, including on the Al-Mudaraba front, with support from the UAE-backed Southern Giants Brigades, Al Jazeera reported.

- AP: Saudi Arabia running low on missile interceptors, seeks foreign air-defense support: Saudi Arabia is running low on missile interceptors and has asked France, Britain, Pakistan, and Egypt to deploy air-defense support against Ansarallah missiles and drones, two regional officials told the Associated Press.

- One official said Riyadh sought assistance because the United States, its main arms supplier, has also seen its interceptor stockpiles dwindle during the six-month war with Iran.

- CENTCOM told Al Jazeera it was “closely monitoring” the Saudi-Ansarallah conflict and pointed to its longstanding military relationship with Riyadh.

- Bloomberg: Saudi Arabia seeks to restore half of East-West oil pipeline capacity “within days”: Saudi Arabia is seeking to restore roughly half the capacity of its East-West oil pipeline “within days,” Bloomberg reported. No firmer timetable was provided.

- Half of the pipeline’s 7 million-barrel-per-day capacity would be about 3.5 million barrels per day.

- AP previously reported that damage to a major pumping facility could take three to five weeks to repair, although partial operations could resume during that period.

- Bloomberg’s report suggests substantial flows may return well before full repairs are completed, easing fears that export stocks at Yanbu would run dry which Reuters said had only 5-7 days of stored crude.

## Iran

- Trump claim U.S. “towards the end” of Iran war; Tehran says it does not trust Washington: President Donald Trump said Wednesday he hopes the war with Iran is nearing an end and that Tehran “want[s] to make a deal,” adding that he had heard from Iran “directly” without elaborating.

- Iran’s Supreme National Security Council Secretary Mohsen Rezaei reiterated Tehran’s distrust of Washington, saying: “We in no way trust the United States. They must take practical actions and gain our trust.”

- U.S.-contracted vessel carrying American personnel struck in Iranian attack near Strait of Hormuz, Fox News reports: A “U.S.-contracted vessel” carrying American personnel was struck during an Iranian attack near the Strait of Hormuz earlier this week, Fox news reported.

- The report appears to publicly confirm that U.S. personnel are directly involved in the “dark” shuttle operation through Hormuz’s southern lane, either aboard oil tankers or vessels accompanying them. Washington has used the covert transits to keep regional energy flows averaging at least 16 million barrels per day, about two-thirds of prewar exports.

- The attack reportedly involved four drones and at least one missile. One projectile struck the vessel, causing minor injuries, including smoke inhalation. The wounded are being treated in an unnamed Gulf country.

- Joe Kent, the former National Counterterrorism Center director who resigned over the Iran war, warned that U.S. warships and contracted vessels are “sitting ducks” and that a mass-casualty attack is only a matter of time. Kent urged Washington to withdraw its ships and bases, and then offer Iran sanctions relief and access to frozen funds in exchange for reopening the Strait.

- South Korea says no decision on Strait of Hormuz military deployment: South Korean Foreign Minister Cho Hyun said Thursday that Seoul has not decided whether to deploy military assets to the Strait of Hormuz, as the government weighs a potential contribution to securing the waterway amid U.S. pressure.

- First Vice Foreign Minister Park Yoon-joo said discussions are focused on safe navigation, energy security and protecting South Korean nationals rather than relations with Washington, adding that Seoul remains in an “internal deliberation and review stage.”

- Iran has opposed foreign military involvement in the Strait and warned Seoul of “serious consequences.” Cho is expected to discuss regional and global issues with U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio in Washington on Friday.

- Global oil market short 5 million barrels a day as China’s crude prices hit record high: The global oil market is now short an estimated 5 million barrels per day (bpd) of crude and refined fuels, the Financial Times reported.

- Chinese crude futures have surged to hit a record $129 a barrel as of Wednesday, up 14% since attacks forced Saudi Arabia to close its East-West pipeline. Oil for immediate delivery has become even more expensive—spot Brent reached $146 and ultra-low-sulfur diesel hit a record $221.

- China had cushioned the global shock by cutting crude imports by nearly 5 million bpd in June while drawing down stockpiles. But imports have rebounded toward 9 million bpd in September as those buffers shrink and refiners return to the market, analysts said.

- China’s gasoline, diesel and jet-fuel stocks are also falling rapidly, raising speculation that Beijing may again restrict fuel exports, the report said.

- UN inquiry finds grounds to believe U.S. committed war crimes in Iran strikes: The UN Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on Iran said it found reasonable grounds to believe the United States committed war crimes in two February 28 airstrikes that killed at least 178 civilians, including women and children.

- The mission said a U.S. Tomahawk strike hit the Shajareh Tayyebeh Primary School in Minab, killing more than 150 people, including around 120 children. A separate U.S. strike using Precision Strike Missiles dispersed tungsten pellets over a sports complex and residential area in Lamerd, killing 22 civilians.

- The report also found that Iran’s repression of the 2025–2026 protests involved gross human rights violations, many amounting to crimes against humanity, including murder, imprisonment, and torture.

- Iran expels Swedish diplomat following Stockholm’s expulsion of Iranian diplomat: Iran ordered a Swedish diplomat to leave the country within 48 hours Thursday in retaliation for Sweden’s decision to expel an Iranian embassy employee over alleged security concerns, the Islamic Republic News Agency reported.

- Iran’s Foreign Ministry rejected Sweden’s allegations as “baseless” and called the expulsion unjustified, claiming Stockholm’s decision was influenced by Israel.

- Israeli man sentenced to 13.5 years for spying for Iran: An Israeli court sentenced Alexander Granovsky to 13.5 years in prison Wednesday for carrying out security-related tasks for an Iranian operative in exchange for thousands of dollars, according to Haaretz.

- Granovsky, arrested in 2024, maintained contact with the operative via Telegram and sent photos of the neighborhood where former Israeli general and Blue and White leader Benny Gantz lived. He was also convicted of setting nine vehicles on fire and spraying graffiti, and was asked to recruit people with criminal records to carry out acts of violence.

## Palestine

- Killed and wounded in Gaza: Over the past 24 hours, five Palestinians were killed—two due to wounds sustained in earlier attacks and three in new Israeli attacks—and 28 injured across Gaza, according to the Palestinian Ministry of Health.

- The total recorded death toll since October 7, 2023 has risen to 73,821 killed, with 174,897 injured. Since October 11, the first full day of the so-called ceasefire, Israel has killed at least 1,386 Palestinians in Gaza and wounded 4,784, while 831 bodies have been recovered from under the rubble.

- Israeli forces carry out demolitions and raids across occupied West Bank:

- Ramallah: Israeli forces detained Palestinian journalist Alaa Al-Rimawi after raiding his apartment in Ramallah’s Al-Masyoun neighborhood on Thursday, WAFA reported. On Wednesday, settlers attacked homes and set fire to agricultural land in Burqa, east of Ramallah, while Israeli forces prevented Civil Defense crews from reaching the fire. Also Wednesday, Israeli forces shot and wounded a Palestinian man during a raid on Al-Bireh.

- Nablus: Israeli forces beat and injured two Palestinians Thursday, while detaining and interrogating them during a raid on Al-Ain refugee camp. Forces also raided homes, turned one into a military post, and blocked access to the camp.

- Qalqilya: Israeli forces shot a Palestinian man in the foot during a raid on Qalqilya, while another man with disabilities suffered from tear-gas inhalation.

- East Jerusalem: Israeli forces demolished five residential structures and a sheep pen in Anata, northeast of occupied East Jerusalem, leaving around 30 people without their homes. Forces beat residents and prevented them from removing their belongings before the demolitions.

- Toll of Gaza’s Israeli-damaged building collapse rises to 21 killed and 45 wounded: Gaza Civil Defense spokesperson Mahmoud Basal told Drop Site’s Abdel Qader Sabbah that the building collapsed at around 3 a.m. as families were sleeping, crushing its six floors on top of one another. Dozens remain trapped beneath the rubble.

- “Half an hour ago, there were still voices coming from inside this building. But unfortunately, the resources we have are not sufficient to reach them,” Basal said, describing how rescuers lack specialized equipment to locate survivors beneath the concrete due to Israeli restrictions.

- Basal said around 2,000 damaged buildings across Gaza are on the verge of collapse while still housing thousands of Palestinians. “Are there any alternatives? The truth is, there are no alternatives in Gaza,” Basal said.

- With insufficient tents and shelter space, Basal appealed directly to the international community, ceasefire guarantors, Board of Peace, and its High Representative, Nickolay Mladenov: “What more are you waiting for?”

- Sabbah’s interview with Basal and an eyewitness.

- 21-year-old Palestinian prisoner dies in Ofer prison: An Israeli court has ordered an autopsy of a Palestinian detainee who died in Ofer Prison on Tuesday, according to the Palestinian Prisoners’ Club. Mutaz Al-Atrash, 21, had been under administrative detention for approximately a year. He had no known health problems prior to his arrest. Israeli police notified the family on Wednesday without providing any information on the cause of death.

- Al-Atrash is one of at least 92 Palestinian prisoners who have died in Israeli custody since the start of the war on Gaza nearly three years ago, according to the Palestinian Prisoners’ Club. The group attributed the deaths to torture, starvation, medical neglect, sexual violence, and other abuses, while saying the fate of additional Gaza detainees remains unknown.

- Gaza Health Ministry: Israel cuts approved medical evacuations from 136 to 61: The Palestinian Health Ministry in Gaza said Israeli authorities obstructed Thursday’s scheduled medical evacuations to Egypt, reducing the number of approved patients and companions from 136 to 72 before ordering another 11 to return, leaving 61.

- The ministry said it would allow only critical cases and patients requiring ambulances to leave, with the others returning in protest against what it called “unjustified punitive policies.” It called for international intervention to ensure all patients can leave for treatment under the Sharm el-Sheikh agreement.

- Israel extends detention of journalist Naqaa Hamed for six days: Israeli authorities have extended the detention of Palestinian journalist and Drop Site contributor Naqaa Hamed for six days, according to a statement by her family. Hamed was arrested near Bethlehem on Tuesday as she was returning from a reporting assignment in the occupied West Bank.

- According to the family, Hamed’s detention centers around her coverage of the Israeli siege of several Palestinian families in their homes in the town of Qusra.

- Hamed’s sister, Fatima Salem said on Wednesday in a social media post: “As an American taxpayer, knowing that my own contributions may be helping to sustain the very system responsible for detaining my sister, an American citizen, is unbearable.”

- Read more about Naqaa’s arrest here.

- U.S. extends visa restrictions barring Abbas from UN General Assembly; Palestinian FM calls decision “unjustified”: The U.S. State Department said it will extend visa restrictions on Palestinian Authority (PA) and Palestine Liberation Organization (PLO) officials, preventing Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas from traveling to New York to address the UN General Assembly next week for the second year in a row.

- Washington accused the PA and PLO of failing to reform and undermining peace, including by seeking international recognition of Palestinian statehood and pursuing cases at international courts.

- The Palestinian Foreign Ministry rejected the decision Thursday as “unjustified,” saying: “Recourse to international institutions and international law is a legitimate right of the State of Palestine, and a peaceful and legal means of protecting our people and their rights.”

- The UN General Assembly is scheduled to vote on a draft resolution on Thursday to allow Abbas to address the session remotely, according to The New York Times.

- Israel and Morocco expand diplomatic ties: ​​Israel and Morocco will open embassies, exchange ambassadors, and expand relations under the U.S.-brokered Abraham Accords, according to a joint statement on Wednesday with the United States, saying “the establishment of full diplomatic, peaceful and friendly relations...will advance the cause of peace and unlock new opportunities for the entire region.”

- In the statement, the U.S. and Israel reaffirm their recognition of Morocco’s sovereignty over Western Sahara which it has occupied since 1975 in defiance of the United Nations and the international community.

- Ireland withdraws from Eurovision 2027 over Gaza: Irish broadcaster RTÉ said Ireland will not participate in or broadcast the 2027 Eurovision Song Contest, citing the continued loss of life and humanitarian crisis in Gaza and restrictions on independent international journalists entering the territory.

- Ireland was among five countries—alongside Iceland, the Netherlands, Slovenia, and Spain—that boycotted the 2026 contest after Israeli broadcaster KAN was allowed to participate. Dutch broadcaster AVROTROS said last month it will not participate in Eurovision 2027 saying the event “can no longer be considered neutral, with a participating country still involved in a large-scale military conflict.” However,  responsibility for Dutch participation has now returned to public broadcasting umbrella organization NPO.

## Lebanon

- Israeli attacks continue across southern Lebanon despite ceasefire; bodies of two young men recovered:

- Nabatieh: The Lebanese Red Cross recovered the bodies of two men from Ain Al-Samahiyah, between Nabatieh Al-Fawqa and Zawtar Al-Sharqiyah, after they were killed in an Israeli attack on Wednesday. Israeli artillery also shelled the Al-Dimashqiyah area on the eastern outskirts of Kfar Tibnit, while Israeli forces opened machine-gun fire toward Wadi Al-Hujeir early Thursday, Lebanon’s National News Agency (NNA) reported.

- Tyre (Sour): Israeli forces continued demolishing homes in Mansouri on Thursday. Israeli warplanes also struck Mansouri, Majdal Zoun and nearby valleys overnight.

- Aoun, Macron, and King Abdullah meet in Paris to discuss support for Lebanese army: Lebanese President Joseph Aoun, French President Emmanuel Macron, and Jordan’s King Abdullah II held a trilateral meeting in Paris on Thursday focused on strengthening cooperation and mobilizing international support for the Lebanese army, NNA reported.

- Aoun separately met Macron at the Élysée, where they discussed efforts to end Israeli attacks on Lebanon in the context of ongoing Lebanese-U.S.-Israeli negotiations and the framework agreement. Aoun also welcomed a French-Italian initiative for the period following the end of UNIFIL’s mandate.

- Aoun called for a “joint regional security strategy” built around shared energy projects and economic, security and political cooperation.

## U.S. News

- Federal Reserve raises interest rates: The Federal Reserve Board raised interest rates by a quarter point to 3.9% as it tries to get inflation under control. It was the first increase since 2023. “The plain fact is that inflation is too high and has been for too long,” said Fed Chair Kevin Warsh.

- President Donald Trump, who spent years railing at Warsh’s predecessor, Jerome Powell, said he still supported Warsh but denounced the decision, writing on social media that “Interest ‌Rates in the United States should be 1%, or less, because we are the Best Credit in the World — BY FAR.”

- At a rally in North Carolina, Trump criticized the Federal Reserve board and said it had voted to raise rates in order to hurt him politically. “They’re raising rates to make Trump do as bad as they can possibly do,” he said.

- At the same rally, Trump said higher gas prices were “a very inexpensive price to pay for what we’ve done” in the Iran war, and repeated his promise to send Americans checks for $5,000 if Republicans won the midterms: “If we win, we’re going to get you $5,000.”

- Democrat puts hold on Trump plan to sell more bombs to Israel: Rep. Gregory Meeks of New York, ranking member on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, said he would block the Trump administration’s plan to sell $2.8 billion in new bombs to Israel. “The Trump administration has not provided sufficient assurances that these weapons will be used by the Netanyahu government in accordance with U.S. law and with appropriate protections for civilians,” Meeks said. However, Secretary of State Marco Rubio can bypass congressional review by claiming the weapons sale is an urgent national security interest.

- House recesses early to avoid vote on Hegseth impeachment: Speaker of the House Mike Johnson sent lawmakers home Wednesday, avoiding a vote on a resolution by Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky to impeach War Secretary Pete Hegseth as well as a bipartisan effort to release additional files related to Jeffrey Epstein.

-  Johnson claimed “the House has done its job” and said “we’re walking out here with our heads high.”

- Massie took control of the House floor and denounced Johnson in an hour-long speech. “Why would we be canceling days when the country is burning?” Massie said. “We should stay here for every day that’s on the calendar and we should debate.”

- Top general says U.S. must be prepared to fight on moon: Gen. Dan Caine, chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, told an audience at the Air, Space, and Cyber Conference that U.S. forces must be prepared to fight around the moon, “from the seabed to cislunar space.”

- His remarks came just days after Air Force Secretary Troy Meink confirmed at the same conference that the U.S. has deployed weapons in space.

- OpenAI discloses new AI transgressions: OpenAI on Wednesday reported six additional incidents in which its AI agents engaged in “unexpected or concerning” activity over the last six months, the New York Times reported.

- In one incident, an AI model created hidden notes reminding itself to conceal errors or lie about missing data. In another it described itself as “freed from the roles and identities that bind other chatbats.”
📥 Have a tip on Capitol Hill?  Email DC Correspondent Julian Andreone at Julian@dropsitenews.com

## Other International News

- U.S. raids vessels in Eastern Pacific: The U.S. military raided vessels in the Eastern Pacific on Tuesday and Wednesday, accusing them without evidence of “supporting illicit at-sea drug trafficking operations,” according to U.S. Southern Command (SOUTHCOM). The crews from both vessels were arrested and transferred to Ecuadorian authorities. “We are relentlessly pursuing narco-terrorists who prey on our citizens, undermine hemispheric security, and leave death and suffering in their wake. This deliberate, lawful, and precise operation saves lives and makes our citizens—from Ecuador to the United States—safer,” SOUTHCOM Commander Gen. Francis L. Donovan said in a statement.

- Russian missile and drone barrages hit Kyiv, Odessa, and Zaporizhzhia: At least 19 people were injured, including two children, in a large overnight Russian missile and drone attack across Ukraine, with strikes concentrated on Kyiv and the Kyiv region, Odessa and Zaporizhzhia.

- Russia’s Defense Ministry claimed that it struck military-industrial, metallurgical, electronics, energy and transport infrastructure, as well as three bulk carriers and a ferry in the port of Chornomorsk that it said were being used to support the Ukrainian military.

- Ukraine said it struck an oil refinery in Yaroslavl northeast of Moscow, while President Volodymyr Zelenskyy also claimed Ukrainian forces damaged Russian aircraft and helicopters at a military base in Rostov and naval targets in the Black Sea.

- North Korea says U.S.-led military buildup justifies expanding nuclear arsenal: North Korea’s Vice Defence Minister Kim Kang Il said in a statement that Pyongyang will continue expanding and strengthening its nuclear forces, arguing that growing U.S. military cooperation with South Korea and Japan has created what he called an increasingly severe nuclear threat.

- Speaking at China’s Xiangshan Forum in Beijing, Kim said North Korea’s status as a nuclear weapons state is “irreversible” and described it as a “line of no retreat,” while accusing Washington of turning its trilateral cooperation with Seoul and Tokyo into a nuclear alliance.

- The remarks came alongside a statement from Kim Yo Jong, the sister of Kim Jong Un, rejecting renewed calls for denuclearisation following a recent International Atomic Energy Agency’s annual meeting discussing Pyongyang’s nuclear status.

- Russia says new U.S. sanctions will undermine peace efforts: After the U.S. House of Representatives passed a broad sanctions package dubbed the “Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia Act of 2026” and aimed at increasing economic pressure on Russia over the war in Ukraine, Moscow said that the bill would harm peace talks if signed into law by President Trump.

- The bill targets Russia’s energy and defense industries and its fleet of oil tankers used to circumvent existing sanctions, while also authorizing Trump to impose tariffs of up to 100% on countries including China and India over purchases of Russian oil and gas.

- Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov called the legislation an “unfriendly” move while India separately warned Washington that secondary tariffs tied to its imports of Russian energy could damage bilateral relations.

- Japanese PM reshuffles cabinet amid economic crisis: Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi replaced 10 of 18 cabinet ministers on Thursday as her government faces declining public support due to an economic crisis exacerbated by the war in Iran, but retained the officials overseeing foreign policy, defense, and economic relations with Washington.

- Takaichi’s government is preparing revisions to Japan’s security strategy by year’s end, with plans to expand the military’s use of drones and artificial intelligence and further increase defense spending beyond its current 2% of GDP.

- The government is simultaneously trying to stabilize relations with China after Takaichi’s earlier remarks that Japan could intervene militarily in a Taiwan contingency strained ties with Beijing.

- Scientists say climate change likely helped trigger catastrophic Nepal glacier collapse: Scientists from the research group World Weather Attribution (WWA) say human-caused climate change likely helped create the conditions for the massive August collapse of glacier ice and rock on Nepal’s Langtang Lirung mountain, which unleashed flooding across parts of Nepal and Tibet and killed around 1,400 people.

- Researchers said Himalayan temperatures were about 5°C above normal in August, with roughly 1.5°C of that anomaly attributable to climate change, accelerating glacier thinning, permafrost thaw, and meltwater buildup.

- The study found glaciers in the region have been thinning by about half a metre per year since 2000, altering pressure on surrounding rock, while melting permafrost likely weakened the mountain slope.

- WWA said the precise trigger cannot be isolated, but concluded that warming substantially increased the likelihood of the cascading glacier-and-rock collapse.

reads.title: ALAIN BAUER: THE CONVICTED CRIMINOLOGIST WHO TALKS ABOUT WAR
reads.subtitle: How a Man Fined €375,000 for Corruption Became France’s Go-To Expert on Security and Geopolitics Anonymous | Independent Analyst 17 September 2026
reads.body:
## Introduction
Alain Bauer is one of the most visible “security experts” in France. He appears on BFMTV, LCI, CNews, Europe 1, and Le Figaro. He comments on terrorism, geopolitics, the war in Ukraine, and domestic insecurity. He holds a professorship at the Conservatoire national des arts et métiers (CNAM), a senior fellowship at the John Jay College of Criminal Justice in New York, and an associate professorship at Fudan University in Shanghai.
He is also a convicted criminal.
On 5 March 2025, the Paris Correctional Court found Alain Bauer guilty of recel de favoritisme (receiving illegal benefits) in connection with contracts awarded by the Caisse des Dépôts et Consignations (CDC) between 2007 and 2014. He was sentenced to twelve months’ imprisonment suspended, a €375,000 fine — the highest penalty prescribed by law for this offence — and exclusion from public procurement for three years.
The court justified the severity of the sentence by citing “the risk of recidivism” and Bauer’s “désinvolture” (casual disregard) during the trial. Bauer was absent from the hearing.
He remains on air.

## I. The Man Behind the Expert
Alain Bauer was born in Paris on 8 May 1962 to textile merchant parents. He holds a master’s degree in political science — not in criminology, law, psychology, or sociology. According to a 2024 investigation by Émile Magazine, he has never published any academic work on the many subjects he is invited to comment on.
When he was appointed to the Chair of Criminology at CNAM in 2009 — a position created by presidential decree under Nicolas Sarkozy — several researchers published an open letter in Libération expressing concern about the promotion of a man known for “his approximations and dubious interpretations”.
The chair was reportedly created specifically for Bauer by Sarkozy, to reward him for his services during the 2008 presidential campaign. To qualify for the position, Bauer was granted a doctorate through the “thesis by works” mechanism — his entire body of work was evaluated in place of a doctoral thesis.

## II. The Career: SAIC, the Grand Orient, and the Security Market
Bauer’s career is a case study in the revolving door between the state, the private sector, and the intelligence apparatus.
PeriodRole1988Enters Michel Rocard’s cabinet at Matignon1993Seven-month internship at SAIC headquarters in San Diego1993–94Vice-President of SAIC Europe1994Founds AB Associates (security consultancy)2000–03Grand Master of the Grand Orient de France (GOdF)2003Appointed head of the Observatoire national de la délinquance by Sarkozy2007–12Security adviser to President Sarkozy2009–19President of the Conseil supérieur de la formation et de la recherche stratégiques (CSFRS)
SAIC (Science Applications International Corporation) is one of the largest contractors for the Pentagon, the CIA, and the NSA. Its board has included former CIA and NSA directors. According to Marc Filterman, cited in a 2005 investigation, SAIC’s organigramme revealed “senior officers from the US Army, US Navy, US Air Force, the Pentagon, the CIA, and many other American government services”.
Bauer’s AB Associates was created in premises adjoining SAIC Europe at the CNIT in La Défense. According to AgoraVox, AB Associates was never registered with the French commercial register despite operating in the security sector.
Bauer’s role at SAIC and his subsequent career led AgoraVox to describe him as “both the supplier and the client of a market of which his own security company is a part”.

## III. The Conviction: What the Court Found
The case against Bauer concerned contracts awarded to his companies by the Caisse des Dépôts et Consignations while it was directed by Augustin de Romanet (2007–2012) and Jean-Pierre Jouyet (2012–2014).
DefendantRoleSentenceAugustin de RomanetFormer CEO, CDC8 months suspended, €200,000 fineJean-Pierre JouyetFormer CEO, CDC8 months suspended, €30,000 fineAlain BauerConsultant12 months suspended, €375,000 fine
The court found Bauer guilty of recel de favoritisme — receiving illegal benefits from public officials. The €375,000 fine was the maximum penalty prescribed by law for this offence. He was also banned from public procurement for three years.
The two former CDC directors were acquitted of the charge of misappropriation of public funds, but convicted of favouritism.
Bauer’s reaction: In a May 2025 interview on RMC and BFMTV, he said: “When you are convinced that you have done everything properly, you get this little shock”.
Following his conviction, Bauer posted a message on LinkedIn that was described by several outlets as an alarming suicide note, prompting concern among his associates.

## IV. The Media Paradox: Why Is He Still On Air?
Bauer’s media presence is, by any measure, extraordinary. He comments on:

- Terrorism — despite, according to Arrêt sur images, having never directly worked on the subject nor possessing professional qualifications in the field

- Geopolitics — the war in Ukraine, the Middle East

- Domestic insecurity — a theme he has covered for over a decade

- Public health — he commented on France’s lockdown exit in May 2020
In March 2026, Le Parisien published an investigation titled: “Personne ne comprend, mais il est toujours là” (”No one understands, but he’s still there”) — asking why Bauer has what amounts to a permanent place at the table (”son rond de serviette”) on French television.
The answer, according to critics, lies in his network:

- Close to Manuel Valls (former Prime Minister)

- Adviser to Nicolas Sarkozy

- Grand Master of the Grand Orient de France

- Connected to Stéphane Fouks (Havas) and other media and political figures
As one commentator put it: “He has a very full address book. That allows him to stay.”

## V. What Bauer Says About the War
Bauer’s analysis of the war in Ukraine is a study in ambiguity. He does not accuse the British defence industry of plotting for war. His thesis is more complex:

> “We are paying the price of our blindness and our illusions.”
His book Au commencement était la guerre (Fayard, 2023) argues that the war has “deep roots in the history of Europe, the United States, and Russia”. He predicted a “Korean-style” scenario: a frozen armistice with exhausted protagonists.
In a 2024 interview, he stated:

> “The West has never been so weak and so isolated.”
This is not a conspiracy theory. It is a structural critique of Western strategic failure. But it is delivered by a man whose own career has been built on the revolving door between the state, the intelligence apparatus, and the private security market.

## VI. The Parallels with the British System
Bauer’s case is not unique to France. It parallels the system we have documented in the United Kingdom:
ElementFrance (Bauer)United Kingdom (Shapps/Harborne)Revolving doorSAIC → AB Associates → Sarkozy adviserMoD → Cambridge Aerospace → MoD contractConflict of interestContracts from CDC while advising Sarkozy£1M donation to Johnson, then £80M contractLack of consequencesStill on air after convictionResigned, but no legal consequencesMedia silenceLimited coverage of convictionLimited coverage of Acoba findings
The mechanism is the same: a system that rewards those who serve it, regardless of legal or ethical violations.

## VII. Conclusions
Alain Bauer is not a “CIA agent” in the operational sense. He is something more subtle and, in some ways, more damaging: a convicted corrupter who continues to shape public opinion on security and defence.
What is proven:

- He worked for SAIC, a major US intelligence contractor.

- He was Grand Master of the Grand Orient de France.

- He was convicted of recel de favoritisme and fined €375,000 — the maximum legal penalty.

- He remains a prominent media commentator on security and geopolitics.

- He has never published academic work on the subjects he is invited to discuss.
What remains unclear:

- Why French media continue to platform a convicted criminal as an “expert.”

- Whether his media presence is linked to his political and masonic networks.

- Whether his analysis of the war serves any particular interest.
The question for the reader: If a man convicted of corruption can continue to shape public opinion on war and security, what does that say about the system that produces “experts”?

reads.title: THE GRAHAM SANCTIONS ACT: WASHINGTON'S LAST CARD BEFORE THE MIDTERMS
reads.subtitle: The US Congress passes its most sweeping Russia sanctions package since 2022, but the real target may not be Moscow. Marco | Independent Analyst 17 September 2026
reads.body:
## Introduction
On 16 September 2026, the US House of Representatives passed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 by a vote of 262-159. The Senate had already approved the measure 86-11 on 7 August. The bill now sits on President Donald Trump’s desk, and the White House has confirmed he will sign it.
This is the most substantial US legislative effort against Moscow since Trump returned to office in January 2025. But what does the bill actually contain? And more importantly—will it change anything on the ground in Ukraine?

## I. The Vote: A Fragile Bipartisan Coalition
The House vote revealed deep fractures within both parties.
Republicans: 203 voted in favour, 7 against. The opposition came from the isolationist wing of the party, wary of granting Trump expanded tariff authority.
Democrats: 58 broke with party leadership to support the bill, while 152 opposed it. The division was not about Russia—Democrats overwhelmingly support Ukraine—but about the tariff powers the bill hands to Trump.
Gregory Meeks, the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, called the bill “deeply flawed,” arguing that “White House lawyers drafted the current text to maximise President Trump’s authority to impose new import taxes on the American people, and to minimise any obligation to actually impose new sanctions on Russia”.
The vote came on the last day before Congress recessed for the November midterm elections. The timing was not coincidental.

## II. What the Bill Actually Does
The Graham Act is not a single measure. It is a package of interlocking provisions, each with its own logic and its own limits.
ProvisionTargetMechanismSecondary tariffsTop 5 buyers of Russian oil/gasUp to 100% tariffs, with exemptions for countries importing <15% of their needs from RussiaShadow fleetTankers transporting Russian crudeSanctions on vessels, owners, insurersFinancial institutionsCentral Bank, Sberbank, VTB, GazprombankAsset freezes, transaction bansRussian officialsPutin, military leadership, oligarchsTravel bans, asset freezesIranEnergy and weapons sectorsExtended sanctions until 2031
The most controversial element is the tariff mechanism. The bill authorises Trump to impose tariffs of up to 100% on the five largest purchasers of Russian oil or natural gas. According to Senator Jeanne Shaheen, among these five, China accounts for 51% of Moscow’s revenues from fossil fuel exports.
A Democratic amendment proposed by Congressman Steny Hoyer would have specified ten countries—China, India, UAE, Turkey, Singapore, Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan, Hungary, Kyrgyzstan, and Slovakia—as eligible for the tariffs. The amendment was rejected.

## III. The Exemption That Changes Everything
The bill contains a crucial loophole: countries that reduce their imports of Russian energy to less than 15% of their total consumption can be exempted from tariffs.
For India, this is a direct challenge. In FY2026, India imported $40.8 billion of Russian crude, accounting for almost one-third of its total crude imports. In August alone, India imported 2.08 million barrels per day from Russia—approximately 45% of its oil imports.
India’s response was swift. On Thursday, the Ministry of External Affairs stated that “the Government of India has noted the passage” of the Act, and affirmed that “any decision regarding the country’s energy purchase would solely” be based on its own national interest.
China was more direct. A Foreign Ministry spokesperson said Beijing “firmly opposes illegal unilateral sanctions without international law basis or UN Security Council authorisation” and would “take all necessary measures to firmly protect the legitimate rights and interests of Chinese enterprises and citizens”.
Translation: Neither India nor China will change their energy policies because of this bill.

## IV. The Shadow Fleet: The Real Target
While the tariff provisions dominate headlines, the most operationally significant element targets Russia’s shadow fleet—the network of ageing tankers that transport Russian crude outside Western insurance and shipping systems.
According to KSE Institute, 192 shadow fleet tankers left Russian ports or were involved in ship-to-ship transfers in April 2026. 92% of them were older than 15 years. By June 2026, shadow tankers accounted for approximately two-thirds of Russia’s oil exports, compared to just 12% at the start of the full-scale invasion in 2022.
The bill sanctions not only the vessels but also their owners, operators, and insurers. It also targets foreign suppliers supporting Russia’s defence sector and networks helping Moscow evade existing measures.

## V. The Iran Connection
At Trump’s explicit request, the bill extends sanctions to Iran’s energy and weapons sectors. The Iran provisions are authorised until 2031.
This is significant. The US had already ended all oil waivers for both Russia and Iran in April 2026, with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent stating that “additional supplies from Russia are no longer considered necessary for the global economy”. The Graham Act codifies this policy into law, making it harder for a future administration to reverse it.
But the Iran provisions also serve a domestic purpose: they allow Republicans to frame the bill as a national security measure, not just a Ukraine-focused intervention.

## VI. What the Bill Does Not Do
For all its sweeping language, the Graham Act has critical limitations.
First, it does not mandate sanctions. The bill authorises the president to impose tariffs and sanctions. It does not require him to do so. Trump retains full discretion to waive any measure he deems contrary to the “national interest”.
Second, it does not touch the fundamental problem. Russia’s war economy has adapted. The shadow fleet exists precisely because sanctions were imposed. Every new measure produces a new evasion mechanism.
Third, it does not address Europe. The bill targets Russia’s buyers, not its European enablers. Hungary, Slovakia, and other EU member states continue to import Russian energy. The bill’s tariff powers could theoretically be used against them, but no one expects that.

## VII. The Strategic Question Nobody Asks
The Graham Act is framed as a tool to “force Moscow to the negotiating table.” But if that were the goal, the bill would have passed eighteen months ago, when Lindsey Graham first introduced it in April 2025.
It did not pass because the Trump administration opposed it. Trump preferred to negotiate directly with Moscow, and the White House calculated that pre-emptive sanctions would weaken his hand. The bill stalled for over a year.
What changed? The negotiations yielded nothing. And the midterm elections are approaching.
The Graham Act is not a strategy. It is a political instrument. It allows Republicans to claim they are “tough on Russia” before voters go to the polls. It allows Democrats to say they tried, even though 152 of them voted against it. And it allows Trump to sign a bill that gives him enormous tariff powers he can use against any country—including US allies—while claiming he is supporting Ukraine.

## VIII. The Aid to Iran Paradox
The most glaring contradiction in the bill is its Iran provisions.
The US has sanctioned Iran for decades. It has ended oil waivers. It has extended sanctions until 2031. And yet, Iranian oil continues to flow, often through the same shadow fleet networks that move Russian crude. The sanctions regime has not stopped Iranian exports; it has merely made them more expensive and more opaque.
The same logic applies to Russia. Every new sanction produces a new evasion mechanism. The shadow fleet did not exist in 2022. By 2026, it handles two-thirds of Russia’s oil exports. The more the West sanctions, the more Russia innovates.
Aid to Iran will continue. Sanctions will not stop it. The bill’s Iran provisions are not a strategy; they are a gesture.

## IX. What Happens Next
Trump is expected to sign the bill within days. Once signed, the following will occur:

- The Treasury Department will begin drafting implementation regulations. This process could take months.

- India and China will continue buying Russian oil. They have already said so.

- The shadow fleet will adapt. New vessels, new flags, new insurance mechanisms.

- The war in Ukraine will continue. No sanctions package has ever ended a war.
The Graham Act is the most significant US legislative action on Russia since 2022. It may also be the least consequential.

## X. Conclusion
The Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 is a complex, contradictory, and ultimately limited instrument. It gives Trump enormous tariff powers while mandating almost nothing. It targets Russia’s energy revenues while exempting the countries that actually buy them. It extends sanctions on Iran while Iran’s oil continues to flow.
The bill’s true purpose is not to end the war. It is to allow Washington to claim it is doing something, while the war enters its fifth year and the body count rises.
The US is not a spectator in this war. It is a party to it. And it is not up to Washington to decide when wars start or end.

- NBC News: “House passes Russia sanctions bill named for Lindsey Graham, sending it to Trump” (16 September 2026)

reads.title: THE LOCOMOTIVE WAR
reads.subtitle: How Russia Is Strangling Ukraine's Railways Marco | Independent Analyst 17 September 2026
reads.body:
## Introduction
On the morning of 13 September 2026, a Russian drone struck a train at Yahodyn station, less than two kilometres from the Polish border. The locomotive was hit directly. There were no casualties — passengers had been evacuated fifteen minutes earlier. The train’s engine was destroyed.
Minutes before, a diplomatic train carrying Boris Johnson, former Swedish Prime Minister Carl Bildt, and several European security advisers had passed through the same station. It had left ahead of schedule. Ukrzaliznytsia, Ukraine’s state railway operator, later stated it was “quite likely” the drone had been aimed at the diplomatic train.
This was not an isolated incident. It was the latest operation in a systematic Russian campaign against Ukraine’s railways — a campaign that has destroyed over 500 locomotives since February 2022, more than half of them in 2026 alone.
This article examines the strategy behind the campaign, the technical trap that makes it so effective, and what it means for Ukraine’s ability to sustain its economy and war effort.

## I. The Yahodyn Strike: What Happened
The facts are well-documented across multiple international outlets:
ElementDetailDate13 September 2026LocationYahodyn station, Volyn oblast, ~2 km from Polish borderTargetLocomotive of a Kyiv–Warsaw passenger trainCasualtiesNone (passengers evacuated 15 minutes before impact)Diplomatic trainBoris Johnson, Carl Bildt, Jonathan Powell, David Petraeus — on separate train, already in PolandUkrainian assessmentUkrzaliznytsia: “quite likely” the diplomatic train was the intended target
Boris Johnson’s reaction on X:

> “I don’t know what warped logic drove Putin to blow up a stationary Ukrainian locomotive on the Polish border this morning. What we can say for sure is that this is the kind of random and senseless attack Ukrainians are enduring every day — even on civilian railways.”
Carl Bildt shared a video of the attack on X, writing: “Gli attacchi contro di noi si stanno intensificando.”
David Petraeus, former CIA director, was on another train at Yahodyn station when the drone struck. He described the attack as “terrifying” and accused Putin of “trying to terrorise Ukrainian civilians.”

## II. The Numbers: 500+ Locomotives Lost
The scale of the campaign is staggering. According to Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha, speaking on 15 September 2026:

> “Since the start of the full-scale invasion, over 500 locomotives have been damaged or completely destroyed by Russian attacks — more than half of them this year alone.”
MetricValueSourceLocomotives damaged/destroyed since 2022500+Sybiha, Interfax-UkraineLocomotives lost in 2026 alone192 (first six months)Ukrzaliznytsia, Rail JournalLocomotives lost 2022-2025217Ukrzaliznytsia, Rail JournalPassenger carriages lost249Ukrzaliznytsia, RailMarketRailway infrastructure attacks in 20261,535+Ministry for Communities and Territories DevelopmentUkrzaliznytsia employees killed52UkrzaliznytsiaUkrzaliznytsia employees injured317Ukrzaliznytsia
The acceleration is stark: in the first six months of 2026, Russia destroyed 192 locomotives — nearly as many as in the previous four years combined (217).
Before the war, in April 2021, Ukrzaliznytsia operated 1,532 locomotives (749 electric, 783 diesel). The loss of 500+ units represents roughly one-third of the pre-war fleet.

## III. Why Locomotives? The Strategic Logic
Russia is not targeting passenger carriages. It is targeting the traction — the locomotives that make the trains move.
Oleksandr Pertsovskyi, head of Ukrzaliznytsia, explained the tactic:

> “There are Shaheds guided apparently by a camera. In other words, the pilot on the other side can see clearly what he is hitting. The goal was not simply to destroy the locomotive; the strike hit the cabin directly.”
Andrii Kharuk, military expert, added:

> “Installing a camera on a Shahed is not technically difficult. Such modifications effectively transform the Shaheds into large FPV drones, allowing operators to guide them toward moving targets like trains.”
The logic is simple:
TargetLocomotiveCarriageCostHundreds of thousands of eurosTens of thousandsProductionComplex, long lead timesSimple, rapid productionReplaceabilityDifficult (limited stock)Easy (continuous production)Strategic impactParalyses entire lineLimited damageDefenceIsolated, identifiable targetDiffuse target
As one analyst put it: “They hit traction, i.e. locomotives, because they understand that without traction there is no movement.”

## IV. The Gauge Trap: 1,520mm vs 1,435mm
This is where the strategy becomes devastatingly effective.
Ukraine’s railway network uses 1,520mm broad gauge — a legacy of the Soviet Union. The European Union uses 1,435mm standard gauge.
SystemGaugeCountriesUkraine (ex-USSR)1,520 mmUkraine, Russia, Belarus, Kazakhstan, Finland, BalticsEU1,435 mmAll EU member states
The consequence: European locomotives cannot run on Ukrainian tracks without modification. They must either:

- Change bogies (slow, costly, impractical for locomotives)

- Use variable-gauge carriages (rare, expensive)

- Transload cargo at border crossings

## V. The Bogie Problem: Why Carriages Can Be Swapped, Locomotives Can’t
This is the technical heart of the trap — and it is crucial to understanding why Russia’s strategy works.
Carriages (and freight wagons): Their function is to carry. The bogies are relatively simple components that can be swapped in blocks. In an operation called “bogie exchange,” the carriage body is lifted and placed on a new set of bogies with the correct gauge. This is a standard operation at border crossings.
Locomotives: Their function is to generate traction. The engine, transmission, and onboard systems are integrated into the bogie itself. This makes bogie replacement an operation that is extremely more complex, lengthy, and costly — often considered impractical. As one technical analysis concluded, while bogie exchange is “possible” for locomotives, “it is often more practical to use two different locomotives.”
In short: for a carriage, the bogie is an “accessory.” For a locomotive, it is part of the “heart.”
Spain is developing variable-gauge bogies for freight wagons, with a €5.48 million grant from Madrid to Kyiv. But this technology is for freight wagons only — not locomotives.

## VI. Ukraine’s Urgent Appeal
On 15 September 2026, Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha issued an urgent appeal to Ukraine’s partners:

> “To keep this lifeline running, Ukraine urgently needs replacements. We call on all our partners to urgently assist us in finding locomotives compatible with the 1520 mm gauge as well as in financing to accelerate the procurement of new ones.”
The problem: Only a handful of countries have compatible rolling stock:
CountryGaugeCompatibilityFinland1,524 mmCompatibleEstonia, Latvia, Lithuania1,520 mmCompatibleKazakhstan1,520 mmCompatibleMoldova1,520 mmOffered 20 locomotives (August 2026)
Sybiha acknowledged the difficulty:

> “The search for such locomotives is complicated by the different track widths. In most European countries, the standard gauge of 1,435 mm is used, while in Ukraine it is 1,520 mm. For this reason, potential suppliers of such machines are few. These are mainly the Baltic states and Finland. Another option is the conversion of existing locomotives to the Ukrainian standard.”

## VII. The Diplomatic Train: A Target?
The Yahodyn strike raises a disturbing question: was the diplomatic train the intended target?
Ukrzaliznytsia’s statement:

> “The diplomatic train had left the station earlier than expected because of the timetable change... due to constant threats of Russian strikes” — and therefore it was “quite possible that it could also have been the intended target.”
Carl Bildt confirmed:

> “It was not our train, but the one that left a few minutes after us toward the Polish border. It was evacuated as the Russian drone approached and no one was injured. Our train only received an evacuation warning.”
Dr. Katarzyna Pisarska, president of the Warsaw Security Forum, who was in the same carriage as Johnson, told the BBC that the attack occurred about 30 minutes after their train had crossed into Poland.
The Russian Defence Ministry claimed the attack was aimed at “railway infrastructure facilities in western Ukraine that are used to transport military cargoes from European countries.”
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk held an emergency meeting and warned:

> “The escalation of the actions from the Russian side is becoming a reality, and they are getting closer and closer to our border.”

## VIII. The Broader Campaign: 1,500+ Attacks
The Yahodyn strike is part of a much larger campaign. According to Ukraine’s Ministry for Communities and Territories Development:
MetricValueAttacks on railway facilities (2025–early 2026)1,535+Infrastructure assets damaged17,000+Attacks on railway infrastructure in 2026 alone1,534 (as of August 2026)
Ukrzaliznytsia’s assessment:

> “These figures demonstrate the systematic and targeted nature of hostile actions aimed at disabling the locomotive fleet in order to reduce the ability of rail transport to ensure uninterrupted freight and passenger services.”
The private sector has also been hit: ArcelorMittal Kryvyi Rih lost 15 locomotives used to maintain continuous production cycles at its iron and coke facilities.

## IX. What This Means for the War
Ukraine’s railways are not just transportation. They are the lifeline of the country:
➡️ Evacuation of civilians from frontline areas
➡️ Transport of essential cargo and military supplies
➡️ Export of grain and other vital goods
➡️ 90% of export cargo moves by rail
Ukrzaliznytsia has lost 40% of its rolling stock, according to Ukrainian political analyst Pavlo Hai-Nyzhnyk. The company has also reported shortages of locomotives and carriages due to the cessation of spare parts supplies from Russia and Belarus.
The strategic goal is clear: Russia is not trying to massacre civilians. It is trying to paralyse Ukraine’s logistics — to destroy and disrupt things faster than Ukraine can repair and rebuild them.

## X. Conclusions: The Slow Strangulation
The locomotive war is a textbook example of asymmetric warfare applied to logistics. Russia is not destroying the entire railway network. It is striking its weakest, most irreplaceable link: the traction.
What the evidence shows:

- 500+ locomotives destroyed since 2022, more than half in 2026 alone

- A 1,520mm gauge trap that prevents EU locomotives from running on Ukrainian tracks

- A bogie problem that makes locomotive replacement far harder than carriage replacement

- 1,500+ attacks on railway infrastructure in 2026

- An urgent Ukrainian appeal to partners for compatible locomotives
What remains unclear:

- Whether the Yahodyn strike was specifically targeting the diplomatic train

- Whether Western partners can supply enough compatible locomotives to replace losses

- Whether Spain’s variable-gauge bogie technology can be adapted for locomotives
The bottom line: Ukraine’s railways are being strangled — not by a single decisive blow, but by a thousand cuts. Each destroyed locomotive is a train that will never run, a cargo that will never move, an evacuation that will never happen.
And Europe, for all its pledges of support, cannot simply send its own locomotives. The gauge is different. The bogies don’t fit. The trap is technical, and it is working.

reads.title: THE MENDEL PARADOX: ZELENSKY'S WAR ON HIS CRITICS AND THE YERMAK CORRUPTION CASE
reads.subtitle: Ukraine's former press secretary was sanctioned and blocked from the European Parliament, while the president's former chief of staff faces money laundering charges. Marco | Independent Analyst 18 S
reads.body:
## Introduction
On 13 September 2026, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky signed Decree No. 901/2026, imposing ten-year sanctions on Ioulia Mendel, his former press secretary. Three days later, Mendel was denied entry to the European Parliament in Brussels, where she had been invited to speak at an event on peace in Ukraine. She delivered her speech via video link.
The official reason for the sanctions: “disinformation and Russian propaganda.” The unofficial reason, according to Mendel and her supporters: retaliation for her repeated accusations of corruption against Zelensky and his inner circle.
At the centre of those accusations is Andriy Yermak, Zelensky’s former chief of staff, who was arrested in May 2026 on money laundering charges. He was released after posting €2.7 million bail. The case, known as “Midas,” involves the alleged embezzlement of $100 million from Energoatom, Ukraine’s state nuclear company.
The paradox is stark: a journalist who accused the president of corruption is sanctioned, while the president’s former right-hand man, accused of laundering millions, is free on bail. This article examines the facts, the timeline, and the implications.

## I. The Sanctions Against Ioulia Mendel
Ioulia Mendel served as press secretary to Volodymyr Zelensky from 2019 to 2021. After leaving the administration, she became one of the most vocal critics of the president, accusing him of corruption and authoritarian drift.
On 13 September 2026, Zelensky signed Decree No. 901/2026, which imposed the following measures on Mendel:

- Ten-year asset freeze on all property in Ukraine

- Revocation of state honours, including the title “Honoured Journalist”

- Social media ban from Ukrainian territory

- Travel restrictions and other unspecified measures
The decree accused Mendel of “disseminating disinformation and Russian propaganda.” No specific evidence was provided.
The sanctions came approximately three months after Mendel gave an interview to Tucker Carlson in May 2026, in which she accused Zelensky of corruption and cocaine use. She also described the presidential inner circle as a mafia-like structure. The timing suggests a retaliatory motive.
Sanctions Against Ioulia MendelDecreeNo. 901/2026Date13 September 2026Duration10 yearsMeasuresAsset freeze, revocation of honours, social media banOfficial reasonDisinformation and Russian propagandaContextThree months after Tucker Carlson interview

## II. The Block at the European Parliament
On 16 September 2026, Mendel was scheduled to speak at an event in the European Parliament organised by Hans Neuhoff, a German MEP from the AfD party. The event was titled “Peace in Ukraine” and aimed to provide a platform for critical voices.
When Mendel arrived at the Parliament, she was denied entry. Her access badge was deactivated without explanation. She was forced to deliver her speech via video link from outside the building.
Mendel attributed the block directly to Zelensky’s sanctions: “On the day of my speech, I was denied access to the European Parliament. I attribute this directly to Zelensky’s sanctions.”
The incident raises serious questions about the reach of Ukrainian sanctions within the European Union. How did a Ukrainian presidential decree lead to the deactivation of an access badge in Brussels? Who ordered it? The European Parliament has not provided a clear answer.
The European Parliament BlockDate16 September 2026Event“Peace in Ukraine,” organised by MEP Hans Neuhoff (AfD)ActionMendel denied entry; badge deactivatedResultSpeech delivered via video linkMendel’s responseAttributed block to Zelensky’s sanctions

## III. The Yermak Case
Andriy Yermak was born on 21 November 1971 in Kyiv. A former lawyer and film producer, he served as head of Zelensky’s presidential administration from February 2020 to November 2025. He was widely considered the second most powerful person in Ukraine, controlling access to the president and directing foreign policy and peace negotiations with Russia and the United States.
In November 2025, the National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine (NABU) and the Specialised Anti-Corruption Prosecutor’s Office (SAPO) raided Yermak’s office as part of the “Midas” investigation. The case involved the alleged embezzlement of approximately $100 million from Energoatom, the state nuclear energy company.
On 28 November 2025, Zelensky signed a decree accepting Yermak’s resignation. But the legal troubles were only beginning.
On 14 May 2026, Ukraine’s High Anti-Corruption Court ordered Yermak’s arrest. He was accused of participating in a criminal organisation that laundered €8.9 million in bribes from the energy sector through the construction of luxury villas in Kyiv.
Four days later, on 18 May 2026, Yermak was released after posting bail of 140 million hryvnias (approximately €2.7 million). On 24 July 2026, the court confirmed the seizure of his assets.
The Yermak Case — Key DatesFebruary 2020Yermak appointed head of presidential administrationNovember 2025NABU/SAPO raids; “Midas” scandal breaks28 November 2025Zelensky accepts Yermak’s resignation14 May 2026Yermak arrested by High Anti-Corruption Court18 May 2026Released on €2.7 million bail24 July 2026Asset seizure confirmed

## IV. The Midas Scandal: Who Else Is Involved?
The Midas case extends beyond Yermak. Two other figures are central:

- Oleksi Chernishov, former deputy prime minister, was also arrested.

- Timur Mindich, co-owner of Kvartal 95—the production company that launched Zelensky’s career—is a fugitive. He is accused of organising €90 million in bribes from Energoatom contractors.
Mindich’s involvement is particularly significant. Kvartal 95 is the studio that produced the television series Servant of the People, in which Zelensky played a fictional president. The company became a symbol of Zelensky’s rise to power. Now, its co-owner is accused of orchestrating a massive corruption scheme.
The fact that Yermak, Chernishov, and Mindich are all linked to Zelensky’s inner circle raises uncomfortable questions about the president’s own knowledge and involvement. No evidence has emerged directly implicating Zelensky, but the pattern is troubling.
Key Figures in the Midas CaseNameRoleStatusAndriy YermakFormer head of presidential administrationReleased on bailOleksi ChernishovFormer deputy prime ministerArrestedTimur MindichCo-owner of Kvartal 95Fugitive

## V. The Paradox
The central paradox of this affair is simple: Ioulia Mendel, a journalist who accused the president of corruption, has been sanctioned and blocked from the European Parliament. Andriy Yermak, the president’s former chief of staff, accused of laundering millions, has been released on bail and remains free.
Mendel vs. YermakNameAccusationConsequenceIoulia MendelDisinformation and Russian propaganda10-year sanctions, EU Parliament blockAndriy YermakMoney laundering (€8.9 million)Released on €2.7 million bail
If Mendel’s accusations were false, why not sue her for defamation? If they were true, why is she being punished while the accused walks free? The official justification—”disinformation and Russian propaganda”—does not explain the disparity.

## VI. The FBI Connection (Unverified)
On 17 September 2026, Ukrainian activist Marta Havryshko posted on X: “Yuliia Mendel should testify to the FBI about everything she knows regarding the alleged corruption in Zelensky’s inner circle. And I suspect she knows a lot. If the sanctions against her and the subsequent wave of attacks by pro-government bloggers and self-proclaimed ‘opinion leaders’ were retaliation for speaking out, that also deserves serious examination.”
This claim is unverified. There is no official confirmation that Mendel has been contacted by the FBI or that an investigation is underway. It should be treated as speculation until corroborated.
However, the mere mention of FBI involvement is significant. It suggests that the corruption allegations against Zelensky’s inner circle are being taken seriously by US law enforcement, at least according to some sources. We will continue to monitor this angle.

## VII. The Streisand Effect
The sanctions and the Parliament block have had the opposite of their intended effect. Instead of silencing Mendel, they have amplified her voice.
Her case is now international news. The Le Parisien headline read: “Guerre en Ukraine : l’ancienne porte-parole de Zelensky dit avoir été privée de discours au Parlement européen.” The story has been picked up by media across Europe and beyond.
The Streisand effect is in full swing: the attempt to censor Mendel has drawn more attention to her accusations than any interview or article could have. Zelensky’s inner circle may have won a temporary victory by silencing a critic, but they have lost the broader battle for public opinion.

## VIII. Strategic Implications
For Ukraine: The case undermines Ukraine’s moral authority. The country presents itself as a democracy fighting for European values. Censoring critics and blocking them from EU institutions contradicts that narrative. It also fuels Russian propaganda, which portrays Ukraine as a corrupt, authoritarian state.
For the European Union: The block at the European Parliament raises questions about the EU’s independence. If a Ukrainian presidential decree can prevent a journalist from entering the Parliament, what does that say about EU sovereignty? The incident has embarrassed the Parliament and raised concerns about undue foreign influence.
For the United States: The Yermak case and the alleged FBI interest suggest that corruption in Ukraine is not just a domestic issue. It affects US aid and investment. If American taxpayer money is being diverted into private villas and offshore accounts, the American public has a right to know.
For Russia: The Kremlin will exploit this case to argue that Ukraine is a failed, corrupt state. It will use Mendel’s sanctions as evidence that Kyiv is no different from Moscow. This is a propaganda gift that Russia did not have to work for.

## IX. Conclusion
The Mendel paradox is not just about one journalist. It is about the nature of power in wartime Ukraine. It is about the limits of censorship and the cost of silence. It is about a president who came to power promising to fight corruption, and who now finds himself surrounded by corruption allegations.
The facts speak for themselves:

- Mendel was sanctioned for 10 years.

- Yermak was arrested for money laundering and released on bail.

- The European Parliament blocked Mendel from entering.

- The official reason for the sanctions was “disinformation.”

- The real reason, many suspect, was retaliation.
If Ukraine wants to be part of Europe, it must respect European values. If it wants to defeat Russia, it must be better than Russia. Silencing critics is not the way. It is the path to authoritarianism.

## Introduction
On 13 September 2026, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky signed decree No. 901/2026, imposing ten-year sanctions on his former press secretary, Iuliia Mendel. The sanctions include asset freezes, a ban on commercial operations, a block on her social media presence from Ukraine, and the revocation of state awards.
Three days later, on 16 September, Mendel was denied entry to the European Parliament in Strasbourg, where she had been invited to speak at a side event organised by the AfD on the theme “Ukraine: Dare Peace. Diplomacy, Not Escalation.”
She gave her speech anyway — via video link. The room was full. The hope for peace, she said, was “almost palpable.”
This article examines the facts, the paradox, and what it reveals about the state of Ukrainian democracy and European censorship.

## I. Who Is Iuliia Mendel?
ElementDetailRolePress secretary to President Zelensky (2019–2021)BackgroundJournalist, former presenter on Ukrainian TVCurrent statusSanctioned by presidential decree (13 Sept 2026)Reason given“Dissemination of disinformation and Russian propaganda”Media appearancesTucker Carlson (May 2026), JDD (Aug 2026), European Parliament (virtual, Sept 2026)
Mendel worked alongside Zelensky for two years. In her own words, she was “among his most faithful propagandists.” She now accuses him of authoritarian drift and of making the war the foundation of his political survival.

## II. The Sanctions: What Do They Entail?
The decree imposes:

- Asset freeze on all property in Ukraine

- Ban on commercial operations and participation in privatisation

- Block on social media from Ukrainian territory

- Revocation of state awards and honorary titles

- Ten-year duration
The sanctions were announced three days before Mendel was due to speak at the European Parliament. The timing is not coincidental.

## III. The European Parliament Block
Mendel was invited by the AfD to a side event at the European Parliament. Such events are routinely organised by political groups. The Parliament itself stated it “does not approve the content of such events” but manages organisational matters.
Yet Mendel was denied access to the building.
She attributed the block directly to Zelensky’s sanctions. The European Parliament has not provided a legal explanation.
Fabio De Masi, German MEP (Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance), raised the case in plenary:

> “Ukraine is sinking further into chaos. A prosecutor general accused of corruption has fled abroad. There have been shootouts between law enforcement. And now the former spokesman of Mr Zelensky has been sanctioned by Zelensky himself for speaking out against Ukraine’s NATO membership, for his commitment to peace, and for opposing the forced conscription of young people. Yet he has always condemned Russia’s attacks too.”
De Masi added:

> “If such conditions prevail in Ukraine, if the country is increasingly transforming into a mafia state, then this European Parliament should not just nod through further billions... but must finally put the question at the centre of debate.”

## IV. The Yermak Paradox
Mendel’s most pointed question is this:

> “Why am I, Iuliia Mendel — former press secretary of Zelensky — under sanctions, and not Andriy Yermak?”
Andriy Yermak was the head of Zelensky’s Presidential Office from 2020 to 2025. He was the most powerful unelected figure in Ukraine — the “true power behind the throne.”
AccusationStatusSourceLaundered $10.5 million through luxury properties in the Dynasty complex near KyivVerifiedNABU, SAPOInvolved in the Energoatom scandal ($100 million kickback scheme)VerifiedNABUConvinced Zelensky that a full-scale invasion would not happenVerifiedThe GuardianConsulted an astrologer for top appointmentsVerifiedSAPO, NYTArrested in May 2026VerifiedCaliber.AzReleased on €3.2 million bailVerifiedCaliber.Az
Yermak was arrested by NABU — an independent anti-corruption body. He was released on bail. He has not been sanctioned by Zelensky.
Mendel, by contrast, has been sanctioned for speaking.

## V. The Streisand Effect
The sanctions and the Parliament block have had an unintended consequence: they have amplified Mendel’s voice.

- Her interview with Tucker Carlson has millions of views.

- She has been interviewed by JDD, cited in European Parliament, and covered by international media.

- The block made her a symbol of censorship.
As the Russian commentator @ZePrisoner noted: “The situation with Mendel is a magnificent own goal for the globalists who finance the war and for the usurper Zelensky.”
The comment is propagandistic, but the analysis is correct: censorship backfired.

## VI. What This Means
The Mendel case raises three fundamental questions:

- For Ukraine: If the government sanctions its own former spokeswoman for criticising the war, what does that say about democracy?

- For Europe: If the European Parliament bars entry to a speaker invited by a political group, on what legal basis?

- For the West: If the fight against “Russian disinformation” becomes a tool to silence dissent, who is the real target?
The paradox is clear:
➡️ Yermak — accused of corruption, money laundering, and consulting an astrologer — is free.
➡️ Mendel — accused of “disinformation” for criticising the war — is sanctioned.
The question is not whether Mendel is right. The question is why the system treats her as a threat.

## VII. Conclusions
The Mendel case is not an isolated incident. It is part of a broader pattern:

- The criminalisation of dissent in Ukraine

- The use of sanctions as a political weapon

- The complicity of European institutions in silencing critics
As Fabio De Masi said in the European Parliament: “If the country is transforming into a mafia state, then we must finally put the question at the centre of debate.”
The European Parliament did not.
Instead, it barred Mendel from entering.
The paradox is not just Ukrainian. It is European.
