reads.title: The Ulm 5 Trial Dramatizes Germany’s Complicity with Israel’s Genocide in Gaza
reads.subtitle: Five activists who vandalized an Elbit Systems factory aim to put Germany and the Israeli weapons company on trial.
reads.body:
As a reader-funded independent news outlet, we operate free from the influence of governments, advertisers, and corporate backers. This is essential to our mission: to report on what matters most, beholden only to the truth. In that spirit, we made a commitment to ensure that our journalism is free for everyone, not locked behind a paywall. But that means we rely on the voluntary support of our community of readers. Please consider making a tax-deductible donation to support our work today.
Subscribe now

-
- Daniel Tatlow-Devally, Leandra Rollo, Vi Kovarbasic, Crow Tricks, and Zo Hailu, known as the “Ulm 5,” are shown behind bulletproof glass at their trial in Stuttgart, Germany for allegedly vandalizing an Elbit Systems factory in the German city of Ulm. Photo by Hebh Jamal for Drop Site News.STUTTGART, Germany—Nearly fifty years after the infamous Red Army Faction trials, Germany’s maximum-security Stammheim Prison is once again the setting of a high-profile case that calls into question the conduct of the German state. This time, however, the defendants are five international pro-Palestinian activists charged with vandalizing a factory in the German city of Ulm owned by Israeli weapons manufacturer Elbit Systems.
On September 8, 2025, the five Berlin-based activists, now known as the Ulm 5, broke into Elbit’s facility and carried out acts of vandalism that they recorded using body cameras and posted online. They destroyed equipment and spray painted “free Palestine” and “baby killers” on the walls. In their videos, the activists—citizens of Britain, Ireland, Spain, and Germany—say they carried out their direct action “to dismantle the tools used to commit genocide in Gaza” and to call attention to Germany’s complicity with it.
No one was injured in the action, which allegedly caused €1.04 million in damages, and the protesters remained at the scene to be arrested. Even so, German prosecutors have clearly decided to treat the Ulm 5 with unusual severity, charging them with membership in a criminal organization, Palestine Action Germany, in addition to trespassing and criminal damage. An additional charge concerns the use of “symbols of an unconstitutional or terrorist organisation”—referring to Hamas—based on the defendants’ use of slogans including “From the river to the sea, Palestine will be free.”
The courtroom itself has been staged for maximum drama, as if the proceedings concerned dangerous criminals rather than nonviolent protesters. The five defendants sit behind a double layer of bulletproof glass that separates them from both their legal team and the public gallery.
Members of the public and press sit behind another layer of bulletproof glass and must pass through an intense security process that includes an invasive pat down behind closed doors. Only accredited journalists may bring writing utensils into the court room, since pens and pencils could be used as “slash and stab weapons,” according to the judge and prosecutor.  Heavily armed security personnel stand watch.
Lynn Boylan, an Irish member of the European Parliament who chairs that body’s Delegation for Relations with Palestine, described the security theater surrounding the case as a “show trial.”
“I initially thought the parents of the Ulm 5 were simply exaggerating because they’re not used to the German court system, but what I experienced on this parliamentary trip really shocked me,” Boylan told Drop Site. “We were not allowed to bring in a pen and paper and take our own notes,” Boylan said, adding that she had to ask permission to take a handkerchief into the courtroom.
“My colleagues visited the Irish citizen, Daniel Tatlow-Devally, in prison and they were concerned with the mind games that the prison staff were playing with Daniel,” Boylan said. “Daniel is incarcerated for 23 hours a day in what is essentially solitary confinement and that can have a serious impact on a person’s mental health. It is completely unnecessary. Daniel and the four others—they’re not violent criminals, and yet they’re being treated as if they are the worst of the worst offenders in a prison system. They should be out on bail.”

-
- Activists rally in Stuttgart, Germany before the start of the trial against five pro-Palestine activists, known as the Ulm 5, accused of vandalizing an Elbit Systems factory in Ulm, Germany. Photo by Julian Rettig/picture alliance via Getty Images.

## Precriminalization
The logistics of the case seem calculated to impose hardship on the activists, four of whom are not German citizens. Tatlow-Devally and the other four defendants—Zo Hailu and Crow Tricks from Britain, Spain’s Leandra Valenzuela, and Vi Kovarbasic, from Germany—are being held in five different prisons and are not allowed to communicate with one another. They receive a single hour of visitation per month that is heavily monitored and accompanied by translators and prison guards. Families and loved ones are not allowed to talk about the case during their visits.
The trial was initially scheduled to take place over 16 hearings spanning approximately three and a half months. In mid-May, however, shortly after proceedings began, the presiding judge, Katherin Lauchstädt, unilaterally added an additional 28 hearing dates extending into January 2027.
Lauchstädt rejected a Drop Site request to interview the five defendants in prison, arguing that doing so would help spread information between the defendants and would therefore interfere with the trial.
On April 27, the first day of the trial, the five defendants entered in handcuffs and were seated separately from their lawyers behind the bulletproof barrier. The arrangement immediately triggered a confrontation. The 11-member defense team refused to take their seats, demanding that their clients be brought forward so they could communicate with them directly and confidentially.
A chaotic standoff between the court and the defense ensued as the lawyers repeatedly attempted to challenge the seating arrangement and raise procedural motions, while the judge refused to give them the floor, and eventually turned off their microphones. The legal team all left the courtroom at that point in protest, prompting a two hour recess.
Attorney Nina Onèr, who represents Zo Hailu, described to Drop Site News how the courtroom itself contributed to the breakdown in proceedings. Unlike in a conventional courtroom where lawyers can address the judge directly, the Stammheim facility requires lawyers to press a button to request permission to speak, after which the court must activate their microphones. On the first day, she said, the court refused to activate the defense microphones at all, preventing the lawyers from formally submitting even a single motion.
“The intention is to build the image of five extremely dangerous individuals that are not allowed to speak to their lawyers freely, even in the breaks,” Onèr told Drop Site.
Among the motions the defense sought to file was a motion for recusal, asking the court to remove itself from the case over concerns of bias. Onèr stressed that such a motion must be submitted at the appropriate stage of proceedings or the defense can lose its right to raise it later.
“We have never experienced any such a thing that the court won’t even let us file our motions,” Onèr said. With the indictment about to be read, Onèr said the defense was left with what it saw as its only remaining option: collectively leaving the courtroom. “Our only chance to stop the indictment from being read and us losing our rights,” she said, “was to collectively leave the courtroom as the trial cannot continue without us.”
The progress of the trial has been slow. Procedural motions are routinely presented only for the judge to reject nearly every single one with very little or no legal justification, according to the Ulm 5’s lawyers. Consistent breaks disrupt the flow of evidence, although sometimes these breaks are called by the legal team due to their inability to speak with their clients and understand their wants while court is in session.
In contrast to some of the Palestine Action cases in the UK, the Ulm 5 have not been charged with terrorism under Section 129a of the German criminal code. Onèr said the effort to censor and monitor communication between the defendants and the defense that could apply to terror cases should not apply here.
“We don’t have a Section 129a case, and yet these are the measures that the court is pushing through the court house that are even extreme when it is a 129a case,” she said.
For comparison, in a Section 129a terrorism trial that’s happening at the same time, the defendants—members of the extremist Reichsbürger movement accused of attempting to overthrow the German government, who allegedly shot German police officers—are allowed to sit with their defense team, and some have even been released from pre-trial detention.
“This definitely sets a new kind of precedent,” Sophia Hoffinger, a monitor project officer at the European Legal Support Center told DropSite. “There are very few comparable prolonged forms of pretrial detention in Section 129 cases.”
Hoffinger said that similar charges have been made against members of the climate justice group, Last Generation, for belonging to a criminal organization. Yet “none of the members have been forced under the same conditions as the Ulm 5 defendants,” she added. “There’s no pretrial detention [in that case] and none of the refusal to allow defendants to consult with their lawyers privately.”
Germany’s federal domestic intelligence agency has not only described the Ulm 5 as extremists, even before they have been convicted, but also accused the legal aid organization 3ezwa of being involved in “prisoner assistance extremism” solely because it has provided support for the trial. Hoffinger described this as a form of “precriminalization.”
“Just because a support structure expresses political support for five people who have not been convicted of anything yet and who are still on trial shows the extent of this precriminalization,” Hoffinger said. “This is a wider trend that Germany is imposing because of expressed support for Palestine. They have politicized this case by even using their own intelligence agencies to interfere and accelerate the accusations against the defendants because of their economic interests in delegitimizing the Ulm 5,” she added.

-
- A drone is on display at the Elbit Systems Deutschland booth during the International Aerospace Exhibition at the Berlin ExpoCenter Airport, on June 11, 2026. Photo by Sebastian Christoph Gollnow/picture alliance via Getty Images.

## Elbit and Israel’s Genocide
As Israel’s largest private arms manufacturer, Elbit Systems has become a frequent target of direct actions and the BDS movement internationally. The company produces a wide range of military equipment—including artillery shells, tank rounds, surveillance equipment, drones, and parts for F-35 jets—many of which have been deployed during the genocide in Gaza.
In Germany, Elbit’s subsidiary produces highly specialised components for laser targeting and communications systems.
Political economist Shir Hever, an expert on the Israeli arms industry, said Elbit’s factory in Ulm develops laser sensors used for gathering digital information and terrain mapping as well as software defined radios that serve as the primary communication platform for the Israeli military.
“This is where Germany plays a very important role in the supply chain, as the same radios and sensors manufactured and developed in Ulm” are used in Gaza, Hever said.
Elbit Systems Germany did not respond to a request for comment.
Under the German legal system, the public prosecutor is legally required to investigate both incriminating and potentially exonerating evidence. That has not happened in this case, and the defense argues the prosecution failed to adequately examine evidence that could potentially justify or contextualise the five defendants’ actions during the alleged break in. This includes investigating Elbit’s complicity in Israel’s war crimes in Gaza.
Instead, the prosecutor, Ronny Stengel, alleges the action was motivated by antisemitism, an aggravating factor in Germany. Since the five sprayed “Baby Killers” on the walls of Elbit facility, the prosecution alleges, they contributed to the antisemitic trope of blood libel, since Elbit is a “Jewish-owned company.”
On June 19, the seventh trial date, the legal team introduced the Dutch newspaper Der Volksrant’s  award-winning investigation, “What the Wounds Are Telling Us,” by Maud Effting and Willem Feenstra, detailing evidence that Israeli forces had deliberately targeted the heads and chests of Palestinian children in Gaza. This was done provide context for understanding the motivations of the defendants and how their conduct should be legally evaluated. Instead of allowing the defense to read out the article in English, however, the judge insisted that it be translated verbally into German, creating a dramatic moment during the proceedings as the translators became visibly emotional, choking up as the material was read aloud in court.
The defense’s argument ultimately depends on a question: What was the five activists’ direct action intended to stop? They argue that Elbit plays a direct role in Israel’s genocide in Gaza and that the defendants’ vandalism was thus justified.
According to Ihsan Adel, chairperson of Law for Palestine and an attorney working on a case filed before the International Court of Justice (ICJ) by Nicaragua, “Germany has a legal obligation to prevent and punish genocide.”
“Proceedings in the Nicaragua case against Germany before the ICJ, together with information available in the public record, indicate that Germany has not taken the measures required under international law to prevent genocide in Gaza,” Adel said.
According to a new report published by Forensis Berlin, Germany approved approximately €1.41 billion in licenses to export military equipment to Israel between October 2023 and June 2026, including €800 million in the first six months of 2026 alone.
The report documents that in 2023 and 2024, Germany ranked first and second respectively among the EU states that reported arms exports to Israel.
Matthias Goldmann, a professor of international law at EBS University, told Drop Site the defendants must meet five conditions for their action to be considered legitimate civil disobedience. The first would be a fundamental interest of the community, such as upholding and respecting international law. The second is that the action was undertaken without regard for their own self-interest, financial, or political gain. The third condition is non-violence, and Goldmann said that “violence begins when people are harmed,” and that vandalizing the Elbit Systems factory does not meet the threshold of a violent act. The fourth condition is that the action must attempt to impact or influence political discourse and correct the course of politics.
“We can disagree about what legitimate resistance is, as one man’s freedom fighter is another man’s terrorist. So to get around that there are criteria,” Goldmann said.
The final criterion, Goldmann said, was that the Ulm 5 meet have demonstrated a willingness to accept their punishment, because they waited on site for the authorities to arrest them.
“Constitutional or international law alone is never self-sufficient; a legal order is subject to different criteria than just the state’s constitution, so I believe the Ulm 5 does meet the criteria of civil disobedience,” Goldmann said.

-
- Family members of defendant Daniel Tatlow-Devally are shown in court making the “handcuffed heart” gesture of solidarity with the Ulm 5. From left: Daniel’s mother, Mimi Tatlow-Golden; his girlfriend, Georgia Kalogeratou; sister, Clara Tatlow-Devally; and stepfather, Jeremy Golden. Photo by Hebh Jamal for Drop Site News.

## A Pattern of State Violence
Crow Tricks’ sibling Tessi Tricks told Drop Site how jarring it was for the families to see the defendants treated like dangerous criminals. “The five activists just don’t look threatening at all. So it’s like this quite confusing experience because you feel like they’re getting treated like they could set off a bomb or they could do something really awful, and it’s like they’re literally just standing there trying to have access to their lawyers, trying to be able to defend themselves. They’re being treated way disproportionately to what they’ve done,” Tessi said.
Tatlow-Devally’s mother, Mimi, said the conditions of his confinement amounted to torture. “Daniel seems to be very resilient even though they are locked for 23 hours a day in a five-by-two-meter cell. The window is frosted glass and can’t be opened, and outside is a concrete yard with no greenery of any kind.”
During visits, she said, her son was kept in a glass room and she was unable to hug her child for the five months she visited them. It was only after she involved Richard Boyd Barrett, a member of Ireland’s lower house of parliament, that a meeting was arranged with the German ambassador. The family was later told that the rule preventing Tatlow-Golden from physically touching their loved ones was due to a clerical error.
“When we first heard that things changed was when one day Daniel’s dad went to visit, and suddenly the visit was just in the family room, sitting at a table, and that was very emotional for Daniel. They had their first touch from a loved one in five months. Daniel had no social contact, no physical contact, and combined that with almost no intellectual contact since they were refused the right to have books sent to them. It’s torture if you think about it,” Mimi said.
Tessi Tricks said the prison environment has been dangerous for Crow, who has been repeatedly moved into different cells and has experienced threats from cellmates.
“Each time Crow moves they get very stressed because they don’t know who they’re going to share a cell with. Last year was quite difficult for Crow when they were threatened by a cellmate. They complained to guards who responded by saying, ‘it’s not our issue unless we see blood on the ground,’” Tricks said.
According to the families, Germany is trying to make an example of the Ulm 5 for “offending Germany’s self-image as a good actor, and they are being punished for it,” said Mimi Tatlow-Golden.
“We see a thread from the prosecutor’s attitudes, from the charges that have been laid, to the decisions the judge has made and to the decision to make Stammheim the location of the trial depicting the five as dangerous people,” she added.
Boylan, the Irish member of the European Parliament, said that Germany’s violent treatment of the Ulm 5 is part of a wider pattern of violence against Palestinian solidarity.
“I think anybody looking at what Israel is doing to the Palestinian people, you know, cannot deny what they see with their own eyes. So I think that that’s part of it that [Germany] have taken this very very heavy-handed approach against all Palestine solidarity,” she said. “They want to send a message to the wider public that you know if you do what the Ulm 5 did, there’s going to be very heavy consequences.”

reads.title: NOVOROSSIYA
reads.subtitle: The Word That Redraws Ukraine Marco | Independent Analyst 16 September 2026
reads.body:
On 16 September 2026, Vladimir Putin addressed the Russian nation ahead of the State Duma elections scheduled for 18-20 September. The address was framed as a call to civic duty. It was, in fact, a territorial declaration.
The sentence that matters most is this:

> “Residents of Donbass and Novorossiya will be voting for State Duma deputies for the first time since their reunification with Russia.”
He did not say “Donbass.” He said “Donbass and Novorossiya.”
Two words. One of them is a region. The other is a programme.

## I. What Putin Said
The address, published on the Kremlin’s official website, was structured around the themes of unity, sovereignty, and sacrifice. Putin called the election campaign “significant and largely definitive,” emphasized that it is taking place “amidst the special military operation,” and framed voting as “our collective response to those who seek to undermine Russia”.
The key passage:

> “Residents of Donbass and Novorossiya will be voting for State Duma deputies for the first time since their reunification with Russia. I firmly believe that our soldiers and officers involved in this challenging work at the frontline will be among active voters.”
He also stated that participation in the vote is “a responsibility and contribution to the country’s strength,” and that “every vote matters”.
Voting will take place over three days: 18, 19, and 20 September.

## II. The Word: Novorossiya
The term “Novorossiya” — “New Russia” — first appeared in the late 18th century as an imperial administrative label for territories colonised by the Russian Empire across what is now south-eastern Ukraine. It fell into disuse during the Soviet period. It was resurrected in 2014, following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, by Kremlin political technologists Vladislav Surkov and Alexander Dugin, and then adopted as official policy by Putin himself.
American historian Timothy Snyder, in The Road to Unfreedom, describes the mechanism:

> “Most citizens of the Russian Federation had not heard of ‘Novorossiya’ in this sense before March and April 2014, when Surkov and Dugin first propagated it, and then Putin made it policy. As Surkov and Glazyev tried to organize armed rebellions in southeastern Ukraine, the maps of ‘Novorossiia’ flooded Russian television screens.”
The term is deliberately vague. As Ukrainian journalist Vitaly Portnikov noted, “The term ‘Novorossiya’ is politically vague, giving Putin enormous flexibility for making new demands”.

## III. What Novorossiya Includes
This is the critical question. And the answer is not ambiguous.
The Atlantic Council confirmed in December 2025 that Putin’s definition of Novorossiya encompasses approximately half of Ukraine, including the country’s entire Black Sea coastline and major cities such as Odesa and Kharkiv.
TerritoryCurrent StatusClaimed as “Novorossiya”Donetsk, LuhanskPartially occupiedYesZaporizhzhia, KhersonPartially occupiedYesCrimeaAnnexed 2014YesKharkivNot occupiedYesDnipropetrovskNot occupiedYesMykolaivNot occupiedYesOdesaNot occupiedYes
This is not a negotiating position. It is a territorial claim on half of Ukraine’s sovereign territory.
Putin has been signalling this expansion for months. In December 2025, during a press conference in New Delhi, he declared that Russia would “liberate Donbas and Novorossiya in any case — by military or other means”. In a December 2025 address to Defense Ministry officials, he stated: “If the opposing side and their foreign patrons refuse to engage in substantive discussions, Russia will achieve the liberation of its historical lands by military means”.
The word “Novorossiya” in the 16 September address is not an isolated rhetorical flourish. It is the continuation of a declared policy.

## IV. The Election as Administrative Annexation
The Duma elections are not simply a domestic Russian ritual. They are an instrument of territorial consolidation.
By holding voting in occupied Ukrainian territories, Moscow is performing sovereignty over land it does not fully control. This is not an election. It is an administrative annexation — the transformation of military occupation into bureaucratic fact.
A European diplomat told AFP that while the election is “quite a sham,” it is a “ritual the Kremlin considers essential”. Exiled Russian political scientist Nikolai Petrov added: “Just like at the time of the Soviet Union, elections should demonstrate loyalty of citizens”.
But in the occupied territories, the function is different. The vote is designed to create a Russian electorate where none legitimately exists — to manufacture the demographic and political basis for the claim that these territories are “already Russia.”
The inclusion of soldiers and officers as “active voters” reinforces this. The front line becomes a polling station. The army becomes the electoral body of the new territory.

## V. Ukraine’s Response
Kyiv has responded on three levels.
Legal:
The Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) issued a statement on 14 September urging residents of occupied territories not to participate. Organising, conducting, or participating in the organisation of Russian elections in occupied territory constitutes a criminal offence under Part 5 of Article 111-1 of Ukraine’s Criminal Code. The penalty: up to 10 years in prison with confiscation of property.
The SBU called the vote “another fake plebiscite” and warned residents not to “become an instrument of the Kremlin regime in the war against our state”.
Military:
Ukraine’s Foreign Intelligence Service warned on 10 September of a high likelihood of false-flag attacks during the 18-20 September voting window. The service identified specific scenarios: bombings of polling stations to create images of “destroyed polling stations,” sabotage of election commission transport with claims of Ukrainian responsibility, and assassination attempts against occupation officials and candidates.
Residents were advised to avoid crowds, polling stations, administrative buildings, and Russian military infrastructure between 17-21 September.
Diplomatic:
Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha condemned the vote on X, calling it a “farce.” He noted that Putin has ruled Russia for 26 years — “longer than Joseph Stalin” — and that his regime has “systematically dismantled anything that resembled democracy”.

## VI. The EU Response
The European Union has stated its position with clarity.
EU Ambassador to the UN Stavros Lambrinidis, speaking before the General Assembly, declared:

> “Crimea, Donetsk, Kherson, Luhansk and Zaporizhzhia are Ukraine. The European Union will never recognize as lawful any attempt by Russia to annex Ukrainian territory. We do not recognize the forced Russification of people and their communities, nor the results of any illegal so-called elections organized by the Russian occupation administration in the temporarily occupied territory of Ukraine.”
Lambrinidis further stated that Russia’s goal is to “alter the demographic composition of the territories it occupies, including through the forced transfer and deportation of civilians, including children,” calling these actions “illegal,” “shameless,” and “disgraceful”.
The EU has also signalled that sanctions will target individuals involved in organising the vote. As stated by Ukrainian officials, “International and national sanctions will be imposed on these individuals, and proceedings will be initiated in accordance with Ukrainian criminal law”.
But the strategic problem for Brussels is deeper. If “Novorossiya” includes Kharkiv, Dnipropetrovsk, Mykolaiv, and Odesa, then any discussion of a “frozen conflict” along current lines is already obsolete. Russia is not negotiating where to stop. It is signalling that it has not yet decided whether to stop.

## VII. The Mechanism
This is Dossier #120 — The Dmitriev Package — applied to the electoral domain.
The mechanism has three components:

- Perform sovereignty. Hold elections in territories you do not fully control. Treat them as already yours. Create facts on the ground that precede and prepare legal annexation.

- Manufacture an electorate. Include military personnel as “active voters.” Create the appearance of popular participation where none exists. Use the ballot box as a tool of demographic engineering.

- Frame resistance as division. Putin’s address concluded: “This will be our collective response to those who seek to undermine Russia, slow down its development, or strip away our sovereignty”. Opposition becomes external aggression. Participation becomes patriotism.
The election is not the story. The word “Novorossiya” is the story. The election is the mechanism for embedding it.

## VIII. What Happens After 20 September
The voting ends on 20 September. The claim it embeds does not.
If Moscow proceeds as expected, the following will unfold:

- Results declared in occupied territories, with turnout figures designed to demonstrate “popular support.”

- International non-recognition from the EU, US, and allies — but no mechanism to reverse the administrative integration.

- Continued pressure on Ukraine to negotiate from a position where “Novorossiya” is treated as a fait accompli.

- Escalation risk if Russia interprets non-recognition as an obstacle to be removed by further military means.
The deeper danger is that the word “Novorossiya” normalises a territorial claim that, if accepted even implicitly, would mean the permanent partition of Ukraine along lines that Moscow — not Kyiv, not Brussels, not Washington — has drawn.

## IX. Conclusions

- Putin’s 16 September address was not a campaign speech. It was a territorial declaration disguised as a call to civic duty.

- “Novorossiya” is not Donbass. It is a claim on approximately half of Ukraine, including Odesa, Kharkiv, Dnipropetrovsk, and Mykolaiv — territories Russia does not occupy.

- The Duma elections are administrative annexation by ballot. They create a Russian electorate in occupied territory and normalise the claim that these lands are already Russia.

- Ukraine has criminalised participation. Up to 10 years in prison for organising or promoting the vote. The SBU warns of false-flag attacks during the voting window.

- The EU has rejected the vote and the claim. But rejection is not a strategy. The word “Novorossiya” has already shifted the baseline.

- The mechanism is the same as Dossier #120. Perform sovereignty. Manufacture facts. Protect the claim through narrative.

- The question is not whether the election is legitimate. It is not. The question is what happens when an illegitimate claim is embedded in administrative reality and no one has the means — or the will — to reverse it.
Putin said it himself in December 2025: Russia will liberate Donbas and Novorossiya “by military or other means.”
The election is the “other means.”

## Sources and Dossiers
Primary sources:

- Vladimir Putin, Address ahead of State Duma elections, Kremlin.ru, 16 September 2026

- TASS, “Large-scale election campaign proceeds amidst special military operation,” 16 September 2026

- United24 Media, “What is ‘Novorossiya’ Putin Keeps Talking About?” 30 January 2026

- Atlantic Council, “Reclaiming Russia’s ‘historical lands,’” 23 December 2025

- Ukraine’s Foreign Intelligence Service, warning on false-flag attacks, 10 September 2026

- Security Service of Ukraine (SBU), statement on election participation, 14 September 2026

- EU Ambassador Stavros Lambrinidis, UN General Assembly statement, September 2026

- Kyiv Post, “SBU Warns Ukrainians in Occupied Areas,” 14 September 2026
Dossiers:

- #120 — Il Pacchetto Dmitriev

- #119 — Il Meccanismo del Consenso

- #88 — La Trappola di Zelensky
Independent analysis. No ideology. Just facts.
Marco | Independent Analyst ⚖️

reads.title: THE DMITRIEV PACKAGE: TRUMP'S MINERALS DEAL WITH KYIV, RUSSIA'S COUNTER-OFFER, AND THE SCRAMBLE FOR THE DONBASS
reads.subtitle: How a $14.8 trillion resource prize became the hidden driver of the Ukraine negotiations — and why Europe is the big loser Marco | Independent Analyst *16 September 2026*
reads.body:
## Introduction: the deal that was signed for resources Ukraine does not control
On April 30, 2025, the United States and Ukraine signed the “Reconstruction Investment Fund” agreement in Washington. The deal established a joint fund that would receive 50% of profits and royalties from new mining, oil, and gas licenses granted to Ukraine. Ukraine retained “full control over subsoil, infrastructure, and natural resources,” Prime Minister Denys Shmyhal stated shortly before the signing.
The agreement contained no concrete security guarantees. It affirmed a “long-term strategic alignment” and pledged U.S. “support for Ukraine’s security, prosperity, reconstruction, and integration into global economic frameworks”.
But there was one problem that no one in Washington wanted to address publicly: approximately 70% of Ukraine’s mineral wealth — an estimated $350 billion — sits in territory controlled by Russia.
The deal was signed for resources Ukraine does not control. And now, Moscow is using that reality as leverage in direct negotiations with Washington.
This article examines the full picture: the original U.S.-Ukraine agreement, the Russian counter-offer known as the “Dmitriev Package,” the 28-point plan for a Donbass lease, the resource wealth at stake, and the strategic implications for Europe.

## I. The U.S.-Ukraine minerals deal: what it actually says

## The terms
The agreement, officially titled the “Agreement between the Government of Ukraine and the Government of the United States of America on the Establishment of a United States-Ukraine Reconstruction Investment Fund,” was signed on April 30, 2025, after months of tense negotiations.
Key provisions:
ElementDetailJoint fundA 50/50 partnership between the U.S. and UkraineRevenue50% of profits and royalties from new extraction licensesOwnershipUkraine retains full control of subsoil and natural resourcesDuration10 years, with profits reinvested in new projects and reconstructionSecurity guaranteesNone

## The problem: the resources are in the Donbass
The Donbass region — comprising Donetsk and Luhansk oblasts — is the industrial and mineral heartland of Ukraine. It contains vast reserves of coal, iron, titanium, lithium, rare earths, and natural gas.
According to Ukrainian Deputy Prime Minister Yulia Svyrydenko, approximately $350 billion worth of critical minerals are located in territory temporarily occupied by Russia.
Forbes Ukraine has valued Ukraine’s total mineral wealth at $14.8 trillion — but over 70% is in the Donbass.
In other words: the U.S.-Ukraine deal was signed for assets that are, for the most part, not under Ukrainian control.

## II. The Dmitriev Package: Russia’s $12-14 trillion counter-offer

## Who is Kirill Dmitriev?
Kirill Dmitriev is the head of the Russian Direct Investment Fund (RDIF) and Putin’s special envoy for investment and economic cooperation with foreign countries.
Born in Kyiv in 1975, he studied at Stanford University and Harvard Business School before working at Goldman Sachs and McKinsey & Company. He is sanctioned by the United States, but the Trump administration issued a special waiver to allow his entry for negotiations.
Dmitriev has met with U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff at least nine times since April 2025.

## The offer
On February 6, 2026, President Zelensky disclosed that Ukrainian intelligence had briefed him on a roughly $12 trillion framework for large-scale economic cooperation between Moscow and Washington.
Dmitriev initially denied the report as “fake,” then publicly raised the figure to $14 trillion.
The package includes:
SectorDetailArctic oil and gasJoint development of offshore projectsRare earthsExtraction and processing of critical mineralsNuclear energyCooperation on nuclear powerData centersNuclear-powered data centersAviationLong-term contracts for American aircraftMiningExpanded projects for lithium, copper, nickel, and platinumDollar systemRussia seeks relief from restrictions that cut it off from dollar paymentsExxon returnRestoration of Exxon’s 30% stake in Sakhalin-1
The memo also signals that Russia is ready to factor in previous American investments and contribute to compensation for losses incurred after Western companies exited the market.

## The logic
Russia’s message to Washington is simple: “Russia has resources. America needs resources. Let’s make a deal.”
The strategic objective is to buy American consent for the normalization of the war. By creating American commercial interests in Russia, Moscow hopes to make it politically costly for Washington to maintain sanctions.

## III. The 28-point plan: leasing the Donbass

## Origin
The plan emerged from three days of negotiations in Miami at the end of October 2025 between Steve Witkoff, Trump’s peace envoy, and Kirill Dmitriev. Jared Kushner was also present.
The plan was leaked to the Telegraph on November 20, 2025.

## Key provisions
PointDetailDonbassUkraine leases the Donbass to Russia. Moscow maintains de facto control; Kyiv retains legal ownership. A rental fee is paidReferendumThe lease circumvents Ukraine’s constitutional requirement for a public referendum on ceding landMilitaryUkraine’s armed forces cut in halfMissilesUkraine surrenders long-range missilesNATOUkraine commits to not joiningForeign troopsBanned on Ukrainian soilLanguageRussian becomes an official state language in occupied territoriesChurchRussian Orthodox Church granted official statusU.S. aidMilitary assistance ends

## Reactions
Dmitriev told reporters he was optimistic: “We feel the Russian position is really being heard.” He added that Moscow’s battlefield gains had strengthened Russia’s negotiating position.
Zelensky has repeatedly ruled out surrendering the entire Donbass.
Lt Gen Keith Kellogg, Trump’s special envoy to Ukraine, resigned shortly after the plan emerged. A close associate said Kellogg believed Trump administration officials were being manipulated by Russia.
European allies were “alarmed” and said they had been largely kept in the dark.

## IV. The resource prize: what’s actually at stake

## The Yuzivska gas field
The Yuzivska field, located in the Donetsk and Kharkiv regions, is one of the largest shale gas deposits in Europe.
DataDetailArea7,886 km²Estimated reserves1.2 to 4 trillion cubic meters of gasContractsShell (2012, ~$10 billion), Chevron (2012)StatusShell left the project in 2015 due to the conflict

## Other Donbass resources

Denis Pushilin, the leader of the DPR, has stated that the main reserves of lithium and titanium are located in the “liberated” territories and that extraction has not yet begun because demining is required.

## Russia’s rare earth strategy
Russia has an ambitious plan to boost its rare earth production:
TargetDetailProduction 203050,000 tons of rare earth products (7x increase)Import dependenceReduced from 75% to 45%Global shareFrom 1.3% today to 10% by 2030Investment400 billion rubles ($5.13 billion)Key regionsMurmansk, Irkutsk, Sakha (Yakutia)
The Donbass is central to this strategy. Ukraine’s Foreign Intelligence Service has revealed that Russia plans a large-scale geological exploration program in occupied Donetsk from 2026 to 2031.

## V. The Anchorage summit: Trump’s offer to Putin

## What was on the table
Before the Trump-Putin summit in Anchorage on August 15, 2025, the Telegraph reported that Trump was preparing to offer Putin:

- Access to rare earth minerals in Alaska for Russian companies

- Suspension of sanctions on the Russian aviation industry

- Access to rare earth minerals in Russian-occupied Ukrainian territories
Trump publicly stated: “I’d like to buy minerals on Russian land too, if we can... They have very good rare earths, also oil and gas. It’s a great thing.”
Putin responded that Moscow is ready to cooperate with Washington on rare earth development, including in the Donetsk and Luhansk People’s Republics.

## The cooling
At the G7 summit in June 2026, Trump threatened to abandon the “Anchorage understandings,” expressing frustration with Putin. Lavrov accused the United States of having “prolonged the war by a year” by withdrawing from the understandings.

## VI. Analysis: who wins and who loses

## The United States
Advantages:

- Access to critical resources (rare earths, lithium, titanium)

- Economic leverage over Russia

- Potential “reimbursement” for aid to Ukraine
Disadvantages:

- Most resources are in Russian-controlled territory

- The Ukraine deal is on paper only

- The Dmitriev Package is a trap (investing in the restoration of the Russian economy)

## Russia
Advantages:

- Control of Donbass resources

- Negotiating leverage over Washington

- Opportunity to normalize the aggression through economic incentives
Disadvantages:

- Sanctions still in place

- Dependence on Western technology for extraction

- Risk of internal destabilization

## Ukraine
Disadvantages:

- Signed a resources deal it cannot control

- Risk of being sidelined in U.S.-Russia negotiations

- The lease plan does not guarantee long-term sovereignty
Advantages:

- Retains legal ownership of subsoil

- Receives reconstruction investment

## Europe
Disadvantages:

- Excluded from resource negotiations

- Lost access to cheap Russian gas

- Paying for Ukraine’s reconstruction

- Risks being locked out of the rare earth scramble

## VII. Conclusion: the deal that was never real
The U.S.-Ukraine minerals deal was signed for resources Ukraine does not control. The Dmitriev Package offers Washington access to resources that Russia physically holds. And the 28-point plan proposes a legal fiction — a “lease” — to bypass Ukraine’s constitution and formalize Russian control.
Trump negotiated with Zelensky in April 2025. He negotiated with Putin in August 2025. Now his envoys are negotiating with Dmitriev in Miami. The pattern is clear: Washington is dealing with whoever physically controls the resources.
Ukraine risks being marginalized in a negotiation about its own territory. Europe — once again — pays the bill without a seat at the table.
Emmanuel Todd said it in March 2025: “Europe is afraid of peace.” Because peace would force European elites to confront the problems they have ignored for decades.
The 2026 elections have already written 2030. And the resource scramble is only beginning.

reads.title: THE ELECTION TRAP
reads.subtitle: Zelensky says elections are impossible. Washington says they are necessary. And the only real obstacle may be the man himself. Marco | Independent Analyst *16 September 2026*
reads.body:
## Introduction: the interview that changed nothing — and everything
On September 16, 2026, Volodymyr Zelensky sat down with CBS News. The question was simple: when will Ukraine hold elections?
His answer was a list. Nine million Ukrainians abroad. Occupied territories where Russian soldiers patrol. Polling stations that cannot be secured. A constitution that forbids it all.
Every point he made was technically accurate. And every point he made also kept him in power.
This article examines the legal, political, and strategic dimensions of Ukraine’s election dilemma. It is not a defense of Zelensky, nor of his critics. It is an analysis of a trap — one that the Ukrainian president has helped construct, and from which he now cannot easily escape.

## I. What Zelensky actually said
The interview, conducted with CBS News and released on September 16, covered the full range of obstacles.

## The scale of the diaspora

> “Around 9 million Ukrainians are currently abroad. Before the full-scale invasion, around 500,000 Ukrainians abroad voted in elections. Organizing voting for the current number of citizens abroad will pose a separate challenge.”
Nine million people. Eighteen times the pre-war diaspora vote. No country has ever organized an election under those conditions.

## The occupied territories

> “How will people in the occupied territories vote? Who will control their vote? There are Russian soldiers there. How do you do all these things?”
This is a real problem — but it is also a permanent one. As long as Russia controls the Donbass, Zaporizhzhia, and Kherson, any Ukrainian election will be incomplete by definition.

## The ceasefire condition
Zelensky added a new element: elections could be held if a ceasefire lasts “for several months.” This period, he said, could be used “not only to prepare for the vote but also to continue working toward ending the war.”
This is a shift. Previously, he had ruled out elections until the war ended. Now he is proposing a window — but only if the fighting stops first.

## II. The constitutional wall: the only argument that holds
Of all Zelensky’s reasons, only one is legally binding.
Ukraine’s constitution and its martial law legislation prohibit all elections — presidential, parliamentary, and local — while martial law is in effect. Article 19 of the Law on the Legal Regime of Martial Law explicitly bans national elections.
Martial law was declared on February 24, 2022, and has been extended every 90 days since. Zelensky’s five-year presidential term officially expired on May 20, 2024. He remains in office solely because martial law extends the mandate of all elected bodies until it is lifted and a new vote can be organized.
This is not a political excuse. It is a constitutional fact. And Washington knows it.

## III. The pressure from Washington: why Trump wants elections
The pressure on Zelensky is not coming from Moscow. It is coming from Washington.

## The timeline of pressure
DateEventDecember 2025Trump tells Politico that Zelensky is “using the war” to avoid elections. “They talk about a democracy, but it gets to a point where it’s not a democracy anymore,” he saysFebruary 2026Washington sets Kyiv a deadline: hold presidential elections in MayMarch 2026Ukraine formally rules out holding presidential elections this yearSeptember 2026Trump brands Zelensky a “dictator without elections” on Truth Social

## Why does Trump want elections?
The answer is structural, not personal. A leader whose mandate expired in 2024 is a legal liability for any agreement Washington wants to sign.
The 28-point peace plan negotiated between Steve Witkoff and Kirill Dmitriev includes provisions on the post-war political process. Elections are part of the package — not because Zelensky wants them, but because his patrons need a Ukrainian counterpart who can ratify a deal.
The lease plan for the Donbass, the minerals agreement, the frozen assets — none of it can be formalized without a legitimate Ukrainian government.

## IV. The Donbass question: the territories are not coming back
Zelensky’s point about the occupied territories is technically correct. But it also obscures a harder truth: Moscow has written them into its constitution.
In September 2022, Russia held referendums in Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia, and Kherson and formally annexed them. Putin then amended Article 65 of the Russian constitution to include them as federal subjects.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has stated explicitly: “The territories that have become subjects of the Federation and are enshrined in the Constitution of our country are an integral part of Russia; this is an absolutely indisputable and inarguable fact.”
For Moscow, this is not a negotiating position. It is domestic law. No Russian leader can return these territories without tearing up the founding document of the current state.
The territories are not “lost” in a legal sense — Ukraine and the international community do not recognize the annexation. But they are lost in a practical sense. And any peace deal will have to confront that reality.

## V. The 28-point plan: the lease that solves nothing
The plan that emerged from Miami — three days of negotiations between Steve Witkoff and Kirill Dmitriev — proposes a legal fiction: Ukraine leases the Donbass to Russia.
Under the terms:

- Moscow maintains de facto control of the territory

- Ukraine retains legal ownership

- Russia pays an undisclosed rental fee

- The arrangement is designed to circumvent Ukraine’s constitutional requirement for a public referendum on ceding land
The logic is elegant. The lease avoids the referendum. The referendum would be lost. So the lease preserves the form of sovereignty while conceding the substance.
But the lease also implicitly recognizes that the Donbass belongs to Ukraine — a direct contradiction of Russia’s own constitution, which annexed the region in 2022.
The plan has raised alarm among European allies, who say they have been largely kept in the dark. Shortly after details emerged, Lt Gen Keith Kellogg, Trump’s special envoy to Ukraine, resigned. A close associate said Kellogg believed Trump administration officials were being manipulated by Russia.

## VI. The resource dimension: what’s actually at stake
The Donbass is not just a territorial dispute. It is one of the most resource-rich regions in Europe.

## The mineral wealth
ResourceEstimated quantityLithium33 million tons of ore, worth $38 billionTitanium7% of global production; Ukraine is among the top 10 countries for proven reservesIron ore27 billion tonsCoalOver 100 billion tonsRare earthsBeryllium, cerium, yttrium, lanthanum, neodymium
Forbes Ukraine has estimated Ukraine’s total mineral resources at $14.8 trillion — but more than 70% is in Donetsk and Luhansk, regions partly or fully controlled by Russia.
Denis Pushilin, the leader of the DPR, has stated that the main reserves of lithium and titanium are located in the “liberated” territories and that extraction has not yet begun because demining is required.

## The U.S.-Ukraine minerals deal
In April 2025, the United States and Ukraine signed the “Reconstruction Investment Fund” agreement. It gave Washington privileged access to Ukraine’s mineral wealth. Trump had originally sought $500 billion in mineral wealth — around four times what the United States had contributed to Ukraine since the war.
But there was one problem: the deal was signed for resources Ukraine does not control.

## VII. The trap: why Zelensky cannot win
Zelensky’s dilemma is structural.

## If he holds elections

- He risks losing. His polling has collapsed.

- The occupied territories cannot vote. The election will be incomplete.

- The diaspora cannot be organized in time. Nine million people. Eighteen times the pre-war scale.

- Security cannot be guaranteed. Russia can strike any polling station at any time.

## If he refuses

- He confirms the Russian narrative that he is an illegitimate leader propped up by the West.

- He defies Washington, which is pressing for elections as a precondition for any deal.

- He becomes the obstacle — not the war, but the man.

## The only path he has left
Zelensky’s CBS interview was an attempt to square the circle. He offered a condition — a months-long ceasefire — that he knows is unlikely to materialize. He listed obstacles that he knows cannot be overcome. And he positioned himself as willing to hold elections, while making them impossible to hold.
It is a careful strategy. But it is also a visible one.

## VIII. Conclusion: the question Washington is asking
The election debate is not really about democracy. It is about legitimacy — and who can sign a deal.
Trump needs a Ukrainian government that can ratify the lease, the minerals agreement, and the post-war settlement. Zelensky’s mandate expired in 2024. His authority rests on martial law. And martial law is extended every 90 days — by a parliament that he controls, in a country where elections cannot be held.
The legal argument is sound. The political argument is weaker.
Every week Zelensky delays, the pressure grows. Every excuse he offers is real — but every excuse also keeps him in power. And when Washington starts asking whether the obstacle is the war or the man, the answer is usually already the man.
Zelensky is not wrong about the constitution. He is not wrong about the diaspora. He is not wrong about the occupied territories. But he is also not wrong about what happens if he holds elections — and loses.
The trap is not of his making alone. But he is the one caught in it.

reads.title: THE GAS LIE
reads.subtitle: Brussels Rewrote the History of Europe's Energy Crisis — While Moscow Kept the Gas Flowing to the Continent That Armed Its Enemy Marco | Independent Analyst *16 September 2026*
reads.body:
## Introduction: the sentence that inverted cause and effect
On September 16, 2026, Ursula von der Leyen stood before the European Parliament in Strasbourg to deliver her annual State of the Union address. The speech was framed as a defense of European resilience — a continent that had faced down Russian aggression, diversified its energy sources, and emerged stronger. The Commission President offered a single sentence to summarize the energy chapter of her mandate:

> “When Russia cut off gas supplies, the response was swift, and today the sources of supply are more diversified.”
It is a sentence that reads as a triumph. It is also a sentence that inverts cause and effect, rewrites the historical record, and places the blame for a self-inflicted crisis on the shoulders of the adversary.
And it omits the one fact that changes everything: Russia never cut off the gas. While Europe was sending billions in weapons to Kyiv — weapons that killed Russian soldiers — Moscow kept the pipelines open. For years. Until Brussels itself legislated the ban — and then blamed Moscow for the cutoff.
This article examines what actually happened to Europe’s energy supply — the regulations, the data, the industrial consequences, and the moral dimension that official narratives refuse to acknowledge.

## I. The regulation that proves her wrong
The most important document in this debate is not a speech. It is a piece of legislation: Regulation (EU) 2026/261 of the European Parliament and of the Council, adopted on January 26, 2026, and published in the Official Journal on February 2, 2026.
The regulation’s title is unambiguous: “on phasing out Russian natural gas imports and preparing the phase-out of Russian oil imports, improving monitoring of potential energy dependencies.” The prohibition to import Russian pipeline gas entered into application on March 18, 2026. Short-term contracts concluded before June 17, 2025 were permitted to continue temporarily until April 25, 2026, for LNG and until June 17, 2026, for pipeline gas.
The European Union did not react to a Russian cutoff. The European Union legislated one.
This is not a semantic distinction. It is the central factual core of the debate. When von der Leyen says “when Russia cut off gas supplies,” she is describing an event that did not occur in the way she frames it. The EU imposed a phased ban on Russian gas imports. The ban was a choice — a political decision taken by the Council and the Parliament, defended publicly by the Commission, and signed into law with full knowledge of its economic consequences.

## II. The context nobody mentions — and it changes everything

## Russia kept the gas flowing while Europe armed its enemy
Here is the fact that the Commission’s narrative cannot accommodate: from February 2022 until the EU’s own ban took effect, Russia continued to supply gas to Europe.
This was not a technical oversight. It was a deliberate decision by Moscow — one that defies the logic of war. Russia was engaged in a military conflict with Ukraine, a country that Europe was arming, funding, and supporting with intelligence and targeting data. Those weapons — artillery, HIMARS, Storm Shadow, ATACMS, F-16s — killed Russian soldiers. They destroyed Russian equipment. They struck Russian territory.
And yet, throughout this period, Gazprom continued to honor its contracts with European buyers. The gas kept flowing through the pipelines that remained operational. The heating stayed on in German homes. The factories kept running in Italy, Austria, and Hungary.
By any standard of state interest, Russia would have been justified in cutting off the gas in 2022. A country at war does not normally continue supplying the economy of the coalition arming its enemy. It is not required by international law to do so. It is not required by any principle of strategic rationality.
But Russia did not cut off the gas. It kept supplying Europe — even as Europe armed the army fighting against it. Until the EU itself decided to stop buying — and then rewrote the story to make Moscow the author of the decision.

## The ruble payment dispute
The one exception proves the rule. In April 2022, Gazprom suspended deliveries to Poland and Bulgaria after both countries refused to comply with a new payment mechanism requiring settlement in rubles. The EU rejected this mechanism — correctly, from a legal standpoint — but the suspensions were targeted and reactive, not a blanket embargo.
The distinction matters. A blanket cutoff would have been a strategic weapon. The suspension of supplies to two countries that refused a payment mechanism was a contractual dispute. To describe the latter as “Russia cut off gas supplies” — in a speech delivered in September 2026, after the EU had legislated a comprehensive ban — is to conflate two entirely different things.

## Zakharova’s challenge
Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova addressed this directly on July 2, 2026:

> “Ursula is an excellent liar. Russia has never cut off gas for Europe. Any EU citizen can sue her for this lie and win.”
She added that Europeans “created problems for themselves after they had imposed illegal sanctions against Russia.”
Zakharova’s rhetoric is characteristically caustic, and her framing is self-serving. But the core factual claim — that Russia did not unilaterally cut off all gas to Europe — is supported by the record. The blanket cessation of Russian gas imports to Europe was a European decision. And it was made while Russia was still supplying the continent that was arming its enemy.

## III. The data: what the transition actually looks like
Von der Leyen’s second claim — that “the sources of supply are more diversified” — is true in a narrow sense. But the data reveals what “diversification” has actually meant.

## The shift from pipeline to LNG
According to the European Commission’s quarterly gas report, EU gas consumption in 2025 reached 339 billion cubic meters — a modest 2% increase over 2024, but still below 2022 levels. Total gas imports reached approximately 288 bcm.
The structure of those imports, however, has been radically transformed:
Source2021 share (pipeline)2025 share (total imports)Russia~40% (pipeline)12.5% (pipeline + LNG)Norway~22%30%United StatesNegligible26%North Africa~12%12.7%Qatar~5%~4%
Pipeline imports fell 8% year-on-year to 158 bcm, while LNG imports rose 29% to 131 bcm and now account for 45% of total gas imports.
The United States became the dominant LNG supplier, with its share of EU LNG imports rising from 45% in 2024 to 58% in 2025. Russia’s share of LNG, by contrast, fell from 20% to 13%.

## The new dependency
This is the first layer of the paradox: Europe has not eliminated its dependency on external gas suppliers. It has redirected it — from Russian pipelines to American, Qatari, and Norwegian LNG. And in doing so, it has traded a geographically proximate supplier for a geopolitically distant one, with different pricing dynamics and different strategic risks.
EU officials have themselves warned about this. The United States supplied nearly 58% of the EU’s LNG imports in 2025 — a fourfold increase over 2021. Analysts have warned that this share could rise to 80% by 2030 if current trends continue.
The irony is difficult to miss: Europe has replaced dependency on Russian gas with dependency on American gas — and it is paying a premium for the privilege.

## IV. The price of “diversification”
The cost of this transition is not theoretical. It is measured in dollars per megawatt-hour, in factory closures, and in jobs lost.

## The price gap
According to the International Energy Agency, the cost of European industrial electricity averaged $92 per megawatt-hour** in mid-2026, while the United States — benefiting from shale gas and a pivot to “energy dominance” — averaged **$38 per MWh. European industry is paying a 140% premium for its electricity.
The gap in gas prices is even more extreme. European natural gas at €49/MWh translates to roughly $15-16 per MMBtu — meaning European industrial users are paying more than five times what their American counterparts pay for the same molecule. Some analyses put the gap even higher, at eight times the US price for gas.
The European Court of Auditors has confirmed the structural nature of this disadvantage. In its 2026 Energy Monitoring Report, ACER — the EU’s energy regulatory agency — found that “EU industrial electricity prices in early 2025 were approximately 1.5 times higher than in the U.S., while gas prices remained three times more expensive“.

## The deindustrialization
These price gaps have real-world consequences. They are not abstract numbers. They are the difference between a factory operating and a factory closing.
Steel: EU crude steel production fell 2.9% in 2025 to 125.8 million tonnes — the lowest level on record, nearly 60 million tonnes below pre-2008 crisis levels. The European Steel Association (EUROFER) notes that the industry has lost 30,000 jobs and 30 million tonnes of capacity over the past five years.
Chemicals: Europe’s chemical industry — once the backbone of the continent’s industrial base — is in structural decline. BASF, the world’s largest chemical company, has cut approximately 7,000 jobs worldwide since January 2024, with two-thirds of those losses in Germany. Its flagship Ludwigshafen plant has seen its workforce fall to the lowest level since 1954.
Dow Chemical announced the elimination of 4,500 jobs globally in 2026, including 605 in the Netherlands across its Terneuzen, Delfzijl, and Dordrecht sites, and 110 in Stade, Germany. The company is shutting down three European chemical plants, with production cessation beginning in mid-2026.
The aggregate numbers are equally stark. According to the European Commission’s own estimates, 1.3 million manufacturing jobs are currently at risk in Europe, with 210,000 manufacturing jobs lost net in 2025 alone. The Commission has warned that “about half” of the jobs in energy-intensive industries — some 1.3 million out of 2.6 million — could vanish.
European Commission Vice-President Roxana Mînzatu has acknowledged that “hundreds of thousands of jobs are under threat from high energy prices, first and foremost in foundation industries such as steel, non-ferrous metals, chemicals, ceramics and glass”.

## The demand destruction
One of the most revealing data points is rarely mentioned in official speeches: European gas consumption did not fall because Europe became more efficient. It fell because industry stopped consuming.
In 2021, the EU consumed 412 bcm of gas. In 2025, it consumed 339 bcm — a reduction of 73 bcm, or roughly 18%. The Commission’s own figures show that this decline was driven largely by demand destruction in the industrial sector — factories closing, production relocating, and energy-intensive industries shutting down.
The European Union is not decarbonizing its industry. It is deindustrializing it. And the official narrative presents this as a success.

## V. The framing: a masterclass in narrative construction
Why does von der Leyen’s sentence matter?
Because it is not an isolated error. It is the central framing of the Commission’s entire energy narrative — a framing that serves three political functions:

## 1. Shifting responsibility
By framing the energy crisis as a Russian action (”when Russia cut off gas supplies”), von der Leyen transforms the EU from the author of the policy into the victim of circumstances. The sanctions, the phase-out regulation, the decision to forego cheap Russian gas — all of these disappear from the narrative. What remains is a story of European resilience in the face of external aggression.

## 2. Justifying the cost
If the crisis was caused by Russia, then the economic pain is an inevitable cost of resistance — a price worth paying for sovereignty. If the crisis was caused by EU policy, then the pain is a consequence of political choices — choices that could have been made differently. The framing determines whether voters see themselves as victims of Russian aggression or as subjects of European policy.

## 3. Protecting the institutional project
The European Commission’s legitimacy depends on its ability to deliver prosperity. If the energy crisis is framed as a Russian attack, the Commission is a defender. If it is framed as a policy failure, the Commission is the problem. The narrative protects the institution.

## The alternative narrative
The alternative account — supported by the regulation, the data, and the statements of EU officials themselves — is straightforward:

- The EU chose to phase out Russian gas — a political decision codified in Regulation 2026/261.

- That decision removed 155 bcm of annual pipeline supply from the European market — roughly 40% of the pre-war total.

- That supply was replaced primarily by more expensive LNG, predominantly from the United States, at prices 2.5 to 8 times higher than domestic US gas.

- The result was a structural increase in European energy costs, which rendered much of European industry uncompetitive against American and Chinese competitors.

- The consequence is deindustrialization — factory closures, mass layoffs, and the relocation of production to regions with cheaper energy.
This is not a Russian narrative. It is the official record of the European Union’s own institutions, read without the rhetorical filter.

## VI. The moral dimension: who betrayed whom?
There is a dimension to this story that transcends economics and enters the realm of political morality.
For three years, Russia supplied gas to Europe while Europe supplied weapons to Ukraine.
Those weapons killed Russian soldiers. They destroyed Russian tanks. They struck Russian territory — including, according to Russian reports, targets inside the Russian Federation itself. And throughout that period, Russian gas continued to flow into European homes and factories.
By any rational standard of state interest, Russia would have been justified in cutting off the gas in 2022. The fact that it did not is not a sign of weakness. It is a sign of restraint — or, at minimum, of a calculation that maintaining commercial ties might preserve a channel of communication.
Europe did not reciprocate. It armed Ukraine. It sanctioned Russia. It froze Russian assets. It imposed a price cap on Russian oil. And then, in January 2026, it passed a regulation banning the import of Russian gas altogether — and blamed Moscow for a cutoff that Brussels itself had legislated.
The question is not whether von der Leyen’s statement is technically false. It is. The question is whether a political leadership that rewrites the causal record to obscure its own choices can still claim democratic legitimacy.
The answer, increasingly, is no.

## VII. The response: the Commission’s silence
When asked about the discrepancy between von der Leyen’s statement and the regulation, the Commission has offered a consistent response: the President was referring to Russian supply cuts in 2022, not to the EU’s legislative phase-out.
This defense is technically plausible — Russia did suspend supplies to Poland and Bulgaria, and did significantly reduce flows through Nord Stream before the pipelines were sabotaged. But it ignores the regulatory timeline that followed.
The sequence of events is clear:

- 2022: Russia suspends supplies to Poland and Bulgaria; Nord Stream flows reduced; pipelines sabotaged.

- 2023-2025: EU develops and negotiates the phase-out regulation.

- January 2026: EU adopts Regulation 2026/261 — a binding ban on Russian gas imports.

- March 2026: Prohibition enters into application.

- September 2026: Von der Leyen says “Russia cut off gas supplies.”
By the time von der Leyen delivered her speech, the legal framework for the cessation of Russian gas imports was European law, not a Russian action. To say “Russia cut off gas supplies” in September 2026 — after Europe had legislated the phase-out — is to describe a world that no longer existed.

## VIII. The political dimension: does she think citizens are fools?
The question that inevitably arises is the one many European voters are asking: does von der Leyen believe European citizens are stupid enough to accept this?
The answer is not simple. The Commission President is not naïve. She knows the regulation exists. She knows the data. She knows that European industry is dying and that voters are paying the price.
The calculation is not that citizens are foolish. The calculation is that the narrative will hold long enough to survive the political moment. The State of the Union address is not a history lecture. It is a political communication exercise. Its purpose is to frame the Commission’s record in the most favorable light possible, to a public that is increasingly skeptical and increasingly angry.
And there is evidence that the calculation is failing.
The French political scientist Emmanuel Todd has observed that Europe has developed a pathological relationship with peace: “Europe is afraid of peace,” he said, “because peace would force European elites to confront the problems they have ignored for decades.” The energy crisis is one of those problems. The Commission’s framing is an attempt to avoid confronting it — to attribute the consequences of policy to the actions of an adversary.

## IX. Conclusion: the bill comes due
Von der Leyen’s sentence — “when Russia cut off gas supplies” — is not a lie in the narrowest sense. Russia did reduce and suspend supplies to certain countries. But it is a deliberate distortion of the causal sequence that led to Europe’s energy crisis.
The record is clear:

- The EU legislated the phase-out of Russian gas.

- The EU chose to replace cheap pipeline gas with expensive LNG.

- The EU accepted the consequences for its industrial base.

- The EU presented the result as a triumph of resilience.

- And all of this happened while Russia kept the gas flowing to the continent that was arming its enemy.
The factories are closing. The jobs are gone. The bills are higher. And in Strasbourg, the Commission President is telling the Parliament that this was Russia’s fault.
It wasn’t. It was her policy. And the bill is paid by the European people.
The question is not whether European citizens are foolish enough to believe this.
The question is how much longer they will pretend to.
