reads.title: Ansarallah advances on Bab al-Mandab; Trump offers to pay Americans $5,000 for midterm votes; U.S. kills 3 in Caribbean boat strike
reads.subtitle: Drop Site Daily: September 10, 2026
reads.body:
- Fighters loyal to Ansarallah, shouts slogans during a rally to recruit more fighters, in Sana’a on September 10, 2026. Photo by Mohammed Huwais / AFP via Getty Images.Thursday, September 10, 2026 – Ansarallah seizes strategic Red Sea port of Mocha, advances toward Bab al-Mandab. Saudi launches more than 50 strikes across Yemen on Wednesday. Ansarallah targets three Saudi cities with ballistic missiles and drones. Pakistan says no military response to Ansarallah attacks on Saudi Arabia under discussion. Seafarer killed, another missing in attack on tanker. Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps claims attack on U.S. aircraft carrier. Report: Iranian strike damages multiple U.S. warplanes at Jordan airbase. President Donald Trump warns Iran “not to get cute,” threatens “very hard” strike on suspected nuclear site. Iran, China, and Russia reject International Atomic Energy Agency resolution. Wall Street Journal: Trump advisers privately warn Iran war could last beyond his presidency. Four Palestinians, including two children, killed in Israeli strike on Beit Lahia home. Israeli strikes hit homes across northern, central and southern Gaza on Wednesday. Israeli forces carry out raids, arrests and demolitions across occupied West Bank. Two Palestinian detainees injured during Israeli prison raid. Palestinian factions reject reconstitution process, warn of exclusion and Palestinian Authority control. Former U.S. Secretary of State Antony Blinken calls report he rejected early Hamas hostage release offer “complete fiction.” Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to sue Haaretz over report he was warned of Oct. 7 attack. Israel destroys homes, wells, and agricultural sites across southern Lebanon despite “ceasefire.” Lebanese army says Israel committed 7,700 violations of U.S.-brokered agreement. Trump administration proposes excluding undocumented immigrants, race questions from 2030 census. Trump to keep El Salvador TPS holders’ protections until “appropriate time.” Trump pledges $5,000 “Trump Dividend” to every American if Republicans keep Congress. Democratic Senator John Fetterman makes video appearance at Trump’s midterm convention. Treasury announces $6 billion bond buyback amid soaring yields, market reacts negatively. U.S. strike in Caribbean kills three. Secretary of State Marco Rubio pledges $45 million in security funding for Ecuador. Eighty-seven missing after ferry fire near Philippine tourist destination. Algeria cuts diplomatic relations with UAE over “provocative or hostile” actions. Thousands protest as Slovenia opens Israeli embassy. British man charged with assisting Russian military intelligence. Cameroon separatists kidnap five teachers, kill police officer in raid. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s flight delayed after Russian drone crashes near Moldovan airport. Russian strikes hit Kyiv petrol station and agribusiness facility in Dnipro.
This is Drop Site Daily, our free news recap We send it Monday – Friday

## Yemen

- Ansarallah seizes strategic Red Sea port of Mocha, advances toward Bab al-Mandab: Ansarallah forces seized the strategic Red Sea port city of Mocha and are advancing south toward the Bab al-Mandab Strait, Reuters reported Thursday. Witnesses separately told AFP they saw Ansarallah forces entering the city, while Saudi-backed troops reportedly withdrew. Yemen’s Saudi-backed government has not officially confirmed Mocha’s fall.

- Ansarallah forces are also nearing control of other coastal areas along the strait as they push to capture all of Yemen’s Red Sea coastline. A military source told AFP that Ansarallah had seized Zuqar Island following rocket attacks and an amphibious assault.

- Bab al-Mandab Strait is a crucial waterway and one of the world’s busiest global shipping lanes that links the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean. It was being increasingly used as the U.S. and Iran to exchange attacks in the Strait of Hormuz.

- Fighting in Yemen since last week has killed at least 500 people, mostly combatants, according to AFP. Nearly 20,000 have fled their homes, according to the International Organization for Migration.

- Saudi launches more than 50 strikes across Yemen on Wednesday: Saudi warplanes carried out 54 airstrikes across six Yemeni governorates within 12 hours on Wednesday, according to Ansarallah military spokesperson Yahya Saree.

- North: Saada, Ansarallah’s main stronghold, and Al-Jawf, both bordering Saudi Arabia.

- Center and east: Marib, an oil and gas region east of Sana’a, and Al-Bayda, a strategic crossroads in central Yemen.

- West and southwest: Hodeidah, Yemen’s main Red Sea port region, and Taiz, a major front between Sana’a and the Gulf of Aden.

- Saree warned the attacks “will not go unpunished.” Saudi Arabia has not confirmed the strikes.

- Ansarallah targets three Saudi cities with ballistic missiles and drones: Saudi-led coalition spokesperson Turki Al-Maliki said Ansarallah forces launched ballistic missiles and drones toward the Saudi cities of Khamis Mushait, Abha, and Jazan on Wednesday, accusing the group of targeting civilians and infrastructure, the Saudi Press Agency reported.

- Saudi Civil Defense separately issued an alert Thursday in Khamis Mushait warning of a potential threat, the fourth such warning within 24 hours, before later announcing that the threat had passed.

- Pakistan says no military response to Ansarallah attacks on Saudi Arabia under discussion: Pakistan said Thursday that it is not currently discussing a military response under the Mecca joint defense agreement following Ansarallah attacks on Saudi Arabia, Reuters reported.

- “There is no such thing under discussion right now,” Foreign Ministry spokesperson Sajjad Haider Khan said. “When time comes, [we] will act under the agreement.”

- The agreement, signed last month by Pakistan, Turkey and Saudi Arabia, stipulates that an armed attack on any one of the three countries will be considered an attack on all. Khan also said there were no plans to expand the alliance.

## Iran

- Seafarer killed, another missing in attack on tanker: One seafarer was killed and another is missing after an incident Wednesday aboard the Gibraltar-flagged oil-products tanker Hercules Star while it was anchored off Dubai, the vessel’s charterer told Reuters.

- Maritime security sources said the tanker may have been struck by a drone, but the weapon has not been confirmed. UKMTO separately reported a ship in the area listing and possibly taking on water after being hit by an unknown projectile. (link)

- Iran’s IRGC claims attack on U.S. aircraft carrier: Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said it targeted a U.S. aircraft carrier roughly 500 kilometers (~310 miles) away on Wednesday, according to Mehr News.

- The U.S. has not confirmed that a carrier was hit and previously said Iranian missile attacks caused no damage or casualties.

- Report: Iranian strike damages multiple U.S. warplanes at Jordan airbase: Multiple U.S. military aircraft were damaged in an Iranian strike on Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Al Azraq, Jordan, early Wednesday, CBS News reported.

- Around eight F-15 fighter jets sustained light damage and were returned to service, while an A-10 Thunderbolt was hit and lost a wing. U.S. forces reportedly fired more than 30 Patriot missiles to intercept incoming Iranian projectiles.

- The strike was part of Iranian retaliation after the U.S. attacked five Iranian oil tankers on Tuesday.

- Trump warns Iran “not to get cute,” threatens “very hard” strike on suspected nuclear site: President Donald Trump threatened further attacks on Iran over alleged renewed activity at Pickaxe Mountain, a suspected nuclear site near the heavily damaged Natanz uranium enrichment facility.

- “We notice there’s a little activity at Pickaxe. I would advise Iran not to get cute because we will have to hit them very hard,” Trump said Wednesday.

- Trump also predicted the U.S.-Iran war would continue until after November’s midterm elections, claiming, “the war will end immediately after the election because they can’t hold out any longer.”

- He argued that short-term economic pain for Americans was worth preventing Iran from developing nuclear weapons. No intelligence assessment has concluded that Iran was close to developing a nuclear weapon.

- Iran, China, and Russia reject IAEA resolution: Iran, China, and Russia jointly rejected a draft resolution introduced by the U.S., Britain, France, and Germany at the IAEA Board of Governors, the U.N. nuclear watchdog’s policymaking body, calling for Iran’s nuclear file to be referred to the U.N. Security Council.

- The three governments said the draft “fails even to make explicit reference to the attacks,” which they described as “the root cause and principal factor underlying the current situation.” They said continuing U.S. attacks have made normal IAEA inspections and safeguards work in Iran effectively impossible.

- The statement noted that Iran nevertheless agreed to provide the agency access to the Bushehr nuclear power plant in mid-September, but said further cooperation requires guarantees that attacks on Iranian nuclear facilities will not recur.

- China, Iran, and Russia also called the IAEA’s June 2025 finding of Iranian noncompliance “politically motivated and far-fetched,” arguing that it paved the way for attacks on safeguarded nuclear facilities.

- Iran’s representative to international organizations in Vienna, Reza Najafi, said the IAEA had never verified any diversion of Iranian nuclear material and accused the resolution’s sponsors of “rewarding the aggressor and punishing the victim.”

- WSJ: Trump advisers privately warn Iran war could last beyond his presidency: Top White House advisers privately warned Trump that the war with Iran could continue beyond his term in January 2029, despite his public predictions of a swift victory, the Wall Street Journal reported, citing U.S. officials.

- Vice President JD Vance, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, and others have discussed the possibility that Tehran could withstand the U.S. naval blockade and other military pressure for years. Trump, however, said Wednesday that the war would end “immediately” after November’s midterm elections because Iran “can’t hold out any longer.”

- Vance publicly declined last week to provide an “artificial timeline,” saying, “It would be irresponsible for us to write out our strategy and our timeline.”

- The Pentagon is meanwhile preparing for a prolonged U.S. presence, with some deployments extended into 2027 and air-defense units potentially remaining without a firm end date.

## Palestine

- Killed and wounded in Gaza: Over the past 24 hours, one Palestinian was killed and 30 injured in attacks across Gaza, according to the Palestinian Ministry of Health.

- The total recorded death toll since October 7, 2023 has risen to 73,670 killed, with 174,682 injured. Since October 11, the first full day of the so-called ceasefire, Israel has killed at least 1,359 Palestinians in Gaza and wounded 4,571, while 831 bodies have been recovered from under the rubble.

- Four Palestinians, including two children, killed in Israeli strike on Beit Lahia home: Four Palestinians from the same family were killed, including two children aged 8 and 12, and several others wounded on Thursday when Israeli forces struck a home in the Beit Lahia area of northern Gaza, WAFA reported. The four bodies were taken to al-Shifa Hospital in Gaza City, while others were reported missing under the rubble.

- Earlier, several Palestinians were wounded after Israeli military vehicles and a drone opened fire toward displacement tents in Jabalia refugee camp.

- Israeli strikes hit homes across northern, central and southern Gaza on Wednesday: An Israeli strike hit a house belonging to the Al-Masri family in Al-Shati refugee camp, west of Gaza City, after the family was ordered to evacuate.

- “They called and ordered us to evacuate. But we’re not resistance fighters or anything. We’re civilians. We have children,” Mahmoud Al-Masri, 37, told Drop Site’s Mohamed Ahmed.

- Ibrahim Al-Shaarawi, 45, whose home was also destroyed, said around 10 families had been living there. “Who told you that the war had stopped? … Every day there’s bombing. Every day there are strikes,” Al-Shaarawi said.

- In central Gaza, a house in Nuseirat refugee camp was struck after an Israeli displacement order, wounding several Palestinians. An order was also issued for another house in western Khan Younis, south of Gaza, before it was struck.

- Watch the dispatch from Mohamed Ahmed here.

- Israeli forces carry out raids, arrests and demolitions across occupied West Bank: Israeli forces carried out raids across the occupied West Bank on Thursday, as Palestinian prisoners’ groups said more than 100 Palestinians, including children, women, former prisoners and journalists, had been detained across the territory over the past week.

- Tulkarm: Israeli forces raided Eco Park, north of Tulkarm, and seized several wild animals from the park on Thursday, WAFA reported. They also detained a park employee.

- Bethlehem: Israeli forces demolished a 170-square-meter home in Battir, west of Bethlehem. Elsewhere in the governorate, Israeli forces detained seven Palestinians, including journalists Sabri Jibril and Muath Amarna, during raids in Tuqu, Dheisheh refugee camp and several areas of Bethlehem.

- Nablus: Two Palestinians were hospitalized after Israeli forces beat them during a raid on Awarta, south of Nablus, on Wednesday evening. Israeli forces also fired live ammunition, tear gas and stun grenades during the raid.

- Two Palestinian detainees injured during Israeli prison raid: Two Palestinian prisoners were injured after Israeli Prison Service units raided several sections of Ganot Prison, according to the Palestinian Commission of Detainees’ Affairs. The commission said the units used stun grenades and rubber-coated bullets during the raid.

- Around 9,400 Palestinian Palestinians are currently held in Israeli prisons, with 3,244 held under administrative detention without charge or trial.

- Palestinian factions reject reconstitution process, warn of exclusion and PA control: Hamas, Palestinian Islamic Jihad, the PFLP, Fatah’s Democratic Reform Current, the PFLP-GC, the Palestinian National Initiative, and the Popular Resistance Committees rejected and expressed “deep concern” over the procedures being used by the Palestinian Authority to reconstitute the Palestinian National Council (PNC), warning that the practices “contradict the principles of national partnership and democracy.”

- The PNC is the PLO’s legislature, intended to represent Palestinians in Palestine and abroad. The factions said members are being appointed through assemblies in several Arab countries that do not represent Palestinians as a whole.

- They condemned “appointment instead of election, exclusion instead of partnership, and unilateralism instead of national consensus.” They accused a powerful faction within the Palestinian Authority of engineering the council to control its decisions, disenfranchise Palestinians abroad, and exclude resistance factions, opposition forces, and independent figures.

- The signatories demanded the process be replaced by national dialogue and a unified election law providing free and transparent voting and proportional representation.

- One year after Doha assassination attempt, Hamas’s Basem Naim tells Drop Site that Israel has not changed course: One year after Israel tried to assassinate Hamas’s negotiating delegation in Doha, senior Hamas official Bassem Naim shared a statement with Drop Site reflecting on the attack.

- Before the attack, Naim said Hamas received a proposal from Trump through Qatari mediators and was given 48 hours to respond. The delegation was meeting to discuss it when Israel attempted to assassinate its members “in the heart of the capital of a mediating state allied with the United States.”

- Naim said the U.S. was “beyond any doubt, complicit in the crime,” and that the failed assassination attempt and the international outrage that followed pushed Washington toward the Sharm el-Sheikh agreement.

- Naim stated that Hamas has adhered to all of the agreement provisions, while Israel continues “the crime of genocide and the project of forced displacement, albeit in a less brutal form” since the agreement. He also criticized the “Board of Peace” for allowing Israel to “continue spreading death, destruction, and hunger everywhere.”

- “There can be no successful wager on breaking the Palestinian will, nor on exhausting the patience of our people,” Naim said. He added that killing individual Palestinian leaders “will not alter the course toward freedom and independence.”

- Blinken calls report he rejected early Hamas hostage release offer “complete fiction”: Former U.S. Secretary of State Antony Blinken denied a Haaretz report that he urged Qatar to wait after it offered to mediate the release of civilian hostages held by Hamas on October 7, 2023.

- Drop Site co-founder Ryan Grim summarized the report as saying Hamas had conveyed through Qatar that it was prepared to return civilian hostages and that Israel refused to engage, after which Qatar approached Blinken. Grim wrote that Blinken “had the opportunity to free every single civilian hostage and de-escalate the situation. Instead he wanted war.”

- Blinken quote-posted Grim’s tweet Wednesday, writing: “For the record, this is false. Complete fiction.”

- Netanyahu to sue Haaretz over report he was warned of Oct. 7 attack: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Wednesday he will sue Haaretz and reporters Shlomi Eldar and Ruth Yaval over a report claiming UAE President Mohammed bin Zayed warned him of a Hamas attack 10 days before October 7, 2023, calling the report “fabricated” and “politically motivated.”

- The Haaretz report claimed then-Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar relayed warnings through an intermediary that he was preparing a “huge surprise” and told contacts “to expect an earthquake.” Bin Zayed’s aides then reportedly passed this to Israel’s Shin Bet, which dismissed the threat, before bin Zayed personally raised it with Netanyahu, who also brushed it aside.

- Netanyahu denied that the phone call with bin Zayed occurred, saying a review of his call log “found no trace of it whatsoever,” and separately accused Palestinian political figure Muhammad Dahlan, who lives in the UAE, of being behind the report.

## Lebanon

- Israel destroys homes, wells, and agricultural sites across southern Lebanon despite “ceasefire”:

- Nabatieh: Israeli warplanes carried out a two-wave strike on Nabatieh Al-Fawqa on Thursday, Lebanon’s National News Agency (NNA) reported. In Mais al-Jabal, Israeli forces carried out a large explosion in the Al-Dabsh area, west of the town, destroying a waste-sorting facility as well as homes and industrial and agricultural structures. A separate Israeli strike on the Marj Harouf–Zebdine road wounded two people on Wednesday, according to Lebanon’s Health Ministry.

- Tyre (Sour): Israeli forces continued demolishing homes and infrastructure in Mansouri, where more than 10 large explosions were reported since midnight, alongside airstrikes and artillery fire. Israeli drones dropped barrels packed with high explosives onto the roofs of homes before detonating them remotely, according to NNA. Israeli forces also blew up artesian wells in the town.

- Lebanese army says Israel committed 7,700 violations of U.S.-brokered agreement: The Lebanese army said Wednesday Israel has committed approximately 7,700 violations of the framework agreement, including opening fire near army personnel and patrols, while escalating strikes and demolitions across southern Lebanon.

- The army said it had fulfilled its obligations by establishing operational control in designated areas and seizing 1,818 weapons and munitions.

## U.S. News

- Primary results:

- Rhode Island State Representative David Morales, a democratic socialist, beat incumbent Providence Mayor Brett Smiley in Tuesday’s Democratic primary. It’s a major win for Reclaim RI, which has spent years working to reshape the state’s politics. Morales campaigned on capping rent hikes, expanding affordable housing, and raising taxes on polluters and corporate landlords, and drew support from Sen. Bernie Sanders and former Mayor Jorge Elorza. Smiley, seeking a second term after winning in 2022, attacked Morales over past support for “defunding the police”—a characterization Morales rejected, saying Smiley was “clinging on to quotes and tweets from over five years ago” and stating he would “not defund the police, a position that I have been very consistent on.” Morales is expected to win in November’s general election in the heavily Democratic city.

- Former CVS executive Helena Foulkes easily defeated incumbent Gov. Dan McKee in Rhode Island’s Democratic gubernatorial primary. McKee, who has served as governor since 2021, faced intense scrutiny over his administration’s handling of the 2023 closure and rebuilding of the Washington Bridge between Providence and East Providence. Foulkes, who lost to McKee in the 2022 primary, is now the favorite heading into November’s general election.

- Trump administration proposes excluding undocumented immigrants, race questions from 2030 census: The Census Bureau proposed a sweeping overhaul of the 2030 census Wednesday that would exclude undocumented immigrants and some legally present immigrants lacking permanent resident status from population counts used to apportion House seats, while also prohibiting race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation questions on the count.

- Census results determine congressional apportionment, redistricting, federal funding, and enforcement of civil rights laws like the Voting Rights Act.

- The proposal would redefine “usual residence” to argue undocumented immigrants lack “a sufficient tie and allegiance” to the country, marking an expanded version of a similar effort Trump’s first administration pursued for the 2020 census, one abandoned by the Biden administration after it was challenged legally.

- Trump administration keeps El Salvador TPS holders’ protections until “appropriate time”: The Trump administration said tens of thousands of Salvadoran immigrants will keep their Temporary Protected Status for now, despite the protections having been scheduled to expire Wednesday, according to a statement from the Department of Homeland Security.

-  DHS said “an announcement on El Salvador’s TPS will be made at the appropriate time” and that Salvadoran TPS holders “retain protection” until then, without specifying when a final decision would come.

- The National TPS Alliance advocacy group estimates about 170,000 Salvadoran TPS holders live in the U.S.

- Trump pledges $5,000 “Trump Dividend” to every American if Republicans keep Congress: President Donald Trump pledged Wednesday at the GOP’s midterm convention in Dallas to send every American adult $5,000 if Republicans retain control of the House and Senate, calling it “the Trump Dividend” and comparing it to corporate shareholder distributions, citing the U.S.’s “tremendous strength and success economically.”

- The promise would likely cost more than $1 trillion and require congressional approval.

- Vice President JD Vance appeared to partially walk back the proposal within the hour, suggesting the wealthy wouldn’t receive payments and that it could be funded by tariff revenue, though such revenue falls far short of the pledged sum.

- Fetterman makes video appearance at Trump’s midterm convention: Sen. John Fetterman (D-Penn.) appeared in a video Wednesday at the opening night of President Trump’s midterm convention in Dallas, describing himself as a “common-sense Democrat” who rejects “the extremes in socialism” and introducing Republican Sen. David McCormick, with whom he pledged to “work together... and defend the steel way of life.”

- The appearance came amid speculation about a possible party switch, which Fetterman has repeatedly denied, telling the Times in July he would “never” leave the Democratic Party, though he recently announced an unusual joint fundraising committee with McCormick.

- The pro-Israel stalwart has noted, however, that a change in Democratic party policy towards against would be a “red line” for him.

- About 69% of likely Democratic voters in Pennsylvania view Fetterman negatively, according to an August Times/Philadelphia Inquirer/Siena poll.

- Treasury announces $6 billion bond buyback amid soaring yields, market reacts negatively: The Treasury Department said Wednesday it will buy back up to $6 billion of government debt in an effort to reduce the costs of borrowing.

- The Department’s repurchases reduce the available supply of longer-dated bonds, increasing their price and lowering their yields, which would then theoretically reduce interest rates across the board.

- The market’s immediate reaction to the buyback was negative, however, with the 10-year yield rising 0.05 percentage points on Thursday afternoon, a 3-year-high, and the 20-year yield rising by a similar amount.
📥 Have a tip on Capitol Hill?  Email DC Correspondent Julian Andreone at Julian@dropsitenews.com

## Other International News

- U.S. strike in Caribbean kills three: U.S. Southern Command announced on Wednesday that its “Joint Task Force Western Hemisphere” had struck a vessel it claimed belonged to narco-traffickers, killing three in the Caribbean.

- Wednesday’s strike is the 69th acknowledged strike in the Pacific by U.S. forces, part of a campaign that has killed at least 230 people who the Trump administration has alleged were trafficking drugs in the region, though several of these incidents have involved civilians.

- Rubio pledges $45 million in security funding for Ecuador: Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced during a visit to Quito on Wednesday that the U.S. would seek $45 million in additional security funding and new equipment for Ecuador, including a 110-foot Coast Guard cutter and five interceptor vessels.

- Rubio also designated the Ecuador-based gang Los Tiguerones a foreign terrorist organization, following similar designations for two other Ecuadorian gangs last year, and announced sanctions on seven former Ecuadorian officials accused of bribery.

- He also claimed that the U.S. campaign against suspected drug trafficking boats has shifted to joint strikes with Ecuador, insisting that the strikes were not aimed at killing fishermen.

- Drop Site’s Camila Lourdes Galarza reported on these strikes on fishermen in April. Her full report is available here.

- Eighty-seven missing after ferry fire near Philippine tourist destination: At least five people have been killed and 87 remain missing after a fire broke out Wednesday evening aboard the ferry M/V June Aster. about 2.2 kilometers offshore of the Philippine’s Palawan province, according to the Philippine coastguard. The coastguard said 42 people had been rescued so far out of the 134 passengers and crew listed on the ship’s manifest.

- Algeria cuts diplomatic relations with UAE over “provocative or hostile” actions: Algeria announced Thursday it would be cutting diplomatic relations with the United Arab Emirates, saying the country had “exhausted all means of preserving bilateral relations” after a series of “provocative or hostile” actions by Abu Dhabi despite “repeated warnings,” according to the country’s foreign ministry.

- The ministry claimed it had summoned the Emirati ambassador and gave him 48 hours to comply with the decision, though the UAE has not immediately responded.

- The rupture follows years of strained ties over the UAE’s normalization with Israel under the 2020 Abraham Accords, and the two countries’ opposing positions on the Western Sahara disput

reads.title: “All I Want Is for the War to End”: Displacement Behind the Front Lines in Yemen
reads.subtitle: Residents of Taiz are grappling with a war that has fully reignited and now arrived, once again, at their doors.
reads.body:
Drop Site’s journalism is free to read because thousands of readers choose to fund it. If our work matters to you, please consider making a tax-deductible donation today.
SUPPORT DROP SITE - DONATE TODAY

-
- Building makeshift shelters in Jabal Zaid displaced persons camp, Wednesday, September 9, 2026. Photo: Khalid Al-Banna.TAIZ, Yemen*—This week, as Ansarallah forces advanced by the hour to seize the port city of Mokha and secure access to the strategic Bab al-Mandab strait off the coast of Yemen, residents of Taiz braced for more fighting.
Over the past week, some of the fiercest battles between Ansarallah (also known as the Houthis) and Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces took place in the hills surrounding Taiz—a crucial trade hub in southwestern Yemen, situated between Ibb, Mokha, Hodeidah, and Aden.
On Wednesday, Saudi Arabia bombed five Yemeni governorates more than 50 times in a single 12-hour span. On Sunday, powerful explosions shook Taiz and several residential areas were shelled. The Yemeni government attributed the explosions to Ansarallah. Ansarallah neither claimed the bombings nor denied them, but the fighting proved decisive ahead of Ansarallah’s capture of Mokha later in the week.
Thousands of households from across the Taiz governorate have been displaced since September 3, when a new round of intensified fighting began. Across Yemen, nearly 20,000 have fled their homes, according to the International Organization for Migration. Over the past week, at least 500 have been killed, according to the AFP, most of them combatants. Among the dead and wounded are civilians, including numerous children.
Drop Site is always free to read. Subscribe today:
Many of the displaced are from Jabal Habashi, a district in the Taiz governorate characterized by greenery, agriculture, and terraced hills. Jabal Habashi has seen the majority of the violence in the area—and its families have experienced among the highest rates of displacement. Because of its strategic position, wedged between Taiz and Mokha, it is a crucial passageway for securing Yemen’s west coast.
Yet, as Ansarallah has been increasingly taking hold of the districts surrounding the provincial capital, which is thus far still under the control of the Saudi-backed Yemeni government, has attempted to retain a sense of normalcy: Its markets are bustling and people walk the streets, despite the presence of military convoys bringing in injured fighters to its hospitals.
“When I heard the explosions I remembered the difficult days of the beginning of the war in 2015,” said Taiz city resident Mohammed Abdulmalik, “and felt with the suffering of the population who witness it nowadays in west Taiz.”

## Civilian Targeting
Drop Site News visited several hospitals in the city of Taiz, including Al Thawra and Al Safwah, speaking with local patients hospitalized with injuries incurred in the ongoing fighting. The aisles of these hospitals were overflowing with patients; the majority of them were injured fighters, although the hospital is treating civilians as well. Ashraf, a 47-year-old construction worker from the Jabal Habashi district, was injured while attempting to flee his village on Saturday with his family, a day after heavy fighting with shelling broke out around him. (Ashraf is a pseudonym used for his safety.)
“We were moving in small separate groups to reduce the risk of being targeted, and an explosion went off. I lost consciousness and fainted, and was later evacuated to Taiz.”
Ashraf woke up in a hospital surrounded by other wounded civilians, including children. Still sitting in a hospital bed, he told Drop Site, “It is always us civilians who suffer the brunt of this war.”
At a private hospital also in Taiz, four injured children were in hospital beds, staying in the same room: three boys and one girl, who was the eldest. The girl and two of the boys were siblings, while the fourth boy was their neighbor.
The children’s guardian, their uncle, told Drop Site he had brought them from the Jabal Habashi district to Taiz city after their home was shelled.
“On Friday, we all stayed home because the fighting was fierce,” he told us. “But by the afternoon, things had calmed down, and the children went out to play in front of the house as usual. Then we heard an explosion nearby and the screams of other children. We ran out and found the four of them on the floor, bleeding.” He was uncertain whether Ansarallah or the Saudi-backed government forces had caused the explosion, as both had been firing at each other.
The uncle said they normally could not afford hospital costs, but an international NGO operating locally funded their stay at the private facility.“I just hope they recover and can return home. Their parents are stuck in the village, as leaving is too dangerous right now. So I am taking care of them for the time being.”

## Families Torn Apart
The Jabal Zaid camp for Internally Displaced People (IDP), nestled between the green valleys of Taiz governorate, is one of several camps that have absorbed at least 5,600 households displaced across the Taiz and Hodeidah governorates in the past week, according to the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA). Residents here live in makeshift tents built from scant, hard-to-source materials.
Rahma, a displaced woman at Jabal Zaid who asked to go only by her first name, told Drop Site News that her family—who was already displaced by fighting a decade ago and living in a different IDP camp—had not only been displaced again, but divided. “When fighting broke out near our [first] camp on Friday, we took our children and fled the area,” she said. “Later that same day, my husband returned to bring our belongings. We waited for him until the next day, but he didn’t come back. We were terrified he might have been killed or injured.”
Rahma later learned from neighbors that he was stuck in the middle of the fighting and no one was allowed to leave the area. Five days later, Rahma’s husband was still trapped in the middle of the fighting.

-
- Nujud Mohammed and her children at Jabal Zaid camp on Wednesday, September 9, 2026. Photo: Khalid Al-Banna.Nujud Mohammed, 28, a mother of six also displaced at Jabal Zaid, described a similar rupture. She is originally from Al Barah, a site that has seen heavy clashes due to its position on the supply route connecting Taiz and Mokha, and has been increasingly targeted by Yemeni government forces and allied warplanes attempting to repel Ansarallah’s advance.
“I tried to return to retrieve our belongings,” she said, “but the road was blocked. We weren’t allowed to reach our old camp to take anything. Our area is now encircled by fighting, and no one can enter or leave. So I returned with nothing. I praise Allah that we are safe, and I trust that He will compensate us for everything we lost.”
For many at Jabal Zaid, the past week is not a first displacement but a second, or third. Nujud’s family fled to Jabal Habashi nine years ago, at the start of Yemen’s civil war, and had lived there ever since.
“Nine years ago we fled because of the fighting in our area. We spent nine years in Jabal Habashi, but on Friday, sudden fighting reached our camp. I immediately took my children and walked from the afternoon until sunset, when we finally found a car that brought us to this camp.”
Surrounded by her children, the youngest of whom is still a toddler, she cooked flatbread over a fire using plastic basins and a makeshift fire. “It isn’t easy to start over in a new camp, but we have been forced to do so because we have no alternative.”

## Camp Without Aid
Nujud and her children now share a single tent with three other families, relying on the goodwill of their new neighbors for food, mattresses, and other basic goods. “No humanitarian organizations have arrived yet,” she said. “Only two representatives from a relief agency came to take our names and ask questions, but no aid has been delivered. We are in dire need of shelter and food.”
Looking at the temporary tent housing her, she said: “All I want at this moment is for the war to end so I can return.”

-
- Mohammed Ahmed and his family in Jabal Zaid camp, Wednesday, September 9, 2026. Photo: Khalid al-Banna.
-
- Mohammed Ahmed and his family in Jabal Zaid camp, Wednesday, September 9, 2026. Photo: Khalid al-Banna.Mohammed Ahmed, 35, a father in the camp, said his family had expected help to be awaiting them once they reached safety: “We assumed that as soon as we reached a safe area, we would receive support from humanitarian organizations, since we know they cannot reach dangerous frontlines,” where their home is. Indeed, many families chose Jabal Zaid precisely because it is considered a safe area, yet no agency has provided aid there so far.
“If this situation continues, our children could starve to death, as there are no job opportunities here and no one to help us.”
Fawzi Al-Habashi, Director of the Better Life Association for Coexistence and Development, a local humanitarian organization that provides food, shelter, and hygiene assistance, said NGOs “have monitored and documented the displacement movement, conducted initial needs assessments, and coordinated with local authorities, providing limited emergency aid to the most vulnerable families based on priority.”
However, as explained by Baraa Shaiban, a Yemeni political analyst who spoke to Drop Site, the suddenness of the displacement, combined with severe funding shortages that have characterized many areas of Yemen (particularly areas controlled by Ansarallah where international aid access has been restricted for years), has hindered the delivery of emergency assistance.
The Saudi-led war against Ansarallah that began in 2015 after the group took over Sana’a spawned one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises and left over 150,000 dead until an uneasy truce was reached in 2022. Many Yemeni civilians are experiencing the clashes as a return to heightened instability, as they see their lives starting over once again, in yet another displacement camp.
As Shaiban put it: “Whatever normality people were hoping to get, it is quickly fading away.”
* A journalist in Yemen contributed reporting.

reads.title: Why We’re Losing the Iran War
reads.subtitle: The US is fighting a 21st Century war with a 20th Century military
reads.body:
I’m a visual thinker, so I just put this “active vs. passive defense” info-meme together. No A.I. was used. The images are from the internet, the text is mine.
We’re fighting this war on the other side of the planet, and our personnel and extremely expensive and difficult to replace assets are sitting exposed above ground. Iran is fighting on its home turf, using its geography to great advantage.
Iran is six times bigger than Colorado, with significantly higher mountains (up to 18,000 feet). Tunneling into solid granite is something Iranian engineers mastered decades ago. Locating and striking a tunnel entrance with a multi-million-dollar standoff weapon does little to nothing to stop Iran from launching their ballistic missiles. These “missile cities” are built like gopher towns, with many entrances. Earthmoving equipment is on standby to clear temporarily blocked entrances, while the others remain operational.

-
- Our 20th Century Navy and Air Force are confronting 21st Century warfighting realities, and they are not prepared. Our current force structure was perfect for [A] enriching the MIC and their political backers and [B] beating the snot out of banana republics as a demonstration of our power projection ability. But now Iran is backing us down, and they are spending only a tiny fraction of the US military budget.

-
-
-
- Note that our 20th Century air force flies at one-tenth the speed of Iran’s hypersonic missiles, and our combat jets carry crews, while Iran’s missiles are obviously unmanned. In today’s “casualty-averse” American political environment, this means our aircraft can only approach the borders of Iran to launch our diminishing supply of costly standoff weapons, lest our planes be shot down over Iranian territory.
This stands in sharp contrast to previous wars, such as Vietnam, Afghanistan or Iraq, where our bombers roamed hostile skies at will, unafraid of ground fire.

-
- And we face a similar problem at sea, as the recent Iranian “test” of a steerable anti-ship ballistic missile that overflew the CVN George Washington demonstrates. Ballistic missiles that can be guided in flight and during their terminal dive in order to strike a moving ship threaten to render our navy obsolete.
This will be a paradigm change on the order of battleships being sunk by land-based bombers during World War Two. Specifically, the sinking of the British battleships the Prince of Wales and the Repulse, on December 10th of 1941. They were attacked and sunk by land-based Japanese “Betty” bombers after departing Singapore.

-
- But just imagine what a porcupine America could become, on a tenth our current military budget, if we quit playing  the global hegemon and sole superpower, even as our economy enters its terminal phase and the global American empire fades away.

Iran has popped the bubble of the facade of American military supremacy, for a tiny fraction of the cost that we’ve squandered on our recurring “forever wars,” which impoverish ordinary Americans even while they further enrich the Epstein Class.

-
- We've already been driven out of the Persian Gulf, and our top military brass are admitting in public that we will probably never return to rebuild our wrecked bases. And Iran has flatly declared that no US warships will ever sail through the Strait of Hormuz again. That is, for Iran, an absolute and unalterable redline. The billion-dollar long-range radars and massive satellite uplink dishes that Iran destroyed with $30,000 Shahed drones cannot be flown in on C-17s, and Iran will not allow foreign ships full of war materiel to enter the Persian Gulf.

-
- Meanwhile, our delusional president posts his own fantasies, which are totally detached from reality. Now, our warships must be resupplied from distant Diego Garcia, instead of from Bahrain, a clear loss. Destroyers must go off the blockade line for a week at a time to sail to Diego Garcia to reload with missiles.

-
- How many of these US bases will be manned and operational when the war is finally over? On September 8th Iran fired barrages of missiles at Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan. There have been significant casualties reported. Will we keep our planes there? Or will they all be moved further back to Israel, or even to Cyprus?

-
- Is this what winning looks like, being pushed backward, far away from the country that we sneak-attacked on February 28?
Operation Epic Fury, AKA Operation Epstein Fiasco, clearly marks the end of an era. I just hope we learn the lessons before Iran gets lucky with a "ship killer" guided ballistic missile. And as far as the defense of American interests in the Western Pacific, well, we can just take that off the table, the way we took the CVN George Washington away from Japan to replace the worn-out Lincoln and its crew.
If America cannot subdue 2nd-tier Iran, (even while expending most of our extremely expensive and difficult to replace interceptors and standoff weapons), we can forget about facing China in a sea and air battle to defend Taiwan, Japan or South Korea. Or for that matter even Guam, the most important America military base located in the “Second Island Chain,” 3,000 kilometers from mainland China.

-

reads.title: Britain finally acts against Israel’s illegal settlements – because people forced it to
reads.subtitle: This isn’t enough. But it’s something to build on
reads.body:
- As British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband announced new sanctions targeting Israel’s illegal settlements, I thought back to exactly a year ago.
Back then, I was in the West Bank – Palestinian land that is illegally occupied by Israel.
I had travelled on a delegation organised by the Christian Palestinian charity Sabeel-Kairos, and if I’m honest, I was surprised Israel let me in after keeping me for interrogation at the Jordanian border.
A couple of days later, they sent me an email revoking my visa, which answered that one.
Help us take on the pro-war, pro-genocide, pro-injustice mainstream media by becoming a subscriber.
In the village of Beit Ijza, I met Sa’adat Gharib and his family. By the time I visited, their home had been completely boxed in by the neighbouring Israeli settlement. Sa’adat told us the surrounding land had belonged to his family. Around the house stood a 26-foot-high metal fence. They lived under the constant gaze of settlers and surveillance cameras.
To get in or out, the family had to pass through an electronic gate controlled by Israeli forces.
Sa’adat told us that the family had been arrested, intimidated and physically attacked. That included attacks on the children. Sometimes, he said, settlers would deliberately walk around the fence naked when his kids were outside.
I went to Hebron and walked down what was once its main commercial street. Much of it has been shuttered, and Palestinians are barred from walking on sections of the street – while Israeli settlers can move freely.
Share

-
- This is apartheid.
One evening, a young Palestinian man I’d met in London took us to a hipster bar in Ramallah. He lived on the outskirts of Jerusalem, where we were staying. But while I could walk freely around Jerusalem, he had only entered the city once in his entire life – as a small child. He couldn’t remember it.
Here is a land where some 770,000 illegal Israeli settlers now live. Palestinian life is being gradually asphyxiated. Palestinians live under military occupation and are routinely detained and incarcerated under a military legal system, including children. Jewish Israeli settlers living alongside them are subject to Israeli civil law.
They endure the routine humiliations of the longest belligerent occupation of our time. Travelling around the West Bank is made nightmarish by Israeli checkpoints. Land is routinely seized. Palestinians are being violently driven from their homes.
In the northern West Bank, Israeli forces have emptied the Jenin, Tulkarm and Nur Shams refugee camps of their residents. More than 33,000 Palestinians were displaced, according to the UN, while huge areas of the camps were demolished or damaged and residents were prevented from returning.
With the support of the Israeli state, settlers are waging a campaign of terror.
Subscribe now
Since 7 October 2023, more than 1,100 Palestinians have been killed by Israeli forces or settlers in the West Bank, including more than 240 children.
This is what I thought about when Miliband announced the sanctions.
At first, I was extremely cynical. I remember talking to Palestinians in the West Bank about the UK’s recognition of a Palestinian state last year. They were entirely dismissive.
They said it was for domestic political consumption, and made no difference to them. If it had been done three decades earlier, they said, then maybe it would amount to something. But the Israeli state was destroying any possibility of a Palestinian state – and the West was doing nothing meaningful about it.

-
- The “two-state solution” has just been a crutch for politicians. When they receive any scrutiny about Israel’s crimes – which is rare – they simply point to their meaningless abstract support for a “two-state solution”.
Subscribe now
Britain’s sanctions are certainly not even close to being enough. Israel is a state committing genocide in Gaza. UN investigators have also found it responsible for war crimes and crimes against humanity. That’s without even mentioning the heinous crimes committed in Lebanon, the illegal occupation of Syrian land, or the disastrous attacks Israel and the US have launched against Iran.
It is a reasonable question to ask why Britain is still conducting any trade with illegal settlements. The direct economic impact of the import ban will be negligible: it will represent only a tiny fraction of the roughly £6 billion in annual trade between Britain and Israel.
But even so, this is a victory won because of those who have ceaselessly campaigned – and because voters, including those who switched to the Green Party, punished Labour at the ballot box.
Those electoral shocks helped bring down Keir Starmer and usher Andy Burnham into Downing Street. Burnham now faces pressure to shore up Labour’s left flank – and that includes taking action on Israel. Recent polling shows support for banning trade with illegal Israeli settlements massively outstripping opposition.
This isn’t enough – but it represents concessions that can be built on.
It doesn’t just mean a ban on imports from illegal settlements. It opens the way to sanctions against companies and individuals whose money or services help settlements expand. That potentially puts Israeli banks and financial companies in scope.
Britain has now officially declared that Israel’s continued occupation of Palestinian land is unlawful, in line with the 2024 ruling of the International Court of Justice. That is – alas! – a new development, and provides a legal basis to push for more action.
Arms export restrictions have been tightened – although the existing carve-out for components supplied through the global F-35 programme remains.
The government is using very careful language, declaring that “there is increasing evidence that war crimes appear to have been committed”. Miliband, the prime minister and the rest of the government obviously know that war crimes have been committed on an industrial scale. A definitive finding, however, would impose certain legal obligations on the government.
Subscribe now
But Miliband explicitly backed legal processes to determine responsibility for war crimes, and said Britain supports the International Court of Justice reaching its judgment in South Africa’s genocide case.
The Global Human Rights sanctions regime is being expanded, allowing sanctions to be imposed not just on those involved in illegal settlements, but potentially on those responsible for violations of international humanitarian law in Gaza.
Miliband also declared that “settler terrorists” are committing ethnic cleansing in parts of the West Bank, and said members of the Israeli government had supported the forced displacement of Palestinians.
All of this can lay the foundations for us to build more pressure – and ensure more far-reaching action.
There were certainly other problems. Miliband denounced the Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions movement, which consciously draws on the successful boycott movement against South African apartheid.
He denounced anyone who questions Israel’s right to exist as “a homeland for the Jewish people” – as though it is somehow outrageous to support a single state (which de facto exists!) with equal rights for all between the River Jordan and the Mediterranean Sea.
That won’t age well.
But you can see from the resulting hysteria that Israel and its cheerleaders are rattled.
Outrageously, that has centred on arguing that taking even these limited measures against a foreign state’s illegal conduct endangers Jewish Brits.
This shameless conflation of Jewish people with Israel’s crimes is dangerously irresponsible.
So no, this isn’t enough.
But it does represent welcome movement – and these concessions were only won because people organised, from the streets to the polling booth.
That includes people like you.
Help us take on the pro-war, pro-genocide, pro-injustice mainstream media by becoming a subscriber.

reads.title: Israeli Strike in Lebanon Kills 12 People From a Single Family, Including 6 Children
reads.subtitle: Israel is once again escalating its bombing of southern Lebanon despite a ceasefire and ongoing U.S.-brokered talks.
reads.body:
Drop Site is a reader-funded, independent news outlet. Without your support, we can’t operate. Please consider becoming a paid subscriber or making a 501(c)(3) tax-deductible donation today.
Subscribe now

-
- A local sheikh gives a final prayer over the body of one of six children killed in a September 7, 2026 Israeli airstrike on the Farhat family home in Kfar Remman, in Nabatieh district, southern Lebanon that killed a total of 12 members of the family. September 8, 2026. Photo by Katrine Dige Houmøller.KFAR REMMAN, Lebanon—“They are killing children. That’s what they’re doing,” Baker Malak said, pointing to the tiny coffins being carried through the streets of the town of Kfar Remman in southern Lebanon on Tuesday. He walked alongside hundreds of mourners in a funeral procession to bury 12 members of a single family, half of them children, killed in an Israeli airstrike on their home a day earlier.
Nearby, mourners carried the coffin of 18-year-old paramedic Ali Shahrour, killed in a separate strike on the town the same day. The procession wound through streets scarred by months of bombardment as an Israeli drone buzzed incessantly overhead.
“When Israel sees that the Lebanese government is doing nothing, they will keep targeting children,” said Malak.
Israel bombed the three-story family home of the Farhat family on Monday morning without warning, reducing the entire building to rubble, and killing three men, three women, and six children between the ages of two months and 13 years. Two other children, both eight years old, were severely wounded in the strike.

-
- The Farhat family home in Kfar Remman, in Nabatieh district, southern Lebanon after a September 7, 2026 Israeli airstrike killed 12 members of the family. September 8, 2026. Photo by Katrine Dige Houmøller.Malak, 45, a resident of Kfar Remman, was a close friend of two brothers killed in the attack, Hassan and Hussein Farhat. Both their coffins were draped in Hezbollah flags during the funeral. Malak told Drop Site he had seen the two men 10 days before the strike. He said they were preparing their children for school after months of closures due to Israel’s bombardment. In the ruins of the family home, schoolbooks, timetables and notebooks lay scattered among the ruins. The Israeli military claimed without evidence that it struck Hezbollah operatives transporting weapons in the area. Malak told Drop Site the house was a civilian home and contained no weapons. Lebanon’s Health Ministry called it a “grave violation of international law.”
During the burial procession, a man’s voice rang out over a loudspeaker: “Stand up and say goodbye to our angels”—referring to the six children among the dead. One of the few survivors, eight-year-old Mustafa Farhat, lost his entire immediate family in the attack—his parents, siblings and grandparents. Badly wounded, he remained at Al-Najda Hospital in Nabatieh.

-
- The funeral procession for 12 members of the Farhat family killed in a September 7 2026 Israeli airstrike on their home in Kfar Remman, in Nabatieh district, southern Lebanon. September 8, 2026. Photo by Katrine Dige Houmøller.The deadly attack on the Farhat home came as part of an escalated wave of Israeli strikes across southern Lebanon that killed at least 27 people, and wounded 69 over the previous three days, according to the Health Ministry. The renewed Israeli assault forced some 20,000 people to flee Nabatieh district last week alone, according to the United Nations.
The attacks come despite a ceasefire and U.S.-brokered framework agreement signed in Washington by the governments of Israel and Lebanon on June 26. The deal requires the Lebanese Armed Forces to disarm Hezbollah before Israel withdraws from parts of the swathe of Lebanese territory it occupies. Hezbollah has rejected the deal, which has been criticized for extracting few guarantees from Israel and placing nearly all obligations on the Lebanese government. An eighth round of talks between Lebanon and Israel overseen by Washington is expected later this month.
The talks have proceeded despite nearly daily attacks by Israel on Lebanon. Between Thursday and Monday, the UN peacekeeping force in Lebanon, UNIFIL, recorded no less than 528 projectiles fired by the Israeli military. On Sunday alone, it recorded 62 Israeli violations of Lebanese airspace—among the highest daily totals since June. UNIFIL also detected Israeli airstrikes inside its area of operations and north of the Litani River. And for the first time since June 21, it also detected a Hezbollah projectile on Sunday, with the group beginning to reengage in retaliatory attacks.
Asked on Tuesday whether the escalation was being driven by one side, UN spokesperson Stéphane Dujarric pointed to UNIFIL’s observations and said: “Everyone can draw their own conclusions pretty clearly.”
Malak said the continuing strikes have only deepened the conviction among many in the south that the framework agreement has failed to protect civilians. “The resistance is the only solution,” he said, referring to Hezbollah. He stressed that people in Nabatieh opposed the Israeli occupation of Lebanese territory in a variety of ways: with weapons, words, or by refusing to leave their land.
Malak remained in heavily bombarded Kfar Remman throughout the war, distributing aid and food, and helping to bury the dead. “I will never leave my village,” he said. “If I ever have to leave, it will be to the grave.”
Since the latest phase of the war began in Lebanon on March 2, nearly 4,400 people have been killed, including more than 250 children, and over 12,400 wounded, according to the Health Ministry. Israel has also targeted health care workers and medical facilities, killing at least 135 emergency workers and attacking 17 hospitals. On Sunday, an Israeli airstrike completely destroyed Ghandour Hospital in Nabatieh al-Fawqa, according to the ministry, which condemned the attack as another violation of the special protections afforded to medical facilities.
At the funeral in Kfar Remman on Tuesday, Karim Saleh, a 32-year-old paramedic with Al-Rissala Scouts— a Lebanese youth and civil defense organization—stood beside the grave of his friend and colleague, 18-year-old paramedic Ali Shahrour who was killed in an Israeli airstrike on his car in Kfar Remman at 1 a.m. on Monday.
Saleh, Shahrour, and two other paramedics, Hadi Farhat and Hassan Hamze, had just finished work at a small restaurant they had recently opened together and Shahrour was driving them all home. Saleh was dropped off first, but shortly after he entered his home, he heard the screech of a missile tearing through the air followed by an explosion. Saleh put on his scouts vest and raced to the scene. Shahrour, Farhat, and Hamze had been struck in the car. People managed to pull out Farhat and Hamze from the burning vehicle just before it exploded. Farhat and Hamze were wounded, but Shahrour was killed.
“Every time I close my eyes I see their faces from that moment. That’s why I’m trying to stay awake, so I don’t close my eyes,” Saleh told Drop Site, his yellow emergency worker vest stained with blood and his eyes red from tears and exhaustion.

-
- Daniel Sharhour (left) the father of paramedic Ali Shahrour, who was killed in a September 7, 2026 Israeli airstrike on his car in Kfar Remman, stands beside Ali’s friend and colleague, Karim Saleh (right). September 8, 2026. Photo by Katrine Houmøller.When Saleh visited Farhat in the intensive care unit in Al-Najda Hospital, Farhat’s first question was “Where is Ali?” He had only just been taken off the breathing tube so that he could speak. Saleh said his friend was in shock, struggling with traumatic memories of the attack. Farhat insisted on attending his friend Shahrour’s funeral Tuesday, but doctors said his condition was too serious to leave the hospital.
“I’m not going to wash their blood off this vest,” Saleh said. “It makes me feel like I’ll always have them by my side.”
Shahrour’s father, Daniel Sharhour, stood beside him. “They killed him in his own hometown. In his own car. In his own country,” Daniel Sharhour said. As he spoke, his voice grew louder, drawing people around him. “I will never forgive what happened to my son. Revenge is hanging around my neck like a necklace. I will take my revenge. I’m not afraid.”

reads.title: Chartbook 473 Germany’s democratic earthquake: the AfD breakthrough in Sachsen-Anhalt and the question of an “alternative to the Alternative”.
reads.body:
SUBTITLE: 
DATE: 2026-09-07T18:36:24.932Z
URL: https://adamtooze.substack.com/p/chartbook-473-germanys-democratic
AUDIENCE: everyone  PAYWALLED: False
CHARS: 11424  WORDCOUNT_FIELD: 1899
Germany’s democracy has suffered an earthquake.
In its regional elections at the weekend, the tiny state of Sachsen-Anhalt - population of just over 2 million souls - gave a stonking 44 percent plurality to the AfD (Alternative für Deutschland). The AfD has pulled off an astonishing transformation of the electoral map.

-
- Despite their remarkable showing, it is not obvious that the AfD will form the next government in Sachsen-Anhalt. The other parties may arrange themselves to keep the AfD out of power. At the national level, the AfD are even further from government. Nevertheless, this result shakes Germany’s political system. It shows how far the familiar political norms of the Federal Republic have disintegrated. Mecklenburg Vorpommern, another small East German state, will vote on September 20th and the outcome may well be similar. The crisis of German democracy has long been forecast. It now seems to be upon us.
The AfD comes in political different shades. In Sachsen-Anhalt it has been officially classified by the German authorities as right-wing extremist. The AfD’s candidate, Ulrich Siegmund, is a charismatic former corporate scent salesman who once tried to convince the government of Berlin that perfuming underground stations with the scent of vanilla would reduce crime. You can’t make this stuff up!
Born after end of GDR, Siegmund both evokes the memories of the Stasi and SED repression and lionizes the memory of a small German state with its own distinct identity, represented by quirky and distinctive machinery such as the Simson moped. When the (Jewish) founders of Simson protested at his instrumentalization of their family’s name, Siegmund dismissed them as unwelcome American busybodies out of touch with East German realities.
Siegmund became notorious for his attendance at a secret meeting at which members of the German right-wing discussed a program of mass “remigration”. This policy position that was once denied, has since come to be espoused by the AfD. Siegmund regards the scandal surrounding his attendance as a welcome publicity coup.
If you want to get a flavor of the right-wing milieu around the AfD in Sachsen-Anhalt, I recommend watching this video of the Simson rally. Check out the dudes in the security cordon!
Also, if you have the stomach for it, check out this casual use of the n-word at a family friendly “rally”.
The AfD are a party of racist xenophobes, to put it mildly.
As has been pointed out, Anhalt was the first German state in 1932 to elect a Nazi Prime Minister. But Sachsen-Anhalt, also has a left-wing history. That alternative is more recent. In the late 1990s, the voters of the state made the SPD the largest party and PDS, the forerunner of Die Linke, came in a strong third. The SPD formed a minority government with the Greens, benefiting from the tacit endorsement of the PDS.

-
- So what needs to be explained is not so much the deep continuity of nationalist sentiment, so much as the collapse of a potential progressive majority. To answer this question, I broadly find convincing the kind of narrative offered by East German journalist and commentator, Jana Hensel.

-
- She argues that the breakdown of trust happened in the 2000s due to the Red-Green government’s dramatic assault on the German model of welfare and labour market administration - known as the “Hartz IV reforms”. These changes, that began to be rolled out in 2003, dramatically increased pressure on welfare recipients and went hand in hand with a surge in the pre-tax gini of inequality. In political terms, Hensel argues, they shocked East Germans out of any illusion of a common, shared community of fate.
Initially, this was profoundly alienating and demotivating. The left-progressive energies of the late 1990s and early 2000s, dissipated. Sachsen-Anhalt’s previous claim to fame in electoral history dated to 2006, when it set the record for the lowest popular participation in a regional election, with a turnout of only 44.4 percent.
The AfD has changed all that. From the lows of 2006, turnout surged at the weekend to 78 percent, up from barely 60 percent in 2021. The main driver and beneficiary of this electoral mobilization is the AfD. Of its huge surge in support by far the largest part came from previous non-voters.

-
- As heroric empirical work by political scientist Julius Koelzer has shown, this mobilization is most dramatic in the rural areas of the state. Not for nothing, political economist Philip Manow speaks of the “democratization of democracy” brought about by Germany’s populist surge. It seems hard to disagree with the basic diagnosis that what we are witnessing is a highly mobilized protest vote against the German democratic establishment couched in terms of a xenophobia and an embrace of national and regional belonging. Heimat has been the rhetorical touchstone of the election. But this reassuring message is paired with a dramatic sense of crisis and the demand that something radical and new needs to be done. Unsurprisingly, right-wing commentators like Ulf Porschardt of Die Welt are declaring the end of the Berlin republic as we know it.
Even those who do not want to share this mood of Untergang, have to reckon with the dramatic vista that this regional election opens up. Faced with a protest vote, it is tempting to ask familiar questions about social disadvantage, the state of the Sachsen-Anhalt economy etc. And it is easy to find answers there for deep seated discontent.
Even by Germany’s modest standards, growth in Sachsen-Anhalt is slow. Unemployment is relatively high. Sachsen Anhalt’s economy was once a major hub of “central German”, state-backed industrialism. The original Junkers factory - home of the legendary JU52 transport and passenger plane - was in Dessau. Sachsen-Anhalt once manufactured rolling stock for the entire Communist bloc. There was a major concentration of chemicals production in the GDR. To say the least, these are not sectors that are doing well. Population is aging and declining.
Against this backdrop, the AfD, like its analogues in France and Italy and the UK, strongly appeals to those who self-identify as “workers”  - 60 percent of whom vote for the AfD - and to those who say they are having financial difficulties - 65 percent vote for the AfD. Neither of those are majority groups in the electorate, but the bias in their vote is telling. Meanwhile, only 30 percent of those with higher education vote for AfD.
But what conclusions follow from this finding? It might seem obvious to say that hard-up, working class right-wing voters should be “won back” by offering them improved welfare measures and price stability. If you ask AfD voters what they worry about, along with their xenophobic concerns about “too many foreigners”, they will mention the cost of living and their concerns for their standard of living. They also mention climate change and the threat of external war.

-
- Sources: h/t Isabella Weber
These are there worries. But if you ask them what they think about the AfD and why they voted for it, economic issues are barely mentioned. What comes first is security, foreigners, woke politics, remoteness etc.

-
- If you are hard up and working-class it would after all be nothing short of bizarre to vote for the AfD in the hope of improved social protection. There are parties in Sachsen-Anhalt offering a progressive welfarist program - notably Die Linke and arguably the SPD and the Greens as well - and the voters are not flocking to them. In choosing the AfD, voters are opting for party that in social policy terms is far to the right of either the CDU or FDP, the traditional pro-business free-market parties in Germany.

-
- Source: DIW
Voting for the AfD in the current landscape, whatever your economic issues, in short, is not a vote to have your economic issues addressed by social democracy, or welfare or government intervention. It is a vote to crackdown on foreigners, which you may imagine may help with jobs and scarce welfare resources. But above all it is a vote for someone who, like you, rejects the status quo, who demands that radical action be taken and is not afraid to break eggs to make omlettes. Insofar as you are voting for a socio-economic vision in voting for the AfD, it is one aptly thoughly clumsily characterized as „nativist producerist deservism“ (Jonas Junack). Where:

- Nativism = A political policy or worldview that promotes the interests of native-born inhabitants over those of immigrants, often driven by fears that newcomers threaten local culture, jobs, or public resources. [1, 2, 3]

- Producerism = A political ideology holding that “productive” members of society—typically working- and middle-class manual laborers, farmers, and small business owners—are exploited by both idle economic elites (like financiers) and non-producing dependents.

- Deservism = A concept centered on the moral categorization of citizens and non-citizens into those who “earn” or “deserve” support, welfare, and legal standing, versus those perceived as free-riders or outsiders. (h/t/ Gemini)
To my mind, if progressive policy hopes to engage with such voters at all - and it is open question whether it should - it must address not just the material realities of relative economic disadvantage, but above all the “outsider” credentials of the AfD.
The racism and xenophobia of the AfD are real. But they are all the more powerful because they serve as a kind of commitment device. People who act and speak in public as right-wing extremists and are labeled as such, establish a claim to authenticity. They establish an identity beyond the “Berlin Republic” mainstream and invite voters to join them. The AfD has worked assiduously to foster and build that community. In the East German states it is now approaching majoritarian status.
To believe that the answer to such a political project can lie reinforcing, reforming and improving the mainstream through improved socio-economic policies is, to say the least, a bold hypothesis. The more obvious conclusion is that to contest the political terrain with the AfD, if that is indeed something we want to do, we need to offer not more of the same (just better), but an “alternative to the Alternative”, an “alternative to the Alternative”, furthermore, that can produce something more than just material benefits. That can produce identity.
When my colleague at Surplus magazine Isabella Weber calls for an “anti-fascist economics, or when Marcel Fratzscher of the DIW calls for a major reform program that is “even more far-reaching” than that 25 years ago with Agenda 2010, they are speaking to the need for bold and radical action. Both have specific economic policies in mind - measures of price control (Weber), a whole raft of ‘reforms” in Fratzscher’s case. But after Sachsen-Anhalt, the central question must be: are such policies enough to found new political identities beyond the current mainstream of Berlin politics? Or is that a mode of politics, which we prefer to leave to the AfD?
I love putting out Chartbook. I am particularly pleased that it goes out for free to thousands of subscribers around the world. But, writing this newsletter takes a lot of work. If you are enjoying it and would like to support the project, sign up for one of the subscription options here. It is the equivalent of a fancy cup of coffee per month!
Subscribe now
